The exercise of the federal jurisdiction is acknowledged to be necessary to the validity of the Manitoba legislation. The Manitoba legislation is, therefore, not final. It is not complete in itself. We are told that the contracts cannot be carried into effect without federal legislation. If, then, the Dominion parliament is to be asked to exercise its undoubted jurisdiction it must examine the contracts on their merits, and it must examine into the resources of the province of Manitoba, on which these heavy liabilities are to form a mortgage, and the whole question must be threshed out at Ottawa, just as it is now being threshed out in this province.
The House will see tbe difference between that opinion and the opinion expressed by the Minister of the Interior this afternoon.
Manitoba has eleven representatives in the legislature at Ottawa, and the territory which is and proposed to be traversed by the Canadian Northern system is represented by twenty-four members. If we add to those the members of the government, who must determine that this is a matter for its deepest consideration, we have of those directly interested in this matter a representation at Ottawa of fully as many as the membership in the Manitoba legislature. There are at Ottawa fully forty members who will take an active and leading interest in determining the merits of this question, and in addition they will be assisted by the advice and counsel of first-rate lawyers, men like Mr. R. L. Borden, the leader of the opposition. Within the government there are several of the ablest lawyers in Canada, men like Mr. Blair, Sir Louis Davies, Mr. Fitzpatrick and Mr. Mills. Manitoba's representative in the cabinet, Mr. Sifton, is a keen lawyer, who is fully competent to analyse the contracts, and who is familiar with railway contracts, having had to do with them in his public capacity on more than one occasion.
The Minister of the Interior did analyse the contract this afternoon to some extent, and he did not hesitate to tell the House that he regarded them as improvident contracts which if he were a member of the legislature he would certainly oppose.
It has been borne in on the minds of the people of Manitoba with great force that while the companies have had superior legal advice and ability at their disposal, the government of Manitoba have been absolutely without any, and in such case the result can hardly be in doubt. If a layman entered a court of law and pitted himself against, an experienced legal counsel, we fancy that he would feel like a fool before he got through with the experiment.

We were told .in the other article that it rested equally on the members of the government and the Dominion parliament.
-and particularly on such members of it as are members of the executive. They are the persons to be dealt with by the electors, who believe a bad bargain has been made.
On the 14th of March last, according to this organ of the government, the responsibility would rest equally on this parliament and on this government; and we were told that patriotically members would stand up and fight .this Bill ; but to-day we are told that the responsibility is to rest entirely upon the legislature of Manitoba. Certainly, the two positions are not very consistent.
On the question of the responsibility of the government, let me read an extract from Sir John Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure and Practice, at page 807 :
Although it is not usual for a minister of the Crown to take charge of a private Bill, it is the special duty of the government, as the responsible leaders of legislation and the chosen guardians of the public interests in parliament, to watch carefully the progress of private legislation in the House and its committees, and see that it does not in any way interfere with the policy of the ministry or the statutory law in reference to the public lands, railways, canals, public works, and such other interests as are entrusted to the Dominion authorities. It is in the standing committees of the House that the supervision of private Bill legislation is chiefly exercised. One of the most important committees of the Commons, that of Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines, has invariably for its chairman one of the ministers of the Crown, and the minister in charge of railways is also one of its members, whose special duty it is to watch closely all legislation that may affect the policy of the government.
So that you will see that the government cannot possibly evade responsibility on this question, because the consensus of opinion with regard to this Bill is that while it is a private Bill, it will be far-reaching in its effects, and that no more important measure has been considered by this House since confederation. We are not sure that this Bill is infra vires. I entertain the opinion very strongly-and this is shared by a great many other members of the House-that this Bill should be referred to the law officers of the Crown in order to ascertain their opinion as to whether it is constitutional or not.
In what respect do you suggest that it is ultra vires ?

The hon. member attended the meeting of the Railway Committee and heard the legal discussion there presented by Mr. Nesbitt and other able legal gentlemen, who certainly suggested that there was grave doubt as to the constitutionality of the Bill.
And took strong grounds that it is unconstitutional.

I must apologize for interrupting the hon. gentleman if that was the case, because I have no recollection of any objection. It may have been stated in general terms, but I have no recollection of any reason being given why the Bill was considered ultra vires.
Mr. Nesbitt argued for half an hour that it was unconstitutional.

The hon. member for Kingston may have inadvertently missed the point, but the hon. member for North Norfolk agrees with me, and I am sure other members will, that grave doubts were cast upon the constitutionality of the Bill by legal gentlemen. That being the case, I think that even yet it would be wise to refer the Bill to the law officers of the Crown and get a short statement upon it. Let me read also from Todd's Parliamentary Government in England, volume 2, page 389, on this same point:
So also, if the interests of the people were likely to be injuriously affected by a private Bill, or if an attempt were made to establish an unsound principle by such means, ministers would be justified in using their influence to oppose it; whilst, on the other hand, ministers would be justified in promoting the passing of a private Bill if it should appear to be desirable for the public interest.
Now, ministers do not contend for an instant that this Bill is desirable for the public interest. In fact, the only authoritative statements which we have had have been from the Minister of Railways and Canals and the Minister of the Interior. One tells us that the Bill is liable to give rise to a grave clash between the Dominion and the province ; the other says he entirely disapproves of it, that it is a bad deal, and he made what I think was rather a monstrous propositon this afternoon when he said that no matter how vicious a Bill the province attempts to pass, it is not for the Federal government to interfere with it-that the province should not be interfered with in any way, tot must be allowed to pass a Bill, even if it should sink the province altogether. I do not think that is a sound principle. I do not see why the British North America Act should have provided a veto power on legislation at all unless it was considered that the Dominion government should exercise a review over provincial legislation of all kinds ; and inasmuch as we have practically a governmental declaration that this is a vicious and improvident Bill and one liable to bring evil upon the province, it seems to me that it is a subject for the review of this parliament, and one on which we ought to think very gravely before we pass the Bill. The hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) this afternoon took what appeared to me to be the very proper position when he said that inasmuch as we are asked to pass the Bill it is creative legislation, and we must pass upon the merits of the Bill, and assume responsibility for it. According to the dictum of the Minister of the Interior, where the power is, there lies the responsibility. That being the ease, responsibility must rest on this parliament and government, because, without our authority the Manitoba legislature is powerless. Let me go on reading this extract:

So also, if the interests of the public were likely to be injuriously affected by a private Bill, or if an attempt were made to establish an unsound principle by such means, ministers would be justified in using their influence to oppose it, whilst on the other hand, ministers would be justified in promoting the passage of a private Bill if it should appear to be desirable in the public interest.
Is the hon. gentleman reading from Todd ?
Yes.

That is with respect to the English parliament. There can be no such thing as a conflict between the central parliament and the provinces in England. Sir John Bourinot would be a better authority on this question.

I have read Sir John Bourinot's work also and the House must agree that he takes a strong position on the same line. We are face to face with ministers passing a Bill which they admit is not in the public interest. The only expressions of opinion we have received from the cabinet clearly indicate that the ministry itself does not believe that this is a wise measure, and yet it is going to render itself responsible for it. I would like to-night to have a positive expression from the ministers present as to whether they believe this? is a good Bill or not ? Such an expression of opinion would influence men like myself. I must say that although I am opposing this measure with all the strength I am capable of, I do not at all pretend to the infallibility which the hon. member for Guysborough charges me with believing I possess. I am exceedingly fallible and may be wrong on this occasion, and if hon. ministers would state their position, that might help men like myself to reach a satisfactory conclusion. I have, from all the study I have been able to give to the matter, come to the conclusion that it is not desirable, in the interests of Manitoba, that this Bill should be ratified; and holding that opinion sincerely, I am offering what opposition to it lies in my power. I could not do less. I have no objection whatever to other members of the House holding what views they deem fit, and I am not here to say that they are not conscientious in the views they do hold. I am not here to question the motives of any member of the legislature, which passed the Bill originally, or any member of this House; but I claim for myself the same rights and privileges as I concede to others. And believing that this measure is not in the interests of the people of Manitoba, I feel it my bounden duty to offer every legitimate opposition I can to its passage. If I did less, I would be recreant to the trust reposed in me by the people of Lisgar.

I have here the remarks made by the Minister of Railways In the Railway Committee on this measure, and while these remarks are not as ample as they should be, I think it pertinent that I should draw attention to them. The hon. minister said :
Parliament could validate any agreement between the province and any company or between two companies, and it would not be abrogating any legislative functions. The present was an exceedingly awkward question, one of greater magnitude than parliament had had before it for many a day.
Surely in view of that statement, no excuse need be offered for the time spent in *discussing this measure.
He might not feel like saying that it was an improvident bargain

No doubt, but he evidently thought It was,
-or that the people, had been carried away, in their desire to get better rates, into making a bad contract, but it was a serious undertaking to ratify the agreement.
If the Minister of Railways did not hesitate to inform the Railway Committee, which is practically a small parliament in itself, that it was a serious matter to ratify that agreement, surely members who stand up in this House and offer all possible objections to it, should not be charged with taking an unfair advantage of the rules of the House.
It might be in the interests of the Canadian Northern and the province of Manitoba to have a tariff of rates as high as possible outside the province of Manitoba in order to neutralize the liabilities of the province under the reduced rates in Manitoba, and in this it appeared to him lay the possibility of a conflict between the provincial government and the government of the Dominion in regard to the control of rates.
Here the hon. minister admits responsibility, and has taken the very stand which we who oppose this measure have been taking in this House.
The question was of sufficient magnitude to demand the most careful consideration, and he was not prepared, on behalf of the government, to express an opinion. It was an extremely important question, and the difficulties in the way could not possibly be brushed aside lightly.
He found out that if this Bill were referred back to the legislature, it might give rise to a grave clash between the government of the Dominion and the government of Manitoba. He points out very naturally that this railway company is likely to charge the highest freights outside of Manitoba on its system in Ontario and the territories. Why ? In order that it might make up for the loss incurred in consequence of the low rates in Manitoba. If that were the ease, the minister stated that that would furnish an occasion for a conflict. If the rates were lower in Manitoba than in the territories on the same system, that would be discrimination and the Federal government might very well call for equali-159
zation of the rates. They might offer a protest against any discrimination in favour of Manitoba and the rates in that province-might be raised. The Minister of the Interior characterized that statement as most absurd, as something that would never occur. Well, we find that the Minister of Railways himself practically suggested this very thing. The hon. minister said that the only control that was exercised by the Federal government upon rates was the adoption or the fixing of a maximum rate. I could not help feeling at the time that if that was the only control which the Federal government exercised over rates, it was about time we had the practice revised, especially in view of the fact that the people have contributed such an enormous sum for the construction of railways in this country. It is about time that we should exercise a more thorough control and allow companies only to fix rates that would cover working expenses and allow a reasonable interest on a reasonably fixed capitalization. I repeat that, especially in view of the aid which was given to this Rainy River Railway, $10,400 per mile, and in view of the fact that parliament took power to control the rates in granting that subsidy, these rates should also be controlled by this parliament, and should be limited to fair working expenses and earnings upon the actual capital invested. When thdt subsidy was voted by parliament two or three sessions ago, I moved, seconded by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver), that the rates of this railway should always be limited to producing 6 per cent on the capital actually invested by the company. I think had that motion been adopted the rates would have been so limited on that portion that Manitoba would not be under the necessity of giving so vast a guarantee in order to secure the supposed boom of the control of the rates. Let me continue to read from the remarks of the Minister of Railways and Canals :
Lieut.-Col. Hughes asked whether the people of Manitoba pay higher rates to Montreal and Boston than the farmers of the western states.
Mr. Blair said that the case which Col. Hughes referred to was governed by the Railway Act. There was a danger, if this agreement was confirmed, that under the operation of the lease and contract the government of Manitoba would, so far as its power went, compel a condition of things to exist which, if it did exist, would compel the Dominion government to take action to redress the grievances of the people discriminated against.
Now, could anything be stronger ? Could you make a clearer declaration with regard to the position we have taken than is contained in these words of the Minister of Railways and Canals ? He clearly foresees that there would be a discrimination in Manitoba as against Ontario and the Northwest Territories, and he intimates that if that discrimination existed it would be proper for the Federal government to step



in and regulate the rates in Manitoba. Now, if you are going to take that power from Manitoba which she supposes she is getting of absolutely controlling the rates, and are going to vest the control in the Federal government, then it must be clear that Manitoba is not getting anything for the vast liability which she is assuming. Surely hon. gentlemen will agree that the position which the Minister of Railways and Canals takes puts a new phase on the question as it appeared to the government and people of Manitoba. That being the case, are we not in duty bound to allow this matter to go back to the Manitoba legislature for ratification ? Should the members of the Manitoba legislature, in view of these statements by the Minister of Railways and Canals, not be allowed to revise that Bill ?
Has not the legislature of Manitoba power to repeal its own Acts ?

There would be a contract, and the Manitoba legislature having made a contract with the Canadian Northern Railway, 1 do not think it would be in their power to repeal it.
Mr. BOY'D. I understand that any legislature has power to repeal any of their Acts.

I am not a lawyer, but I do not think it would be competent for the Manitoba legislature to repeal any Act of this nature involving a contract that they have passed. I would invite the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to answer the question which the member for Macdonald has asked.
I would have to get all the facts about it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: But offhand? Perhaps the hon. member for Guys-borough (Mr. Fraser) could answer it ?
There is no need of It. Hon. members on either side of the House are not called upon to answer questions off-hand. I would not give any opinion on it.

Perhaps I should have hesitated about asking this question. I might get a bill in the morning for legal advice. Perhaps if I had sent over a retainer, I might have been able to get an opinion. But the House will agree with me that if the Manitoba legislature passes a Bill embodying a contract, and obligations had been undertaken because of that contract, it would not be competent for the Manitoba legislature to repeal it.
If the conditions are not carried out they can repeal it.

If I thought they were competent to repeal this legislation at any time, I would sit down and not say another word. Now, I continue to read from the report with regard to the position of the Minister of Railways before the Railway Committee :
Mr. Cochrane suggested that the same condition exists in Ontario with regard to the rates on freight from Chicago to the seaboard passing through Ontario.
Mr. Blair said that it did not, and he quoted the provision of the Railway Act which provided for eases when there was competition and it was necessary to make the rates in order to secure trade. He suggested that there should be a clause embodied in the Bill in the terms of the General Railway Act providing against discrimination in rates and against secret rates or concessions, and there could he, he said, no objection to such a clause going in the Bill, and the presence of such a clause in the Bill would he advantageous and have a restraining influence.
Mr. Lash, on behalf of the Canadian Northern Railway, said he would accept the clause suggested by Mr. Blair.
The clause as suggested was as follows, and it was embodied in the Bill :
3. Nothing in this Act or in this indenture contained in the schedules hereto, or done in pursuance of this Act or of the said indentures, shall (a) divest or limit, temporarily or otherwise, the rights or powers (under existing or future legislation of the parliament of Canada) of the Governor in Council, or of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, or of any commission or other authority, respecting any matter or thing, obligation or duty ;
It will be seen that with a clause like that in the measure, the legislature of Manitoba is not going to have the control that the speeches of the Premier, Mr. Roblin, and the Attorney General, Mr. Campbell, judging by the extracts I have given, must have led the people to believe they were receiving.
(b)	place the government of Canada, directly or indirectly, under any liability, obligation or duty with respect to any payment, matter or thing in the said indentures provided for or referred to ;
(c)	authorize the Canadian Northern Railway Company to charge or demand any higher rates for the carriage of freight or passengers than those heretofore or hereafter fixed under the authority of existing or future legislation of the pariiament of Canada, by the Governor in Council, or by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, or by any committee or other authority.
That clause having been inserted in the Bill, who will say that it is the same Bill that passed the Manitoba legislature ? This clause served notice upon the legislature of Manitoba that it is not to have the control of rates which the members of the executive sought to lead the people to believe that they were receiving. I do not say. I have no desire to say. that the members of the executive wilfully sought to mislead the
-MAY 13, 1901
Manitoba legislature or tlie people of Manitoba. I am not here to impute motives of any kind. But, taking fairly the expressions of Mr. Roblin and Mr. Colin H. Campbell, I think that any fair-minded man would certainly say that they understood that the legislature was going to have control of rates. It is perfectly true that in one expression used by the Attorney General, Mr. Campbell, which has been read by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), he did indicate that the Federal parliament would still have the right to exercise the same authority. But in the statement of the Stli of February, which was read by the hon. member for Labelle, he positively assured the people that they were receiving the absolute control of rates. That was the burden of the entire song. This is what was to be received in return for the vast liability the people of Manitoba were asked to assume. Now, it must be perfectly clear to all reasonable men that, in view of the clause I have read, Manitoba will not and cannot have the control of rates that she expected to have. That being the case, it seems to me a most reasonable proposition that we should allow this Bill to go back to the legislature of Manitoba for ratification ; and if the legislature chooses to ratify it, it can do so within a week or two. In that case the responsibility would rest with them, and this parliament and government will have done its whole duty to the people of Manitoba. I do not see why such a reasonable proposition should be refused. I marvel that the Prime Minister should take the responsibility of forcing this measure through when he could relieve himself entirely of responsibility by accepting the amendment of which I have given notice, and which I shall move at a later stage of the proceedings.
With regard to the limitation of rates, it seems to me that the clause which says that before the government can lower the rates the company must be heard, and their interest taken into consideration, does not give the government of Manitoba any right to limit rates greater than is given'to the federal authority, as represented bv the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. The interests of the company would be taken into consideration in any attempt made by the federal authority to exercise control of rates. And in this case, what better control is given to Manitoba than the rights enjoyed by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council ?
Now. I want to say a word in regard to the financial position of Manitoba. I want to make a statement in regard to the gross liability which is assumed under this railway bargain. The statement has been made from time to time in the House, I made it myself and it has been used by other members. that the province of Manitoba was assuming a liability of over $17,000.000. The premier of Manitoba called my atten-159*
tion to the fact that that was an exaggerated statement and that the liability of the province would not be over $13,000,000 or $14,000,000. I presume that the figures were arrived at in this way : The Northern Pacific system is being acquired on a rental basis, taking the value of the road at $7,000,000, and if the' government acquire the road at any time as they have a right to do, they must pay $7,000,000. That would be the first gross amount. Then, there is the interest on the bonds on 290 miles of the Rainy River road for thirty years which would amount to $5,800,000, or, in round figures, $0,000,000. That would make $13,000,000. Then, I suppose the additional amount is made up in this way : The government of Manitoba not only guarantee the bonds for thirty years but also guarantee the payment of the bonds themselves at the expiration of the thirty years, and that would amount to some $6,000,000 or $7,000,000, so that the province would pay during the thirty years $5,800,000, and at the end of the thirty years be liable for the bonds themselves which would be something over $6,000,000. That is probably the way that this gross amount was arrived at. I am quite sure that nobody desires to misrepresent the facts. I think they are sufficiently grave themselves without any exaggeration and I gladly avail myself of this opportunity to offer the explanation which I have given.
I want to refer briefly to the position which the lion. Minister of the Interior took this afternoon on the Bill and I want to congratulate him on the very clever speech which he made. He rarely speaks that he does not make a clever speech. However, I am convinced that there was a good deal of sophistry in his position and that when it is examined by a legal man, somebody better qualified than I am, I think it can be shown to be entirely fallacious in its conclusions. However, in my own poor way, I will attempt to offer a word or two upon his remarks. He pointed out first that the Bill simply gives the two companies power to contract and that we are in no sense responsible, that we are merely giving to the Northern Pacific Railway Company the power to contract. I take the position that the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) takes, and in view of the fact that he has been a cabinet minister, and is recognized as a very able man, his opinion is of considerable value, that we do not only give the power to these companies to contract but that in passing this measure we pass an enabling Act without the passage of which it would be quite impossible that this bargain could be consummated, and inasmuch as the hon. Minister of the Interior laid down the dictum that where the power lies, there rests the responsibility, and inasmuch as we are called upon to pass this enabling legislation, then, the responsibility


must rest upon us. If Manitoba is left to herself and Manitoba can by the passage of such legislation as she can pass authorize the contract the case would be different, but we are asked here to pass an enabling Act, and because we do pass that Act we take the responsibility on our own shoulders and we must be prepared to accept that responsibility. We do more than enable one company to contract with another ; we pass upon the contract itself. If we were only asked to say that the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Northern Pacific Railway Company might be allowed to enter into a bargain there would not be so much cause for complaint, but, in this Act which we propose to pass, is recited the contract as a schedule and we must take the responsibility for that contract. We cannot avoid that responsibility. Without our passing this Act this contract could never be validated. It would be null and void. Why then say that we have no responsibility and that we are doing nothing ? I may be wrong. I have not the advantage of a legal mind, but I think that I have a little common sense, and it seems to me that the proposition of the hon. Minister of the Interior is one entirely averse to common sense. It is not reconcilable with common sense at all. Inasmuch as the schedule and this arrangement are set out in this Act which we are about to pass we must pass upon the merits of every sentence of that contract and we are going to be held responsible for it. If repudiation comes in Manitoba, if the predictions made by some hon. gentlemen prove true, and I sincerely hope they will not, the responsibility must rest upon us. Speaking for myself, 1 would be delighted to find if the Bill becomes law that the gigantic ventures will prove a success, because every interest 1 have is in Manitoba, and it is in defence of my own interests and of the interests of the people I represent that I take the stand I do to-night. If the time comes, however, when the predictions of those who think as I do that it will prove disastrous for the province, are realized, then, I say, the responsibility must rest upon the Federal government and upon the parliament of this country. To the Federal parliament the people of Manitoba will resort and will ask it to pay the debts that bring ruin to Manitoba. Why should you not ? They will be able to say to you that when you passed this Act you knew more than they did, that when we, the legislature of Manitoba, voted for the Bill, we believed the representations that were made to us by the executive that the absolute control of freight rates have been secured and was guaranteed to us. A minister of the Crown had stated clearly and hon. members of the House had said that Manitoba had not obtained that control, and in the face of that fact you passed that Act, and, therefore, we come to you and say that you must pay our debts, that we Mr. RICHARDSON (Lisgar).
are unable to pay ourselves. That is a grave position, but It is only fair and right that we should understand that when we pass this legislation we will be held responsible in the long run. That is why I appeal and why I have appealed to the government to pause in this matter, and to say: We decline to take absolute responsibility in regard to this measure. We say to the legislature : We hand you back this matter. We are not going to take the position of overriding your legislation, of overriding the legislature, we are not going to veto your legislation but we simply pass it on this condition : That in view of the developments since this Bill was brought before the Canadian parliament iyou have the right to say for yourselves whether you do think this Bill should finally pass into legislation. The Minister of the Interior told us that there had been no protest forwarded to this government by the minority of the Manitoba legislature. I do not wish to say anything that would be offensive to the minister, but it does seem to me that that Is a puerile objection. Did not the' minority register their protest by voice and vote against this measure in the provincial assembly, and do we not know that the political associates of the Minister of the Interior who follow Mr. Greenway, solemnly took the ground that this legislation was improvident and was not in the interest of Manitoba ? It does strike me that it would be superfluous for the minority to send any ; formal protest to this parliament. The Minister of the Interior warned the House that | the refusal to pass this legislation would be liable to give rise to serious agitation in Manitoba. I doubt that statement, but even if it is correct it could only be correct to a very small extent. The minister has a logical mind and he will see that if my motion is adopted and we say to the Manitoba legislature that they should reconsider the'r Bill in view of the developments at Ottawa, that would prevent any agitation against this parliament. Let me call the attention of the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sifton) to the fact that the Minister of Railways stated that if we did pass the legislation it might give rise to a grave clash between the province and the Dominion, and that is one of the grounds on which I oppose the Bill. The Minister of the Interior gave it as his impression that even without this legislation here the government of Manitoba would be able to guarantee the bonds of the railway. If that be true, let Manitoba deal with this matter, and why should the Dominion parliament be called upon to confer power upon Manitoba to enter into this improvident bargain. As to the lease on the Northern Pacific and Manitoba system, I cannot for the life of me see how tliis railway is going to be made pay. The consideration that it cannot pay has led many right-thinking people to the conclusion that the contract is absolutely improvident. The returns furnished by the Northern Paefic Railway itself show

that during the year 1900 there was a loss on the Manitoba system of $185,000 on operating expenses alone, to say nothing of their not being able to pay any interest on fixed charges. In view of that loss on operating expenses how can it be expected that this road will pay handsomely when it is operated by another company ? Under a different management it is true the road may lose less, but I cannot see how reasonable men on the Manitoba system of $185,000 on oper-ting expenses and interest on fixed charges. And, if it fails to do that, what will be the result ? The resources of Manitoba consist in her per capita allowance and in some revenue which she derives from licenses, &c., amounting in all to about $700,000. For the last few years the province has been unable to meet its expenditure out of its ordinary revenue, and she has been drawing upon capital for some considerable time. She has been obliged to draw upon the school fund deposited with the Federal government in order to make up her deficit, in addition to borrowing money on provincial bonds. The delegates who came down here say that the annual outlay under this contract will be $600,000 ; but suppose it is $442,000 only, as those in favour of this Bill allege, Manitoba has no resources out of which to make good that deficit. She cannot go on borrowing money and paying her debts out of capital, and if she loses only $200,000 under this contract the House will see that the financial position of the province will be seriously jeopardized. The grant for schools by the provincial government has been doubling -during recent years, and the demands are increasing as settlement progresses. Manitoba is obliged to make up these deficits out of capital account. That being the case, if we fasten this liability upon the province, I believe it will be obliged to come back to the Federal government for relief, and it would be exceedingly difficult for us to refuse to grant that relief, because we shall be responsible for having fastened on the province the financial obligations which "brought it into that position.
Now, I want to say a word with reference to the remarks addressed to the House by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd). He said that the opposition to this Bill originated with a few agitators in Winnipeg. I do not think that was a perfectly fair statement of the case. I think even the Minister of the Interior will agree with me when I say that the entire Liberal party was opposed to it. I do not think there was an exception. Mr. James Ashdown was mentioned to-night as an exception. as a strong supporter of the Bill, as holding up both hands for it. I do not think that was an accurate description of his position. As a member of the board of trade, Mr. Ashdown agreed with a majority of the committee appointed to consider the question, that if certain amendments were made to the Bill they would
withdraw opposition to it. Those amendments have, of course, not been made. We are told, however, that the improvements suggested will be put in the mortgage when it is executed. On that point I entirely agree with the position taken by my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) that we ought to have this mortgage laid on the Table of the House before we ratify the contract. It is exceedingly important that we should have an opportunity to protect the people of Manitoba in connection with this contract if it is the decision of the House that the Bill must be forced through. As I stated when speaking previously on the question, we want to have the mortgage laid on the Table in order that we may see that those provisions which men like Mr. Ashdown have asked to be placed in it are placed in it. In discussing that matter with the premier of Manitoba-and I do not think he will accuse me of violating any confidence in the matter-he said that until the mortgage was executed, it would be difficult to lay it on the Table. I replied that although the mortgage may not be executed, we ought to have the mortgage as prepared laid on the Table, so that if the House finally decides to ratify this Bill, we may be able to examine the mortgage and see that the conditions which the majority of the Board of Trade asked to be placed in the mortgage are placed in it. We could at least do that much for Manitoba.
Now, let me reiterate that I believe the entire Liberal party-I do not know a single exception-are unanimously opposed to this legislation. Mr. Ashdown, though called a Liberal, was formerly a Conservative. In addition to the Liberal party, the entire labour party in Winnipeg, and I presume they have associated with them the labour men throughout the province, have denounced this legislation as not carrying out the idea of governmelit ownership at all. The president of the labour party said that the Bill, instead of being government ownership of railways, was the government ownership of railway debts. Then, what do we find with regard to the Conservative party? We find that most of the leading Conservatives there are very hostile to this measure. It is quite true, they have been designated by politicians on the other side as not being thoroughbreds ; but be that as it may. many of them are heartily opposed to the Bill. I read a list of Liberal-Conservatives opposed to this Bill, the names being taken from the Winnipeg Free Press, the organ of the Dominion government, and a paper over which my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior exercises a very important influence :	Mayor Arbuthnot, of Winnipeg;
Mayor Dickey, of Carberry ; ex-Mayor Gilroy, of Winnipeg; ex-Mayor Andrews, of Winnipeg ; Mr. Gilroy has been a candidate for political honours in the Conservative interest ; so has Mr. Andrews. Andrew

Kelly, of Brandon, a prominent Conservative ; J. H. Haslan, the Conservative candidate for Selkirk in the last Dominion election. Mr. A. M. Nanton, of Winnipeg, a prominent Conservative ; Mr. J. H. Brock, of Winnipeg, one of the most prominent Conservatives in the province of Manitoba, and a brother of the hon. member for Centre Toronto ; Aid. Fry, of Winnipeg, another prominent Conservative. Just to show that Conservative opinion is as much opposed to this Bill as Liberal opinion, let me read a short editorial from this government organ. It is headed ' Take a vote on it,' and says :
There are several stout Conservative papers in the west opposing the terms of the railway contracts now before the Manitoba legislature. A Manitoba paper which has been friendly to the party led by Mr. Hugh J. Macdonald, the Portage la Prairie Graphic of the 3rd inst., says:
' The Canadian Northern contract now before the local House is one of those measures which should be referred to the people. There are two reasons why this should be done. The vital importance of the measure to the province, by far the most important measure that has ever come into Manitoba politics, marks it as one upon which the people should pronounce first hand. The other reason is that the present government was elected on a platform of public ownership, and while this deal offers several of the advantages of public ownership, it does not give us public ownership, while entailing some of its risks. The proposal of the member for Lakeside is a good one, and we would suggest that Mr. McKenzie should not wait for a cabinet minister to accept his challenge, but should resign at once in the event of the third reading of the Bill being delayed.'
During a discussion of this Bill in the Manitoba legislature, Mr. Young, of Delor-aine. a brother of Senator Young, and Mr. McKenzie, the Liberal member for Lakeside, a local constituency in the constituency of my hon. friend from Macdonald, both offered to resign their seats and make the issue of their re-election the merits of this railway bargain ; and their offers were not accepted. Their offer was not accepted, because the government must have felt that their candidates would certainly have been defeated.
Nearly the whole Conservative press is opposed to the contract, and scarcely a prominent Conservative in the province of Manitoba, outside of the members who voted for the Bill, approve of it. The Montreal Gazette opposed the contract from the start, and only the day before yesterday had an article deploring the provisions of the Bill and trusting it would not become law. The Ottawa Citizen, the Calgary Herald. the Montreal Star, the Belleville Intelligencer, which is controlled by Sir Mackenzie Bowell, the Hamilton Spectator, and the Toronto News, have all expressed themselves adverse to this deal. And among the financial and commercial publications opposed to it are the Canadian Trade Review, the Mr. RICHARDSON (Lisgar).
Monetary Times and the Winnipeg Commercial, I do not know of a single Liberal paper, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, that has expressed itself in approval of this transaction. Some of the comments of the Conservative press are very strong. Sir Mackenzie Bowell's paper says that if it does not ruin the province, the province will be very fortunate. And the other papers denounced it in the same strain. In view of the fact that this deal is condemned both by Liberal and Conservative papers, in view of the fact that the labour party is unanimously opposed to it, and that both Liberals and Conservatives of prominence have denounced it, we may reasonably assume that public opinion is decidedly opposed to the ratification of this contract.
The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) said that I was elected by the votes of the Conservatives of the constituency of Lisgar. There is no doubt that a large majority of the Conservatives of Lisgar cast their ballots in my favour, but I must also say that without a vote of a very large number of Liberals in the county of Lisgar I would not be here to-night; and it is my firm conviction that were it not for the fierce campaign waged against me, I would have had a majority of at least 2,000 electors. The people of Lisgar, I believe, desired to pay me the compliment of returning me by a large majority, because of the position I took in defence of their rights.
Let me show the House what sort of tactics were resorted to against me. A few days before the election, a type-written circular was sent practically to every Liberal voter in Lisgar. That circular originated in the office of the Liberal organizer in Winnipeg. It was a forgery, and was signed ' The Central Conservative Association.' It was written as if it were intended for Conservative voters only, and what did that circular say ? It said that in the name of Sir Charles Tupper it was desirable that the mask should be withdrawn, and he wanted the faithful to understand that R. L. Richardson had made a deal with the Conservative party, and had sold himself out politically to that party. The circular further stated that it was important, in the interest of the Conservative party, that R. L. Richardson should be elected, because he had made a deal by which he was going to take over the Winnipeg Telegram, a Conservative paper, and amalgamate it with his paper, and that he would be very useful to the Conservative party as editor of the Conservative paper in the capital. Emissaries went all through the concessions of that constituency armed with that circular, and saying tp 'my old Liberal friends : What do you think of Richardson now ? Here is a circular issued by the Conservative party of Manitoba : it is intended for Conservatives. but it has dropped into the hands of Liberals.
I rise to a question of order. What have we got to do with this circular ?

For a time I allowed the hon. gentleman to proceed, because there was a reference made to the manner in which he was elected. But, I think he has gone far enough, and he would do well to get back to the Bill.
I was just going to return. I had just one other statement to make.
We will take it for granted.

The hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) says the House is not interested1 in this matter, but I find I am receiving much more attention when I refer to this matter than when I speak upon the Bill. I would not have referred to it had not the hon. member for Macdonald stated that I was misrepresenting the people who elected me. I admit that I got a good Conservative vote in the constituency, but I would not have been elected without a very large Liberal vote, though the hon. member for Macdonald may be correct in saying that I would not be here if I did not get the Conservative vote. I may say, however, that I am here representing both Liberals and Conservatives. I ran as an independent, I got votes on both sides, and I am here as representing all the people of Lisgar. It lias been said to me : You are taking your political life in your hands by opposing this Bill. The Liberals who opposed you in Lisgar will not support you, and the Conservatives who supported you will not support you again. I realize that there may possibly be some force in that statement, but I am not in public life for the purpose merely of holding down a seat in this House. I desire in the interests of the people of Lisgar to stand up against this Bill. It is immaterial to me whether, in taking this position, I shall sacrifice my seat in this House. I would sooner do right and sacrifice my seat, than to be wrong and hold my seat. My experience in public life has not enamoured me with being a member of parliament. A man who takes an independent position has got no flowery path to pursue in public life. I care not the snap of a finger whether I sacrifice my seat in this House, or whether I shall ever appear here again ; but, I shall at least know that in opposing this measure I have acted conscientiously, and. as I believe, in the interest of my constituents. I trust the House will pardon this personal allusion.
The hon. member for Marquette also referred to me as having advocated government ownership, and that now- I was opposing that principle. I gathered from his remarks that he thinks this railway deal brings government ownership to Manitoba. I entirely differ from the hon. member in
that conclusion. My conviction is, that if we pass this Bill we will put back for all time, certainly for thirty years, government ownership of railways in Manitoba. Government ownership can only be effectively carried out by the federal power. The provinces may, to some extent, control the road-beds, and by virtue of the assistance-which they give to railway companies, may ask for certain rates ; but, inasmuch as it was clearly laid down in the Railway Committee by eminent legal authorities, that no province can own or control a railway outside of its limits, I think that opinion deals a fatal blow at the idea of effective government ownership by provincial authorities. The longer I study the railway question the more convinced I am that government ownership is the only effective solution of the transportation problem. I was surprised to find, these last few days, that the Hon. Joseph Howe, one of the greatest statesmen Canada has known, in his speeches and letters, indicated that government ownership was bound to come in due time.

I would call the attention of the hon. member to the fact that the Bill does not include the subject of government ownership; therefore, I desire that the hon. gentleman direct his remarks to the Bill.

I would suggest to the Chairman that this Bill is by many regarded as securing the government ownership of these railways and government control of the rates, and I submit that I think I am strictly within the lines in pointing out that this is not secured. However, I would not like to transgress any further, if I am out of order. But, the whole contention of the hon. member for Marquette was, that I was to blame in opposing this Bill, because it provided for practical government ownership and control of rates. If the Chairman is still of the opinion that, under the circumstances, I cannot continue that line of argument, of course, I will accept his ruling.

I am certainly of the opinion that it does not include the question of the government ownership of railways, and therefore I think it would be irrelevant to discuss the question of government ownership in the discussion of this Bill.
It was in connection with this Bill that we discussed the question of government ownership. I was just saying that I was being twitted-
Oh, go on and talk.
That is my ruling.

I would like to refer to a statement made by the hon.

member for Marquette (Mr. Roche), who said that the Northern Pacific Railway was Introduced into the province of Manitoba under the condition that it should not charge higher rates than were charged by the Canadian Pacific Railway. I may say that the hon. gentleman is slightly in error in regard to that point. A maximum rate letter was obtained from the Northern Pacific by the government of Mr. Greenway at the time the bargain was made, and that maximum rate letter called for a reductiop of 3 cents per 100 pounds in the rate on wheat from points in Manitoba to Lake Superior. X myself saw the tariff issued by the Canadian Pacific Railway, I think, in October, and the rate was 24 cents per 100 pounds on wheat from Manitoba points to Lake Superior, but as soon as this bargain was made between the Greenway government and the Northern Pacific Railway, by virtue of which this maximum rate letter was issued, and which reduced the rate from 24 to 21 cents per 100 pounds, the Canadian Pacific Railway withdrew its tariff and issued a new one, making the rate 21 cents per 100 pounds from Manitoba points to Lake Superior, so that, an actual and positive reduction of 3 cents per 100 pounds in the rate from Manitoba points to Lake Superior was obtained. In addition to that, the incoming rates on general merchandise were reduced on the Northern Pacific from 25 per cent to 33J per cent. Because of the reduction on the Northern Pacific the Canadian Pacific Railway was obliged to meet the rate, so that the introduction of the Northern Pacific in the province of Manitoba meant a very considerable saving in freight rates to the people of Manitoba.
I do not know that I have anything further to say at this stage of the proceedings. I have two or three amendments which I propose to move when the time comes, but I felt it desirable that the remarks which I have addressed to the committee should be addressed to it on the preamble of the Bill, in the hope that the government might see its way clear to accepting the amendment which I propose, and have this Bill come into force only upon being ratified by the legislature of Manitoba, after being referred back to that body. I have some memoranda which I shall present to the House when the amendments come to be considered, but in the meantime I will content myself with making a final appeal to the government to accept my proposal and allow this Bill to go back to the legislature of Manitoba for final ratification. When this matter was first introduced to the public the premier of Manitoba referred to the fact that his party was elected on the questions of government ownership of railways. He told the audience that it was not time in Manitoba to adopt that principle, that the people in the province of Manitoba would not be willing to entrust the operation and ownership of railways into the hands of politicians at the present time, but he claimed that he had made an arrangement by which all the advantages without the drawbacks of government ownership were obtained. I do not wish to discuss the question of government ownership, but I am surprised that the hon. gentleman who preceded me (Mr. Richardson, Lisgar) was called to order for referring to this matter, because I was charged in the Railway Committee with being false to the principles that I have stated here several times when 1 declared myself to be in favour of the government ownership of railways. I am pleased that the discussion has lasted as long as it has, and I claim that there has been no obstruction placed in the way of the passage of this Bill. Until to-day the character of the debate was even more remarkable than the Bill itself. With one exception it was not until to-day that any supporter of the Bill would say so. It was not until to-day that the Manitoba members would give their reasons for supporting the Bill. In fact, until to-day the response of the members of this House to all our argument was :	We
do not care about it. But the difficulties that we have all along pointed out are now recognized to exist. I would not speak on the preamble if any who are in authority would give us hope that the propositions we have put forward would be accepted. There is one amendment on the Order paper that I cannot for the life of me un-del-stand why it should not be accepted. It proposes that we should pass this Bill and that it should not become law until the legislature of Manitoba had passed upon it again. I have not the slightest doubt that if the legislature should remain of the same opinion as it was when it made the contract, the railway companies would be glad to accept the same terms. 1 have had the opinion of a gentleman who had reason to look carefully into this deal, and he told me that the bargain was so one-sided that if it had been made by an individual and if it were taken into a court of law, it would probably be declared void on the ground that the maker of the bargain could not possibly
have understood what he was doing when he entered into it. The Minister of the Interior told us to-day, what should have been recognized long ago, that the question before us is the passage of a railway Bill; that it includes an agreement with a second party, but that the railway companies can in no way involve that second party unless we give them the power. It always has been the procedure of this parliament for us to examine into the merits of proposed railway amalgamations, and it is our right and our duty to do so. Even if a shareholder of one of the companies asking amalgamation appears before us, he is listened to. In this case the appellants to us are the people of Manitoba. The Minister of the Interior looked at this purely as a matter between this railway company and the legislature of Manitoba, and he seemed to forget that it is the people who are appealing to this parliament. We are not here as representing corporations, but we are here supposed to look after the interests of the people, and to see that they are amply and thoroughly protected. The member for Labelle has pointed out to the House that under the contract included in this Bill, it was altogether likely that different rates would prevail in Manitoba from these prevailing in Ontario and the Northwest Territories, and that in all probability they would be higher in Ontario than they would be in Manitoba. The certainty then was that the people outside of Manitoba would appeal to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, and as a remedy against this discrimination the Minister of Railways and Canals told us m the committee that it would be competent for the Privy Council to either lower the rates outside of Manitoba, or to increase the rates within the borders of Manitoba. The probability would be that the contention would be made that the rates outside of Manitoba were as low as they could possibly be, and therefore it would be incumbent upon the government to order that the railway rates in the province of Manitoba shall be raised. This seems to have been overlooked by the Minister of the Interior, and it would certainly bring this government into contest with the government of Manitoba. That I think has been demonstrated to the satisfaction of the members of this House. Before we are asked to pass this preamble, we shall have a definite statement as to whether this is to be provided for or not. It has been claimed by some hon. gentlemen that there has been too much discussion upon this matter, and that the subject has been practically talked to death. I do not agree in that view. The discussion has been altogether one-sided until to-day. but I believe that a great deal of good has been done because the result of our efforts has been to point certain defects in this measure. It was only to-day that those in favour of the Bill spoke.
My hon. friend (Mr. Puttee) is perfectly aware that one single member on the other side occupied the floor for two days, and that we did not have a chance to speak at all.

I made one exception. The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) this evening, for the first time in my knowledge, questioned the opposition of the people of Winnipeg to this bargain. Last Monday night I produced a great deal of evidence in this House as to the feeling of the people in the city of Winnipeg and also in the province at large in opposition to these deals ; and until to-night I have not heard that fact questioned. I wish to state most emphatically that public opinion in the city of Winnipeg is as nearly unanimous in its opposition to the railway bargain as it has been on any question I have ever known. I produced evidence from the leading journals of public opinion in the city. I cited the action of the city council, who were opposed to the deals, because they were advertising the sale of $1,000,000 worth of debentures, and on the recommendation of tlieir finance committee they took up this matter. I referred to the action of the board of trade, who did all they could to induce the government to meet their wishes and make the bargain decently fair, so that they could support it, and finally, after being told time and again that everything would appear in the mortgage, they lost all faith and went on record as opposed to the Bill. I referred to tlie Trades Council of Winnipeg, who, as believers in government ownership, were opposed to the Bill from the start, also the Labour party, which is a political organization. I quoted extensively from the Winnipeg Commercial, the only business publication in the west, and certainly as reliable as any paper in this country can be-a paper whose opinions are not swayed at all by political reasons, but which looked at the question simply as a matter of business. I referred to the public meetings in Winnipeg, which condemned the deal absolutely. The bon. member for Macdonald said that the meetings were practically in favour of the bargain, and that if the people present had been given a chance to vote, the majority would have been in their favour. The Tribune of Saturday, March 16, giving an account of the public meeting, said :
The success of the public meeting at the Winnipeg theatre last night for further discussion of the railroad deal was interfered with to some extent by an exhibition of organized rowdyism, for which the supporters of the railway deals are responsible. It was known as early as yesterday morning that organization for this purpose was going on, and fearing trouble extra police had been stationed in various parts of the theatre. The interruptions were conducted by what appeared to be a gang of navvies, who had secured a portion of the upper gallery. But their shouts were ill-timed, and showed the Mr. PUTTEE.
utmost ignorance of the questions under discussion. The ignorance of the gang, however,, was most superbly shown, when they even interrupted Messrs. Sproule and Samson Walker, who were speakers on the side of those who had engaged them:
The theatre was packed to the doors and the great bulk of the audieneq was thoroughly in sympathy with the resolution condemning the deal and asking for the protection of thg Dominion government in the matter.
I should not read this and have It put on record if it were not that I have had information from other sources which corroborates it. The description of the same meeting in the Winnipeg Free Press is as follows :-
The mass meeting held in the Winnipeg theatre last night to consider the railway deal was an affair of immense proportions. The spacious theatre was filled to the roof with au enthusiastic crowd, which, when the resolution was put to a vote, voted overwhelmingly in favour of it. The crowd was good-natured and noisy at times, but not disorderly, and the noise was the result of the efforts of an organized gang of disturbers who were opposed to any discussion of the matter, and who were assisted by a band of foreigners, navvies and shantymen who had been paid for this purpose, and marched to the theatre before it opened and seated in the top gallery.
Only to-day I received a communication from a gentleman in Winnipeg who was at that meeting, and he corroborates exactly the statements made by these papers. I recognize, of course, that the papers are generally supposed to lend a partisan colouring to their reports; hut it is only fair to say that the papers of Winnipeg, like the papers of metropolitan cities, have got to a considerable extent beyond that style of newspaper reporting. There was a deliberate attempt at that time to falsify the personal opinions of the citizens of Winnipeg In regard to those deals. The hon. member for Macdonald happened to be in the city that night, and an Innocent spectator at the performance.
I submitted last Monday evening a great deal of evidence to show the condition of public opinion as expressed in the press. I have in my hand a number of letters from different parties giving expressions of-private opinion. I know what weight is attached to a private expression of opinion, but many of the statements sent me, I think, accurately gauge the sentiment of the people of Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba. One gentleman writes me that the public has its mind made up as to the course to he pursued in the event of this deal becoming law, and that is to elect a government, at the first opportunity, pledged to repudiation, and that government will be neither Liberal nor Conservative, but a coalition of men from both parties. The attitude of the province, this gentleman says, is one of solid disgust, which will show itself with terrible effect whenever the opportunity offers, and he advises the

government to strengthen the militia contemporaneously with the passing of this Bill. Only in a few places is the contract at all approved of, and those are places which are in the expectation of public favours arising out of it, such as Emerson where a bridge is promised and where the Great Northern is expected to have a station. The writer of this letter is a gentleman who was unsuccessful in the last provincial general election, and who was one of the principal advocates of the very strongest platform on which the party now in power stands, namely, the government ownership of railways. He also is ex-mayor of the city of Winnipeg. I have also a letter from another gentleman who took a very active part in the last provincial election and who thoroughly understands the sentiment of the province in this matter.
Name.

The gentleman is Mr. W. R. Mulock, and he writes that the sentiment against the deal is practically universal.
The hon. member for Macdonald laid great stress on the fact that when the Canadian Pacific Railway became aware of the nature of the bargain they offered the Manitoba government some $5,000,000 or $6,000,000 spread over the next five years, and that he claimed should be taken as the value of the present bargain. I do not agree with the hon. gentleman on that point. That simply shows conclusively that the argument advanced by the hon. member for North Norfolk is well-founded, namely, that in the next two or three years freight rates will certainly come down. I do not know whether the Canadian Pacific Railway are favouring this deal or not ; I do not know whether they are in collusion with the parties to this deal or not, but there is every probability that the rumour to that effect is pretty well founded ; but their offer of $5,000.000, spread over the next five years, would in any case be a low offer for an absolute monopoly. If they could get such a monopoly at that price, they would certainly be getting it cheap. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, through its president, before this deal was made public, offered the provincial government an arrangement that seemed to be a very profitable one. But. there is no evidence that this is the value we should put upon this,bargain. As the premier of the province said, and quite rightly, they could not consider it as an alternative offer, because the people of Manitoba were anxious to get away from that monopoly, and to strengthen it even with the advantage of five millions on the other side would be out of the question. I do not think we should be called upon to pass this Bill without intimation being given whether any of these amendments of which we have had notice, will be acepted. I think I have stated the case fairly when I
say that though the matter was before the committee for four days, it did not receive proper attention, that it was not amended as it might have been if we had gone into both sides of the question. I do not think the preamble should be passed at all until we have an expression of opinon from the government. At all events, I will claim this much, that I have taken this Bill seriously, that the people of Manitoba are opposed to it, and we have a right to expect this parliament to protect the province. I have shown my sincerity, at all events, in believing that the province is against it by offering-and I think it is one of the best propositions made-that the matter should be referred to the people of the province. I do not think the proposal to refer it back to the legislature is adequate. The Manitoba legislature would probably be called together immediately and pass the measure.

On section 3,

Before section 3 is carried, I must say at once that the government, having accepted the responsibility of the principle of the Bill, my position is quite similar to that of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). The Minister of Railways made it clear in the committee that he wanted to introduce this clause as a warning to the government of Manitoba as to the spirit which animated the Federal parliament in adopting this legislation-that is, that the Federal government would keep its full power to interfere at any time to prevent Manitoba interfering with other people's rights in this regard.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope hon. gentlemen will keep order for a little while. I think any disorder is lowering to the dignity of the committee.

The clause reads as follows :
3. Nothing in this Act or in the indenture contained in the schedules hereto, or done in pursuance of this Act, or of the said indentures shall :
(a)	divest or limit, temporarily or otherwise, the rights or powers (under existing or future legislation of the parliament of Canada) of the Governor in Council, or of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council or of any commission or other authority, respecting any matter or thing, obligation or duty;
(b)	place the Governor of Canada, directly or indirectly, under any liability, obligation or duty with respect to any payment, matter or thing in the said indentures, provided for or referred to ;
(c)	authorize the Canadian Northern Railway Company to charge or demand any discriminating rate for the carriage of freight or passengers or to allow or make, any secret or special tolls on rebates, drawbacks or concessions, or any higher rates for the carriage of freight or passengers than those heretofore or hereafter fixed under the authority of existing or future legislation of the parliament of Canada, by the Governor in Council, or by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, or by any commission or other authority.
If I understand the bearing of this clause, it means that if any individual or place feels that the rates imposed on the country by the government of Manitoba under this Act interferes with or discriminates against them, they can come to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council for redress. The point has been raised in the committee and in this House-and so far it has not been denied in any way except by the Minister of the Interior. by saying it -was a childish absurdity, while in the Railway Committee the Minister of Railways admitted that it was worthy of considerafion-the point has been made that the government of Manitoba might fix the rates so that there would be no discrimination against any part of the province while interfering with the rights of another province or the whole Dominion. Therefore, I gave notice that I would move, as I do so. seconded by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Richardson) that after the word ' any discriminating rate,' these words be inserted :

-in favour of or against either (1) any individual or corporation, or (2) the people or shippers of or from any particular place, section, district or province.
I do not see how, if the government are in good faith, as I am sure they are, in desiring that this warning to the government of Manitoba should be effective, if they really intend to exercise the powers that are included, I do not see what objection there can be to the amendment I am now moving.
I do not move it with any idea of making the measure satisfactory to myself-I am opposed to the whole Bill, but when it is demanded by the majority, I submit to the majority. But I do not see why, if this warning is to be given against interfering with the right of people or localities in Manitoba, it should not be a warning against interfering with the rights of the people and localities in other provinces, a warning that they are not to take such steps as will divert the trade to American railways, or to use their powers to the injury of the intei'ests of the people of the Northwest, of Ontario, or of any other section. After all, if this adds nothing to the clause, it cannot do harm. If the government are sincere in saying they are ready to maintain the rights of the rest of the country in ease they are interfered with, what objection can they have to this amendment ? I submit this amendment to the committee, hoping the committee will accept it, not as a movement to defeat the Bill, but simply to emphasize the reservation made by the Minister of Railways and Canals.

I will say to my hon. friend from Labelle that if this Bill were before the Railway Committee, I do not think I would have any serious objection to his amendment, in fact I would have none at all, because in my judgment it adds nothing to or detracts nothing from the sense of the clause we have before us. The clause now reads as follows
Nothing in this Act or in this indenture contained in the schedule hereto, or done in pursuance of this.Act or of the said indentures shall . .	. . authorize the Canadian Northern Railway Company to charge or demand any higher rates

	,
Or any discriminatory rates. Now, there is no doubt that if a person is discriminated against he has the right of appeal to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. The Canadian Northern shall not be authorized to discriminate against any person, it shall not be authorized to discriminate against any place. If any place is discriminated against it will have the right of appeal to the Railway Committee. In the same way if this discrimination is made against a person, or a particular locality, or against a province, there would be the right of appeal to the Railway Committee. I do not see that the amendment is needed.

In my opinion the amendment adds nothing at all to the value of the clause. Those who may be discriminated against have that right under the General Railway Act. Everything the hon. gentleman wishes to secure by llis amendment is already provided for in the Act.

I desire to say only one word. The hon. member for Labelle has attributed to me statements and purposes which I did not make or entertain when this Bill was under consideration before the Railway Committee. I did not suggest the inclusion of that section in this Bill in any way, shape or form; it d'id not emanate from me. The gentlemen who were promoting this Bill introduced a special clause for the purpose of affording some assurance to, I presume, some persons on the committee who had doubts as to whether the action of parliament in passing this Bill would in some degree impair its power and authority in the premises, that it would have no such effect.
All that I suggested in the committee was that inasmuch as the object of the amendment which had emanated from the promoters of the Bill, and by which it was proposed to say that nothing in the Act should interfere with the power of the Railway Committee in respect to rates; that is to say, that the rates could not be made any higher than the rates fixed by the Governor in Council under the Railway Act, and that inasmuch as the clause only referred to the question of the raising of rates, I thought it would be reasonable to also add a clause having reference to discrimination, or to the making of secret rebates or other arrangements which are clearly declared against by the provisions of the Railway Act. At the same time, I took special care to convey to the committee my own opinion, that we were thereby not at all strengthened in our position ; that it was not necessary that we should make that declaration, that nothing wm could do or say would add to the powers of the provincial legislature or derogate from our own powers, that we were not conferring any powers on them and that we were taking none from ourselves. So that, when the hon. gentleman suggests that this clause was inserted at my suggestion he is entirely in error and he is forgetting the statement I made upon the subject. I would have a very serious objection to this amendment, the hon. gentleman must, if he is familiar with the Railway Act, know that it does not profess to deal with the question of the regulation of rates where that regulation appertains to the traffic which goes outside of the country. It has not been thought expedient, in any legislation which has passed this country, to make provision in such a case. This amendment refers to

the subject -with the view of making such a provision, and I think it would not he expedient to adopt it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Do I understand that in the Railway Act there is no power on the part of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council to prevent Manitoba, if she should choose to do it, sending the trade of the west to the United States ?
The MINISTER OB' RAILWAYS AND CANALS. I certainly do not think that the Railway Act deals with the question at all of the transfer of business to the United States. I do not find anything in it that deals with the question. The Railway Act does not provide for the classification of goods "which are carried out of the country into a foreign country or which may be brought from a foreign country on a through rate. We have declined to confer upon the Governor in Council any power to classify such goods for the purpose of having a rate fixed and we do not regulate the rate on such traffic.

Then, this throws a new light on the subject, and it adds very much to the seriousness of it. This shows that the government have no power under the Railway Act, according to the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, to prevent Manitoba from sending her trade to the United States. Therefore, I think I shall be able to show that question is a very important one, and when we come to the third reading, I think this should be made a little clearer than it is now.
Amendment (Mr. Bourassa) negatived.
