With a view of preventing the Manitoba government to discriminate against the rights of the people of the other provinces, or to divert the trade of Canada to the United States, I have moved an amendment to the third clause. . The Prime Minister told us that the power to prevent this lay with the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, but two minutes later the Minister of Railways told us that such power did not rest with that body. Well, we should know where we stand. There is no doubt from what we have heard from the Minister of the Interior, that the province of Manitoba will take the power, and probably a little more power than they are given under this law. It has happened in that province that where the constitution was plain, and where the highest tribunal in the land had declared the constitution was there, the government of Manitoba found a way to break the spirit of the constitution. If the government of Manitoba have already found a way to raise such a political agitation that the government of Canada did not deem it advisable to see that the constitution should be respected where the constitution was clearly on the side of a certain section of the population-and I am not prepared to say that the government of Canada was wrong in not interfering in that matter-I say that when we are creating an authority which may bring about a clash between that province and the Dominion, it is our duty to examine our position carefully. The Minister of Railways now tells us that there is nothing to prevent the Manitoba government from diverting the trade of that province to the United States. That is the point I raised in the Railway Committee, that is the point I raised on Monday last, that is the point that for eight days I have endeavoured to get explained by the Minister of Railways. But it is only at two o'clock in the morning, after a protracted debate and on a slight amendment to a subclause, that the minister chooses to throw light on the subject, and Ms light is that there is nothing in the Railway Act to enable him to protect the people of the rest of Canada against undue interference by the province of Manitoba. The minister tells us that he does not want to introduce into any private or special legislation, powers that we already possess under the Railway Act. Is this ordinary legislation ? No. It is entirely unprecedented legislation and it calls for unprecedented safeguards. The Minister of Railways has charged me with misquoting his words, and if I have done so, I ask his pardon, because I want to be fair to everybody ; but does the minister charge any one with misquotation who says that he stated in the Railway Committee that the powers given under this Bill to the Manitoba government might be the cause of a great clash between Manitoba and the Dominion. I suppose the hon. gentleman will not stand up now and state that he did not say those words, because all members of the committee are witnesses of them. Besides that, I understood the hon. gentleman to say that it would be a good thing, though per haps it would not do much by law, to introduce this as a warning to the government of Manitoba. The hon. gentleman says I misquoted him. All right ; I take that back; but I do not take back the statement that he said that this Bill would cause a grave clash between one of the provinces and the government of Canada. The hon. gentleman raised the question that on account of certain rates being adopted by the government of Manitoba, it might be the duty of the Dominion government to interfere to raise their rates in order to prevent them diverting the trade of this country to American lines. The hon. gentleman did not commit, himself very much on the details ; in fact, he has not been very committal on this Bill from the beginning till to-night. But, after the declaration made by the hon. gentleman a few minutes ago, this country is entitled to know what would be the effect of this legislation. On the one hand, the Prime Minister says they already possess that power, and the Minister of Railways says they do not possess that power. 1 would like to know what power they do possess, and the country would like to know.
Is the hon. gentleman not aware, from the debate that has taken place to-night, that in 1899 ?1,000,000 worth of Manitoba freight has gone out over the Northern Pacific system to Duluth ?

I do not mind at all what has happened. If something wrong has been done, that is no excuse for another wrong being committed. What may have been done is nothing to us. We are here to deal with one piece of legislation. That piece of legislation may be the cause of great trouble between one province and the Federal government. That special piece of legislation is the result of such a popular agitation as was pointed out to this House this afternoon by the hon. Minister of the Interior as justifying no Dominion interfer-
508/

ence with the province in regulating their railway facilities. Such an agitation is what induces one of the members of the cabinet to stand up and vote for a Bill of which he disapproves, against which he says he would have spoken and voted had he been a member of the legislature which adopted it ; and now this parliament is called upon to sanction that legislation on the sole ground that the provincial feeling in Manitoba is so strong that it would not tolerate interference. If that feeling is so strong that w* are not free to oppose this legislation, what will the feeling be once the legislation is passed and the government have to interfere on behalf of the rest of the country ? I know it is useless to protest against this legislation ; but at this the last stage of the Bill, I will not let it pass without protesting once more against the way it has been conducted. No one has stood up to say a word for the measure except two members from Manitoba, who made a very weak defence of it. No one spoke for it until after four days of discussion ; and I think it was time to make some defence when the only minister who spoke on the Bill stated that he intended to vote for it although he was opposed to it. The discussion is not a good certificate to the legislation nor to our responsibility. I have been accused of posing for virtue; but I have no direct interest in this legislation. Whatever may be the consequences of it to the people of Manitoba, I do not mind so long as I have no responsibility in the matter ; but the moment we are called upon to vote for the ratification or the sanction of the legislation, that moment we become responsible for it. Under this piece of legislation, a provincial government may be in a position to work against the trade of the rest of the country, to nullify the work we are doing daily in this parliament to build up our transportation facilities ; and when we have the declaration of the Minister of Railways and Canals that under the Railway Act the government have no power to prevent that, it is imperative, even if it is useless to speak for those who have no axes to grind in this matter to express once more their full and true thought on the question.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I understood, Sir, that at the start the great opposition to this legislation was because Manitoba had not full control of rates. My hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) now opposes it because Manitoba has too much power to control rates and may discriminate against the other provinces. provinces Manitoba will have power to discriminate. I am sure the hon. gentleman does not wish to be unfair to me. I have based my opposition to the Bill on this ground at every stage.

I think I can very safely appeal to the members of the Railway Committee who heard what I had to say when this Bill was under consideration there, that I did not make any statements or convey any intimation to the committee to the effect that it was not entirely within the competence of this parliament, notwithstanding the passing of this Act, and without the clauses which are introduced in it, to prevent the Northern Pacific Railway charging discriminating rates. I never hesitated to say that the power of parliament was left unimpaired ; and while I stated that, I do not hesitate to say that I feared, and I fear at this moment, that there may be such a reduction of rates forced by the action of the Manitoba government upon the Canadian Northern Railway as to lead the Canadian Northern, even with the approval, if it were necessary, of the government of Manitoba, to impose higher rates on traffic on portions of their line outside of the province of Manitoba, so as thereby to reduce the loss which will result from operations within that province. That is where I fear there may be difficulties occurring, and to that extent I have not swerved in my opinion as to the consequences which might ensue from the carrying out of this agreement. When I stated a moment ago that I could not subscribe to the additional amendment proposed by the hon. member for La-belle, I had in my mind the provisions of the Railway Act, and those provisions have reference to the case of traffic which goes out of this country into a foreign country, in respect of which the Railway Act does not propose that the Governor in Council shall exercise any authority or control or undertake to say what shall be the rates imposed. The Railway Act provides, in the first place, that there shall be a uniform classification of rates fixed by the Governor in Council, that the various classes of freight shall be put under different classifications, and these shall be uniform over the whole of the railway, and the same rates, under certain conditions and classifications contained in the Act, which shall be imposed by the company, shall be uniform on one part of the line with the rate which is charged on that same classification

upon other portions of the line. That is what the Act means when it says that railway companies cannot discriminate. Having declared under the authority of parliament what shall be the uniform classification of the different classes of freight, then what does parliament go on to say :
The company, in fixing or regulating the tolls to he taken for the transportation of goods, shall, except in respect of through traffic to or from the United States, adopt and conform to any uniform classification of freight which the Governor in Council, on the report of the minister, from time to time, prescribes.
That means that the companies shall not be called on to conform to the classification of freight where the freight is carried outside of Canada or brought inside of Canada to or from the United States.

It is abundantly clear that our power in this regard, so far as railway rates are concerned, is clear and definite. It was in the endeavour to make it clear that the amendment is not in accord with the principle of the Railway Act, and would seek to impose on this particular traffic restrictions and obligations which are not imposed on railway traffic in any other country or in any other part of Canada, that I called attention to its character.

I just want to add a word to what the hon. member for Labelle has said. It is a remarkable spectacle to find an entire government and its supporters put through a Bill, which, I believe, they unanimously consider an improvident one-a Bill concerning which I do not believe there are three members on that side who are not of the opinion that it is one that would work injury to the province of Manitoba. That being the case, I cannot allow this House to divide without saying that we are presenting to-night one of the most remarkable spectacles ever witnessed in the House of Commons. I could not help wondering what Liberals like Papi-neau, Baldwin, Lafontaine, Alex. Mackenzie, Geo. Brown and Edward Blake, would think 160

The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright)

5098 moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
That is is expedient to make provision for a subsidy, not exceeding a sum of one hundred thousand dollars per annum, for a steamship service between a port or ports in Canada and a port or ports in France.
He said : The House will remember that for many years we have had on the statute-book an Act whereby $50,000 a year was appropriated as a subsidy to encourage trade with France. The House is also aware that during all these years we have found it impossible to obtain any proper service for that money. We are at present about to propose to the House a subsidy not to, exceed $100,000, for which, however, we expect to obtain a largely increased service. The service will be not quite but nearly double what was proposed in the original Act, that is to say, if it is carried out. The minimum service will be eighteen voyages, however, instead of 24, 12 to be performed during the summer months, and six during the winter months. They will probably be from the ports of Montreal and Quebec during the summer, and from the ports of St. John or Halifax during the winter as is the case with several of our other subsidies. They go to northern ports in France, probably to Havre and Boulogne, having the right to go also to the Mediterranean ports if it is found expedient. These are the chief modifications which we propose to make in the Bill we propose presently to introduce, founded on this resolution. Of course, the House is aware that all these grants are in the nature of the case largely experimental ; and while I am sure that, all will agree with me in thinking that it is very desirable indeed to extend our trade with France, which has a population of 40,000,000, a well-to-do population, and where, if we can introduce articles of food products more especially, we may look to do a very considerable business ; still there are, no doubt, owing to the French tariff and other causes, rather serious difficulties in our way. These we hope to overcome to a considerable degree by the creation of a line which we hope will ply if not weekly, at any rate once every ten days, between Canada and France.
The present traffic with France, as the House is aware, amounts to nearly $6,000,000 a year, exports and imports, $5,800,000, I think, is the exact figure. Of this the greater portion are imports from France. But we have been of late years extending and increasing our trade with France, and there is a reasonable hope, if we obtain a permanent line of steamers, of making a very considerable advance. Moreover, there are certain articles largely consumed in France Which I think we could deal in to a verv great advantage. For example, in the article of pulp, there are good hopes of a large increase in our trade. At present their supply of pulp comes, I am informed, almost
entirely from the Scandinavian countries, but apparently there is no reason why wre should not be able to compete with them on favourable terms. We are also in hopes of being able to sell respectable quantities of iron and possibly of coal to France, especially if we have the advantage of conveying them in steamers directly to a French port, which, under the French law, would be necessary in order to obtain the benefit of their traiff. In the article of manufactures we have already developed a considerable trade, principally in agricultural implements, and we hope to do more. There is some trade in lumber ; how far that can be extended, I am not exactly in a position to say, but still there is a reasonable possibility that it may be done. In the matter of food products, there would no doubt be a considerable chance for development if we can induce the French government to give us some moderate concessions. As the House is aware, a treaty was made by our predecessors with the French government under which certain articles are admitted under their minimum tariff ; but it was a condition of that treaty, in effect at any rate, that a line of steamers should be subsidized to France, and without that, as I have mentioned, under the French tariff, it is very difficult to obtain anything like the full value of the concessions that have been made to us.
It lias also appeared to the government that the present is a proper time for attempting to increase our trade with France. I am happy to say that a great deal of attention was paid to the Canadian exhibits which were displayed at the recent exposition in Paris. A good many orders have been obtained, I am told, in consequence of the impression that was made on the French public by reason of the exhibits there produced ; and there is, I think, ground for believing that we may to a considerable extent increase and develop our trade, even in the last named articles. Practically, I may add, this is a joint subsidy. Under the French law considerable bonuses are granted to ships making ocean voyages. One-half of these vessels would foe under the French register, and will obtain the benefit of the French subsidy ; one-half of them will bear the English flag and obtain, of course, our subsidy. The House is aware that the articles at present imported from France are chiefly articles of luxury, articles of the nature of silks, of fine woollens, of wines and brandies, and fancy goods generally. There are some other articles, but those constitute the staples. Of course I am not yet in a position to say what results may follow, but I think there is reasonable ground of belief that the money we propose to expend in this way will be found not to be thrown away. In the first instance we may probably not exceed the subsidy now on the statute-book, which amounts tb $50,000 a year ; but we have taken provision

that in case an additional number of steamers are put on we may be at liberty to increase the subsidy to $100,000, but not more. I think the subsidy which, under these circumstances, would be earned by French vessels employed, would nearly if not altogether equal ours.
I have further to add that although this contract is being made with the Franco-Canadian Company, that company have agreed to form a new company to which this contract is to be assigned, which company will be largely composed of Canadian stockholders. The gentlemen whose names are given to us as having agreed to take an interest in it, are gentlemen well known in this community whose names I think are sufficient guarantee that the enterprise will be prosecuted with all reasonable vigour. I will give the House the names of the principal incorporators of the new company to which the present company) propose to assign the the contract with the government. We have not been able to wait for the full incorporation of this company, owing to the necessary legal delay which must elapse before they can receive their charter. But we have agreed with the promoters of the Canadian company that their contract should be assigned to the new company. The principal incorporators are the Hon. Itobt. Mackay, of Montreal ; Mr. Henry Miles, Mr. Alfred A. Ayer, Hon. Geo. E. Drummond, Hon. Alfred Thibaudeau, Mr. Blumhart, Hon. Melvin Jones, J. R. Booth, of this city, E. B. Douglas, and Mr. Clergue, of Sault Ste. Marie. Those, I think, are all the facts material to the consideration of the proposition of the government ; but of course when we go into committee I shall be glad to give any further details.
The hon. gentleman spoke of food products ; what business does the hon. gentleman expect to do in that line V

The corporators expect to do a considerable trade in that article ; it is probable also that a considerable trade may be developed, specially with the Mediterranean ports in the article of coal, which is daily becoming more and more needed for French manufacturing purposes. We entertained hopes that there may be considerable development in the iron trade also.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Will any provision be made for cold storage in connection with this line ?
That will be done by my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture in the usual way.

speechtext: Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the resolution.

Can the minister inform us as to the development with the trade Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
with France since we have a new tariff arrangement ?

We have had no direct line of steamships, and that seems to be almost a sine qua non of any considerable development. But I can give my hon. friend roughly the figures. In 1896, our exports to France were $581,000 in round numbers ; in 1897, they were $690,000 ; in 1898, they had increased to $1,025,000 ; and iu 1899, to $1,557,000-1 think that was largely due to the export of foodstuffs. Last year the exports were $1,374,000. Thus the increase in our exports since 1890 has been about 150 per cent. Similarly with our imports : 1890, $2,782,000 ; 1897, $2,500,000 ; 1898, $4,090,000 ; 1899, $3,879,000 ; 1900, $4,464,000. This, as will be seen, makes the total trade, exports and imports, nearly $6,000,000 a year, as against $3,364,000 in 1896. The imports are mainly articles of luxury-silks, tine woollens, brandy, spirits aud fancy goods.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: By what route do these imports come now ?

I have been informed that the trade its to a considerable extent done through American ports, but some direct to Montreal. It is not at all unlikely, although we have no means of tracing it, that our exports to France are really in excess of these figures, for I have very little doubt that a good deal of the exports credited to the United States are really Canadian goods sent via New York.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
I believe we have a very large potential trade with France, and that the best way to encourage that trade is this scheme of subsidizing a direct line of steamers. Let me call the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the advantage which would result to us from interesting our commissioner in France in the development of that trade. I do not know whether we receive from time to time reports from that commissioner as to the prospects for increased trade with that great country. The commissioner is no doubt aware to what an immense extent the trade with the United States has been increased through the efforts of their consular agent abroad. Side by side with this encouragement of a direct line of steamers with France, I think we should be kept fully informed as to the lines of trade that might be opened up with France. I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if we receive regular reports from our agent in France, and, if not, whether it should not be feasible to provide some means to keep the country informed of the commercial needs existing in France, and, if necessary to send for that purpose what seems to me would need to be but an inconsiderable sum of money. We have an agent there

wlio is an intelligent man as those who know him are aware. If something were done in the line I suggest, I think it would materially aid the object we have in view.

I have no hesitation in saying that if our agency In Paris were put upon a better footing, we should attain a considerable commercial result. Mr. Fabre has been paid the paltry sum of $3,000 a year. He has received those who have come to him, and has done his best to furnish them with information as to Canada. I know personally that hundreds of callers visit his office. Unfortunately, the office has not been equipped on a commercial footing. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) is quite right in suggesting that improvement should be made. Before last year, I had travelled a good deal in France and other continental European countries as well as In England, but never with the same view as when I was there last year. In the execution of my duties as Canadian commissioner to the Paris Exposition, I had the advantage of meeting many people of all classes, including many interested in all branches of commerce, in mining and so on. rue establishment of a direct line of steamers cannot fail to bring results that will surprise us. We are selling to France to-day a good deal of pulp-wood timber, and paper also, i have no doubt that hereafter we shall be able to sell many things that we do not sell now. At this season last year-I think I have stated this in the House before, but it will bear repetition-I paid one, two and even three francs for a single apple. That may seem ridiculous, but it is true. I need hardly say that I did not buy many of them. But it is true that in April and May people are compelled to pay for some classes of fruit simply ridiculous prices. With our system of cold storage and with a direct line of steamers we could export our fruit to France and sell it at very fine prices indeed. And what is time of fruit is true of other things. We can sell iron, coal, furniture, pianos and other things. Our furniture was the only line in which we were not represented in the Paris Exposition as we should have been and as we might have been. But in spite of the inferior samples that we had there, a good many orders have since been sent from France to our manufacturers. But to assure success, we must, as my hon. friend has suggested, have a better agency -not that Mr. Fabre is not an able man, but he is not a commercial man, and moreover he is not equipped as he should be.
Coupled with that policy which will be actively pushed, it will be necessary to equip our agency better than it has been in the past. I do not say that we will be bound to spend a large amount of money, but we must have in Paris a commercial man who knows Canada thoroughly well and of course can speak both English and
French. Our American neighbours are doing an immense trade with that country, and there is an American chamber of commerce in France. Our agency there will also be able to reach Belgium, which is taking a deep interest in Canada to-day. The group who are working with the King of Belgium, and who have carried out such important enterprises in the Congo, have settled With us. They are erecting a large pulp and paper mills at the Shawinlgan Falls. Those men command millions. Both BT-ench and Belgium capitalists have invested largely in Russia and lost large amounts of money. I have been in a position to know that they have lost immense sums. Well, all those who know the economical condition of the continent will admit that there is plenty of money in France and Belgium. The people there do not know what to do with it at times, and invest it right and left. Canada is a good field for investment. Our laws are becoming better known. Those people know that capital and labour are safe here, and if we give our attention to the continent we will draw capital from these countries by leaps and bounds, especially as considerable of their capital has been invested elsewhere and has not brought the results which it will necessarily bring here.
Perhaps we will be able also to bring about closer and better relations between these two mother lands, if I may speak as a French Canadian, and I believe that to be a very legitimate ambition. It is surprising what magnificent results are brought about by closer relations. The two races have lived in peace and harmony, and I do not see why England and France, which are among the foremost civilized nations in the world, should not also live in peace and harmony. From that standpoint, I have no doubt that the policy which was initiated by the late government, and which we are continuing, will have results that both sides will applaud.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. J. Israel Tarte).

speechtext:
I have for a good many years been of the opinion that our agent in France is only an ornamental gentleman ; and if he is to be depended on soley for the development of our trade in connection with this steamship line, I am afraid our efforts will be a failure. He may be a very good man in some lines, but what those lines are I am unable to say. I have nothing to say against the gentleman personally, whom I do not-know. He may be a very good man for work to which he is adapted, but it is very importent, if we hope to develop trade with France, that we should have in that country a live commercial agent who is more familiar with Canada's resources and products. There is no doubt a good deal of truth in what the hon. minister has said as to the large amount of capital on the continent looking for investment, and if we make it known that there are many lines in this country in which that capital may

be profitably invested, no doubt our progress will be considerably accelerated. A friend of mine who is living in France writes me that lie is struck with the large amount of capital lying there idle and the desire of the people to invest, if they only knew where to invest it safely and profitably. But we would certainly require to have a live commercial agent in that country, who would be on the alert for possibilities of extending our commercial relations with France and with Belgium as well.
If we hope to succeed in establishing a trade with France in the food lines, we will have to do something with regard to cold storage. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says that the Minister of Agriculture will attend to that matter, but I would take this opportunity of pointing out that in that connection there are several considerations to be kept in view. There is the speed of the journey, and there are the freight charges and the question of cold storage, on the satisfactory solution of which will depend largely our trade with that country. The lion. Minister of Public Works spoke of the cost of apples in France, which would indicate a profitable market for that product ; and while it may not be necessary to have cold storage for apples, they will require a species of cold storage until land ed. I notice that we get a good deal of wines and brandy from France, and am not aware what our temperance friends on the opposite side would think about increasing that trade, but, as regards wines, many people hold the opinion that temperance habits would be promoted if our people would drink light wines instead of strong liquor. We get a considerable quantity of silks and satins from France and also woollens, but I do not see how the French woollens can compete with the English make, when the latter has the preferential rate in its favour.
We get a class of goods which does not come into competition with the English.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Will these boats make a trip every week ?
We hope to have a weekly service, but for the first year we only expect a fortnightly service in summer and a monthly one in winter. We will not pay more than $50,000 for that service.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
No doubt the money spent advertising our country at the great exposition will have fruitful results, but we should have a good lively commercial agent there.
I do not think our present agent is a man of that character. He may be valuable in some lines, but that is not his line.
I am very glad to see the spirit in which this resolution is
They could if they were under British register.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Mr. Fabre is a man whose services we should not think of dispensing with. He is not a commercial man. but he has made a large circle of acquaintances in commercial circles. He is a very useful man. We should have a commercial agent in France. There is a great deal of interest taken in us in France now. If my hon. friend from Toronto will remember, a few years ago there was an exhibition in which a great many French people took part. They were so well pleased with that venture that before I left they asked if Canada would not have an exhibition on a large scale either at Toronto or Montreal. Although they are French they said that they preferred Toronto, because they had been so well treated there, and they have been selling in Ontario since then pianos and expensive things of that kind. My hon. friend has observed the name of Mr. Lyman .Tones among the promoters of the line. This is because the Massey-Harris Company have established a very large trade in France already, but with this new line they will double and treble that trade. They are selling implements in France where these implements are not known as they should be. They are only beginning to be known. We had a trade last year amounting to $5,500,000 with France, and, as the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) has said, this does not represent the volume of business we are doing with France. There is in Montreal a large circle of French peo-
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. J. I. Tarte).

speechtext: If they were under British register or that of any other country which participates in her, coast clearing trade, they could take cargoes from one port in the Dominion to another port. A steamer under French register could not take any molasses from the port of Halifax to Montreal, while a Norwegian or an Italian steamer could. These French steamers could not participate in our coasting trade. While they could take freight from France to different ports in the Dominion, or from different ports in the Dominion to France, they could not take freight from one port in the Dominion to another port in the Dominion under French registration.

I would be glad to support any legislation in favour of increasing our trade with other countries in which it can be done profitably. For that purpose, I presume it is necessai^y to give subsidies in some cases but particularly to establish communication with countries to which we can export goods. There is no question that it is necessary to hunt for markets for our products. For that purpose, the first essential is to have a good agent in that country ; an agent who will look up all the lines of trade that can be most profitably engaged in there. I do not know what are the qualifications of the gentleman who now represents us in France, but whether he be suitable or not for the purpose, I contend that it is the duty of the government to get the vei-y best man possible when we are going to subsidize steamers to develop that

trade. I would vote in favour of such a subsidy only on the condition that these boats are equipped in a manner suitable to carry on the trade. The minister (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) says that is a matter with which the Minister of Agriculture has to deal.
The MINISTER OF1 TRADE AND COMMERCE. As to the question of cold storage.
Mr. SMITH (Wentworth), Whatever department lias to deal with it, it is most important to secure that these steamers should be equipped so as to carry perishable products.
Hear, hear.

I am not so sanguine as is the Minister of Public Works that we can find in France a market for a large quantity of our fruit, but doubtless with a direct line of steamers something may be done. France is our largest competitor in the British market in some lines of fruit, especially pears ; but we may perhaps find ,a market for our apples there at some seasons of the year.
Peaches also.

In order to carry our apples to France under proper conditions we must have the holds of these vessels thoroughly ventilated. I have heard it stated frequently that the reason we cannot make satisfactory arrangements in this respect with the steamships running to Britain is because the contracts are already let and we cannot compel the steamship companies. We are now about to enter into a contract with a steamship company, and now is the time to make the bargain that we shall have the latest improvements to carry our perishable products across the ocean in good condition. We heard a few days ago in the Committee on Agriculture that our cheese deteriorated in value to the enormous extent of about three million dollars last year, because it was not carried to Britain in good condition. That was due entirely to the poor equipment of the steamships and the railway cars in this country. If we are going to develop a trade with France, we must provide in this contract a hard and fast bargain that the holds of these vessels must be so ventilated that their temperature will not be higher than the temperature outside the vessel. The temperature of the ocean air outside the vessel is sufficiently low to enable us to carry even pears, as well as almost all kinds of perishable products, across the ocean and deliver them in the European markets in infinitely better condition than with cold storage, and this can be secured at practically no expense. The cost of fitting up a steamer with proper ventilating apparatus is merely nominal compared with the cost of a cold stor-Mr. SMITH (Wentworth).
age plant. I presume that butter would require cold storage, but almost all our perishable products require only this forced ventilation. We voted the other day a small subsidy for a steamer running from Annapolis to Great Britain for the purpose of carrying apples, and from the statements made in this House it is apparent that although the subsidy was voted purposely to accommodate the apple trade, no arrangements were made to carry these apples properly, and the hon. gentleman who spoke on the question told us that the returns showed that the apples arrived in England in a rotten condition ; in fact, that it was the worst shipment of apples that ever went from Nova Scotia. This will show how important it is that we should take precautions when we are subsidizing steamers. If we are going to develop a trade in perishable products with France, we must have the holds of these vessels thoroughly ventilated, and that stipulation should be made now when we are voting a subsidy to a new line.

The suggestion just made by my hon. friend (Mr. Smith, Wentworth) is a most admirable one, because any one who knows the nature of our trade with France, knows that a great portion of that trade will be in perishable products. Now, when we are making the contract, is just the time to provide for the cold storage which is necessary. I have no doubt that if ever we develop extensive commercial relations with European countries, and particularly with France, we will do a large business in perishable products, including, of course, meats. The hon. Minister of Public Works knows the price of meat in France.
Two francs a pound.

Yes, and I believe we could therefore compete successfully in that market. Any one who is well acquainted with Mr. Fabre will know that what the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) stated is absolutely true. At the same time I must add very promptly that it would be very great folly to dispense with Mr. Fabre's services at present, because he is extremely useful to us in France. We all know that in promoting commercial relations with European countries, side by side with commercial aptitude, you want a man who is something of a diplomat, and Mr. Fabre fills the bill in that respect perfectly. I would suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce the advisability not only of giving us proper commercial representation in France and in Belgium, with which our chances of trade are very great, but also with some other European countries. I believe that we can develop a very large trade with Italy, perhaps not quite to the same extent ns with France, but much on the same lines. The same remark applies to Germany. I believe sincerely that we might very easily stand

some retrenchment in the amount of money we pay to immigration agents, who, to a very large extent, do not benefit this country, and with half that amount I believe that we could pay proper commercial agents who would greately develop our trade with the European continent. Those who have read Edwin Williams' book upon the cause of the decadence of British foreign commerce, know with what insistence he demonstrates how the Americans have developed their foreign trade by the employment of skilful commercial agents. I think we could take a leaf out of Edwin Williams' book, because I believe that money spent in that direction would give returns a hundred fold.

I may, perhaps, be permitted to say a few words with reference to the subsidies which are granted to steamships. It is true that the steamship line which we ran from Annapolis last year did not give satisfaction to the parties interested, but it is only fair to say that this service was demanded by the people, who supposed that it would be of great value to them. Previously to this year, at all events in the near past, the fruit-growers of Nova Scotia were of the opinion that it would be necessary for them to have cold storage for the shipment of their fruit. They have changed their minds in that regard, and after investigation and experience, they are now satisfied that all that is necessary is proper ventilation of the holds. I understand that provision has been made by the government by which any steamer putting in forced ventilation shall receive half the cost of installing the same. I would urge upon the minister that all contracts for subsidies to steamers plying from the ports of Nova Scotia-and I think, probably, it would apply to St. John, N.B., as well-should have in them a stipulation requiring them to install a forced ventilation plant when carrying cargoes of fruit. I have brought this matter to the attention of the House before, and I take this occasion to impress it upon the mind of the minister, because the people of the country are unanimous in their opinion that it is a thing which should be done. If that is done, we are satisfied that the fruit can be carried with the utmost safety. If that is not done, and the subsidy is given to a line of steamers calling at these ports, then, it prevents competition which would otherwise take place, because the shippers are satisfied that if the business were left open to competition, other lines of steamers would install the necessary ventilation in order to carry the fruit to the other side in proper condition.

It is pleasant to find a resolution which we can all agree on and heartily support. I think this resolution is a move decidedly in the right direction, for developing the trade of the country ; but I thoroughly agree with my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule), and my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), that we want to go further and appoint business agents in all these countries. I thoroughly believe that if we had proper business representatives in different countries, it would pay us to stop all the expenses we now incur on account of immigration. Immigration would follow, and we should have a much better class of immigrants than we have had in the past. As regards the suggestion that this is an occasion when proper equipment should be provided for the carriage of our products in a businesslike manner, I think that is certainly worthy of the consideration of the government; and if it is necessary to ask for a further sum of money for that purpose, I am sure that this side of the House would join with the government in providing whatever is necessary to carry out the business properly.
From what port will these vessels sail in winter ?
From maritime ports.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I did not mean to convey the idea that Mr. Fabre's services should be dispensed with, but that he is not a suitable man to promote the development of trade, and therefore it would be necessary to appoint a live commercial agent; and I think we might go further and have an agent in Belgium as well.

I quite understand that the hon. gentleman's remarks were not intended to disparage Mr. Fabre's capacity as a diplomatic representative agent. I may say that the point raised has been receiving- the consideration of the government, and we are now considering the question of improving our commercial facilities in France and elsewhere. The matter of cold storage has been more particularly under the direction of the Minister of Agriculture. I may add that tlie Prime Minister informs me that he hopes soon to have the pleasure of welcoming informally an agent of the French government in a semi-official capacity, with whom we hope to confer as to getting further advantages and privileges from the French government ; but these negotiations are not at a stage where we can make any statement to the House in regard to them.
Resolution reported, read the first and the second time, and concurred in.
The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 141) further to amend the Act respect-tag ocean steamship subsidies.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
Bill (No. 130) to amend the Railway Act (Mr. Fitzpatrick), read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.

This Bill is merely to provide for arrangements which may he made by the creditors of insolvent railway companies, to enable them to wind up the company or reorganize it-practically applying to railway companies those provisions of the Winding-up Act which are applied to other financial institutions in the country. The provisions of this Bill are adapted from the Imperial Railway Companies Act of 1807.
Will the Solicitor General explain how the franchise of the old company passes to the new company ?
The franchise remains absolutely vested in the company. It is simply a scheme for a rearrangement of the liabilities of the company.

I am sorry to have to admit that I have not read the Bill until now ; but what I cannot understand is, what benefit it is to the creditors of the company to classify and rearrange their securities if the company itself is unable to run its trains.
The benefit is that the liability of the company might be wiped out in some quarter.
They might wipe out the liability in two ways-by transferring the franchise to somebody, or by an Act of parliament.

The company has a certain amount of liability, bonded debts and ordinary liability. In order to relieve itself of these liabilities, there is a scheme of distribution provided to which the creditors are obliged to assent. It may be in the interests of the bondholders, as well as the shareholders to have the liabilities of the company reduced, and this scheme is for the purpose of enabling a company to arrange with its creditors in such a way as to reorganize the liabilities and induce the creditors to accept so much on the dollar.

It is compulsory reduction and getting rid of debt. Why not let the creditors get a judgment, as they can under the provisions of the Railway Act, and then work the road, and if necessary, come to this House for a franchise?

This is a more satisfactory proceeding. Under the present law, you can get a judgment against a road and then proceed to sell it and have the assets distributed by the sheriff. But you cannot liquidate the liabilities in that way, unless you dispose of the whole enterprise, whereas it may be important to all

interested to keep the railway in the hands of those who originally started it and rearrange the liabilities. This law has been in force in England since 1867, and worked very satisfactorily. At present, take a road running through different provinces, you cannot sell that road and have a proper distribution of the proceeds.
You can sell the franchise of the road, and if you buy the franchise you can get from this House the right of running it.
Let the hon. gentleman refer to the case of the Manitoba and North-western and see how that system works.

There is a provision in the Railway Act enabling the creditors to take possession of the road under an order of the court, and when they have been in possession a certain time, they can come to this House and get a franchise.
But what is the object of all these involved proceedings ?

All that requires legislation, and in the meantime the affairs of the company are in a state of confusion. It has been found in England very useful indeed to have a power of the kind proposed in this Bill vested in the court. If my hon. friend has followed in any degree at all the practice in England, he will find that the system is exceedingly popular and has been found to work very advantageously. The result is that the various interests in the country-bondholders, stockholders, preference holders and whatever they may be-are brought before the court. The whole case is presented and objections are considered by the court. Then a scheme of assessment of all the interests is proposed by the judicial tribunal and usually accepted, and the machine then starts on a sound and healthy basis, with all its entangling difficulties removed, and matters on a satisfactory and smooth footing. Such matters cannot be settled in any other way so effectively as by this system, and I wonder we have not had it in operation long before this. I hope there will be no objection on the part of the committee. It is not a novel experiment at all, but one which has worked well in England.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Take the ordinary Winding-up Act, applicable to all our corporations. An exception is made with regard to railway companies. You can extinguish liabilities by the Winding-up Act, but that Act does not apply to railway companies.

I am in sympathy with the object of the Bill, but why has the jurisdiction been vested in the Exchequer Court ?

Would it not, as a matter of convenience, be better to give jurisdiction to the court of the domicile of the railway. On the question of notice, I see that the Bill, in two instances, provides for notice in the Canada Gazette only. In our country the bondholders very seldom read the Canada Gazette and perhaps such notice would not be sufficient for the parties interested.

It is important to have a scheme of distribution made by a court over which we have direct authority ourselves. Besides the railway to which this Act will apply will be railways running through different provinces, and it is doubtful if a provinica'l court would have the right to distribute the assets of corporations running in different provinces. It is better to have the whole matter under the control of one special court, the jurisdiction of which cannot be doubted.
In the liquidation before the court, can the court lessen the first or second class security or make a rearrangement ?

This cannot be done without the approval of the creditors themselves. You get your scheme of distribution, which must be prepared by the creditors among themselves. All that the court does is to ratify that which the creditors have agreed to, or upon cause shown- for instance, in a case of an irregularity-the scheme may be readjusted by the court. The whole thing starts with the creditors and is all dependent on their concurrence and consent.
The most important part is the voluntary liquidation scheme. Whether the creditors would always be safe is questionable, though it would be very convenient for the railway company.

The case referred to certainly illustrates the necessity for this Act. Their Lordships of the Privy Council said that they look upon it as a curious anomaly in our legislation that we did not have applicable to railway companies
a scheme which is applicable to all our other financial institutions.

Section 2 of the Bill gives an idea of its scope. If a railway unfortunately got into debt and some heavy creditor was pressing it, the company may appeal to the court and have a decision satisfactory for the benefit of all the creditors. I think the Bill a very proper one.

The Bill is in the right direction but does not go far enough. There was no better illustration of its necessity than we had in the legislation passed a few years ago in reference to the Kingston and Pembroke Railway. A road goes into the hands of a receiver, but we know that the receiver can do nothing but receive and disburse. He cannot formulate any scheme, or do anything for the extension of business or the promotion of the interests of the road generally. But, under the first section, it is only when the company is unable to do anything else that the directors are to be the moving parties in a matter of this kind. As I said, that is all right so far as it goes, but it seems to me that it ought to go further, to allow some one else to be the moving party in preparing a scheme, and then it should go so far as to allow the court to sell the franchise of the road. Where the court is seized of the whole matter, it should be in a position to adjust the claims of the creditors and, if anything is left, to protect the shareholders.
The Solicitor General says that this is to be done by the consent of the creditors. But I do not see anything in the Bill providing that the consent of the creditors is necesary.

Section 5 provides :
The scheme shall be deemed assented to by the holders of mortgages or bonds, under the authority of the Railway Act

And so on.
But I mean the ordinary creditors of the road.
Probably the hon. gentleman refers to the class covered by section 6 ?
No, they are not the ordinary creditors. They are not provided for.
Look at section 8.
Well, we shall strike it after awhile.
You cannot jumble all classes together, making the Bill unintelligible. There must be a separate provision for every class of creditors.

But I do not see
any provision for getting the consent of

the ordinary creditor ; for instance, the man iwho holds his judgment against the road.

As we go through the clauses, I think the hon. gentleman will find that provision is made for all that it is necessary to provide for.
On section 11,
There is no provision for the ordinary workman, for instance, who has a claim against the road.

The ordinary creditor is not affected hy this Bill. This relates to the mortgage creditors and shareholders. Section 12 provides that the creditors have a right to be heard as against the scheme. But their claims remain.

I think the Solicitor General is mistaken. Section 1 speaks of a ' scheme of arrangement between the company and its creditors.' The word ' creditor ' is used in a general sense, and the ordinary creditor needs to be provided for as well as the others. This Bill ought to apply to the line which, for instance, a man who furnishes material and whose claim has not been paid. He ought to have the opportunity of setting this Act in motion as well as the shareholders.
It is not the shareholder, but the preference creditor.
This gives a general creditor the right to come in and be heard, and this is the first time that this class of creditor has been mentioned.
The creditor has to satisfy the court that he might in some manner or other get his claim, if this arrangement was not carried out, but all the others have to be consenting parties to it.

I think the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Britton) is very "reasonable, whether those who are not consenting are going to be affected by this proceeding, that is to say, when all the special creditors mentioned here eoncur and they agree to wipe out claims for wages, claims for material supplied, &c. That is an idea that naturally suggests itself. My contention is that this scheme of distribution does not affect those claims. Perhaps I may be wrong. I will not ask the committee to dispose of the matter until I have a chance of looking into the matter further.

If you apply the principles of the Insolvent Act to railways, it is simply for the purpose of getting rid of those creditors, there can be no other object. If the Solicitor General intends to look into the subject, he will see that this Bill has that effect.

I would ask the Solicitor General to consider whether it might not be well to incorporate in this Bill proceedings for the sale of the road under certain circumstances. That is something we have not got at present in Canada. Whenever a road is insolvent and a readjustment is necessary, the company has to come before us to be authorized to carry on its undertaking, and we have to make some new legislation ; whereas here we have now a court established for considering the case of an insolvent railway, and why not go one step further and have this court authorized to sell the franchise of an insolvent railway.

As I view it, it would be improper to give to any court the right to dispose of a franchise. That is a matter which is conferred by parliament upon a certain number of individuals, and if the franchise is to pass to other parties it seems to me that parliament must exercise control over that franchise when it passes into other people's hands.
At one o'clock, Committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.

Previous to the adjournment I was called upon to consider the question as to whether or not this Bill would affect creditors who are not specially mentioned therein, or outside creditors. I have had an opportunity of looking at the cases, and I find that there is a formal decision under the corresponding section of the English Act. That is section 18 from which our section 13 is taken verbatim. It is there decided that this section makes the scheme binding Only upon persons assenting to it or bound by it; that is, those who have actually agreed to it, or those, who, not having agreed to it, are declared by the previous sections to be bound ; in other words, the majority and the minority of the various classes whose votes are taken (per Lord Cairns in re Cambrian Railway Company's scheme, 3 ch. 278, p. 296). The question was further discussed afterwards in the case of Stevens vs. Mid-Hants Railway Company, 8 ch. 1064, where it was held that outside creditors and unpaid land-owners are not bound by the scheme.
Is the wording of this section precisely similar to the wording of the English Act ?

If you take our section 13 I will read the English section 18, and you will see that they exactly correspond :
The scheme, when confirmed, shall be enrolled in the court, and thenceforth it shall be binding and effectual to all intents, and the provisions thereof shall, against and in favour of the com-

pany and all persons assenting thereto or hound thereby, have the like effect, as if they had been enacted by parliament.
That is word for word ?
Yes, word for word. This Bill of ours is taken from the Railway Company's Act of 1867, par. 6 to par. 19 inclusive. We take practically these paragraphs and make of them a special Bill.
I take it from the remarks of the lion. Solicitor General this morning that the government have considered the advisability of vesting the Exchequer Court with jurisdiction in these matters ?
Yes, we thought that being a federal court it would be the best court to dispose of matters of this sort which are under the control of the Federal parliament.

The point that I wish to bring to the attention of the hon. Solicitor General is this ; I suppose, under the general Act referring to the Exchequer Court, that if it should be found necessary to have proceedings of this kind, for instance in the district of Montreal, the court, for the purposes of section 12, might sit in Montreal to hear the directors, creditors, shareholders and other persons before confirming the scheme of settlement. I suppose the court would not necessarily have to sit in Ottawa.

The Exchequer Court necessarily would, in connection with a matter of this sort, follow the practice which it has followed heretofore, that is to say, sit in the different provinces for the convenience of the persons interested in the scheme.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following resolutions
1.	That the Governor in Council may from time to time advance and pay to the corporation of the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, in addition to the moneys authorized to be advanced to the said corporation by the Governor in Council by chapter 10 of the statutes of 1896 (first session) and by chapter 47 of the statutes of 1898, such sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of one million dollars, as are required to enable the said corporation to construct such grain elevators and other terminal facilities as are necessary properly to equip the port of Montreal.
2.	No such advance shall be made unless the plans, specifications and estimates for the works to be performed by the said corporation and
on which the money so to be advanced is to be expended have been first submitted to and approved by the Minister of Public Works.
3.	The said corporation shall, upon an advance being made, deposit with the Minister of Finance .and Receiver General debentures of the said corporation equal in par value to the advance so made (which debentures the said corporation are hereby authorized to issue), and such debentures so issued shall be of such amounts as the said Minister of Finance and Receiver General determines, and shall bear date on the day when such advance is made, and shall be repayable within twenty-five years from the date of their issue, and in the meantime shall hear interest at the rate of 3 per centum per annum, such interest to be payable half-yearly, on the 1st day of July and the 1st day of January in each year.
4.	The principal and interest of the sums so to be advanced, as aforesaid, to the said corporation shall be paid by the corporation out of the revenue of the corporation mentioned in section 8 of chapter 10 of the statutes of 1896 (first session), and shall he a charge upon said revenue in the same manner and to the same extent as if the sums so advanced had been borrowed by the corporation under said chapter 10 of the statutes of 1896 (first session).
He said : Mr. Speaker, I think it will be agreed that throughout all the discussions that have taken place in this House on the question of transportation it has been generally admitted that whatever may be said regarding the needs of other ports, it is of the utmost importance that the port of Montreal should be properly equipped. Now, the question has been, What is the best method by which to provide the desired accommodation ? Up to a few months ago it was thought that a business concern commonly known as the Conners syndicate, was to provide accommodation in the way of elevators and other facilities at the port of Montreal, but owing to various causes the promoters of that enterprise failed to obtain the necessary capital. Other schemes were then advanced to serve the same purpose, schemes which involved guarantees and so forth. The conclusion which the government reached was that it is not desirable to grant aid through the hands of private enterprise, but that if these facilities are needed, as we believe them to be, at the port of Montreal, the wisest course would be that the government should grant this aid to the harbour commissioners, who are public trustees, and leave to them the working ont of the necessary details. The Harbour Commissioners of Montreal have already received considerable advances from the Dominion treasury, but it is only right to say that they have promptly paid the interest on these advances, so that, in the case of the loans to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, they are not gifts but loans on which they have paid a fair rate of interest. In 1896 we advanced to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal 82.000,000. partly in renewal of old loans and partly for improvements. In 1898 pro-

vision was made for a further advance to the harbour commissioners, and schemes have been outlined for the construction of tiie piers and so forth in that port which will ultimately take up the amount so authorized, $2,000,000, so that for the purposes of elevators, which Is the particular object in view now, it is necessary to make a further and special provision. We have therefore determined to ask the consent of parliament to a further appropriation from time to time, not exceeding $1,000,000, to be furnished as may be required to the harbour commissioners for the purpose of providing elevators and such other terminal facilities as in their judgment may be deemed necessary for the equipment of the port. I think I would be correct in saying that the general feeling of the House will be that if money is to be advanced for securing proper harbour facilities it will be best advanced through the medium of the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, who may be relied upon, both from their local interest and pride, to see that these funds are administered for the good of the port.
What are the other terminal facilities ?

The expression is put in rather that the harbour commissioners will not find themselves restricted. The great purpose of the grant is for the building of elevators, but incidentally there may be found something else which will require to be done. We have not desired to restrict the harbour commissioners too closely, although the money is granted for the purpose of erecting elevators.
What is the indebtedness of the harbour commissioners now ?
The indebtedness of the harbour commissioners is $2,000,000 now, on which they have paid interest up to date.

Some of the leading newspapers in Montreal have lately been advising very strongly that the harbour commissioners should refuse to pay any further interest upon the advances which have been made to them as they were entitled to these as gifts, and in view of this, I think we may consider this question in the light of a gift.
That is a very dangerous admission. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) ought not to admit that.
Some time ago it was stated that Mr. Clergue made an offer for building these elevators and that another company-I forget the name-also made an offer.

I do not recollect Mr. Clergue's scheme. There was a proposal made to the Harbour Commissiou-Mr. FIELDING.
ers of Montreal, but we came to the conclusion that it wg.s not desirable to wait for private enterprise any longer but to have this grant made to the commissioners, because time is passing and in the delay of private enterprise we are suffering a delay which may be very dangerous to the business of the St. Lawrence.
WTill this grant be placed in the hands of the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal to be spent in any direction they please, or is it simply for the purpose of building elevators ?

Of course, the whole sum is not at once placed in the hands of the harbour commissioners. This is an authority for the government to advance the Montreal Harbour Commissioners such amounts as may be deemed proper for the purpose, not exceeding $1,000,000. The principal purpose is for elevators, although the expression ' other 'terminal facilities ' is also used. The plans and specifications of the proposed works must be submitted to the hon. Minister of Public Works and have his approval.
ilr. BROCK. Is there any expert evidence before the government that such elevators as they are going to build in Montreal will be in the interest of transportation generally, or is it specially in the interest of the city of Montreal that this advance is to be made ? I think that the country at large, which is granting this money, expects that there should be something before the government to show that the money expended in Montreal is for the general advantage of the country. We have heard a good deal said about the port of Quebec. The question is a very large one and It is desirable that some expert engineering evidence should be before the government and before the country when this large sum of $1,000,000 is being advanced, so that it will not be found afterwards that this money has been completely wasted and that some other port will be a more desirable port. We know very well that the Grand Trunk Railway Company are diverting a large portion of their trade from the port of Montreal to Portland. If it can be shown that the establishing of a harbour at Portland will place the farmers and other producers of this country in closer touch with Liverpool at a lower rate of freight, I think it is well for us to consider before spending such a large sum of money in Montreal if it is going to have the effect which it is expected it will have. I fear myself that it will be found before many years that a cheaper means of getting the freight out of the country will be found and if that is the case we will look back with regret at this large sum of money which is being spent in Montreal without having sufficient evidence before us to show that this is the best port available.
512]

The government are not giving any sum of money to the port of Montreal-not one cent. The government are advancing money to the harbour commissioners on bonds that are given us and upon which the interest has been faithfully paid in the past, as I have no doubt it will be in the future. The debt of the harbour of Montreal, according to the last report dated the 10th of July, 1900, was $3,822,000. It Is a little more now; it is, in round numbers, $4,000,000, with an average interest payment of 3J per cent. As I said, every dollar of the interest has been paid so far and in that same year there was a surplus of $52,927. In other words, the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal are perfectly prepared to meet all their obligations. The amount of money that we had power to advance them in 1898 and 1899 is all engaged in the works that are now being carried out.
That is the last $2,000,000 vote ?

Yes. The whole amount is engaged in the works that are now being carried out. The House will perhaps remember that in 1899, before I left for the other side on account of illness, the sum of $500,000 had been placed in the estimates of the Department of Public Works to build an elevator in Montreal. The item was struck out after 1 left Ottawa. My colleagues explained to me that difficulties had arisen and that they had made up their minds that it would be better not to go on with that policy. Then, the Conners syndicate came along and made the offer that the House knows of. The big American railway companies immediately started a powerful opposition against the Conners syndicate to prevent the American capitalists who are associated with Mr. Conners from getting the money he required to carry out the undertaking. A few months ago Mr. Conners notified the harbour commissioners that he had failed, that he could not possibly raise the money that he expected to raise. Then several offers were made, and Mr. Booth made an offer. The Montreal Board of Trade, the Chamber of Commerce, and the harbour commissioners considered very seriously the question as to what was the best thing to do. The Montreal Board of Trade were unanimously of the opinion that the time had come when the government should build these elevators, or advance the money to build them. In other words, they pronounced themselves very strongly in favour of public ownership. I may say that I altogether share their views. The government of Canada own the canals. It seems to me that we should be the masters of our terminals. The Montreal Harbour Commissioners are only trustees for the government : they are the trustees for the country. They will have full control of the rates to be charged at these 161
elevators as they have control of the rates charged in the harbour itself.
After a good deal of consideration and negotiation, we came to the conclusion, as the Minister of Finance stated, that it was better to advance one million dollars to the harbour commissioners to help them to build an elevator, warehouse, etc., and to complete, so far as that amount can, the harbour accommodation. The ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Haggart) asked what it was intended to do with that money. The primary object is to build elevators. I may say that in my opinion a big warehouse should also be erected. It will be also necessary to have these works equipped with railway tracks, and so on ; and permanent sheds will have to be erected and supplied with every modern improvement, so as to allow the freight to be handled cheaply. The hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) alluded to the fact that the Grand Trunk Railway seemed to have finally settled in Portland. What reason did they publicly give for their action in that respect ? The Grand Trunk Railway authorities stated that they would not have followed that policy if the port of Montreal had been properly equipped, and in that I believe them. The port of Montreal was not equipped, and it is not equipped to-day, to handle the large trade that the Grand Trunk Railway was carrying to it daily. The Grand Trunk Railway used to have hundreds and hundreds of cars waiting for the freight to be handled, and as they could not put up with that they moved elsewhere. I may also say that the Grand Trunk Railway Company complained very bitterly that the municipal authorities did not deal liberally with them. Every one who views the matter from the standpoint of handling trade and commerce cannot fail to realize that not a single one of our Canadian ports is equipped as it should be. The port of Montreal is not equipped as it should be ; the port of Quebec is not equipped as it should be; the port of St. John, although not badly equipped, is nuc equipped as it should be ; Halifax has not what it should have, and the ports on the great lakes have not what they should have. I say that the whole thing has to be overhauled.
What does Halifax want ?
Well, I hope we will have in a short time a fast line of steamers.
To Sydney ?

I was saying that the whole St. Lawrence route, from the upper lakes down, would have to he equipped and overhauled. A good deal has been said about the different advantages of the port of Quebec and the | port of Montreal, and so on. For me, that



3s not the question. Those ports have each their natural advantages, and their natural 'difficulties. The port of Quebec is 160 miles further down than the port of Montreal, but, on the other hand, it has magnificent natural facilities. I have no doubt whatever that in the near future the larger ships will not come to Montreal, but will stop at Quebec.
Hear, hear.

All the same, the import trade that will stop at Quebec will have to come by the St. Lawrence route to Montreal as the final distributing point, and most of the western trade from the lakes will come to the port of Montreal, to be transhipped for the ocean voyage. If it were not a sure thing that the port of Montreal will be equipped as it ought to be, then Buffalo and the other American ports would get the trade which is in store for us. We have been, perhaps, a little too slow, although we must not complain. This young nation has done great things. We have spent millions and millions of money to build railways ; we are beginning to get our ports in order. Recrimination is no good in our days ; we must view the future and the future alone, and we must put our heads together without political distinctions, because there is no party politics in these broad questions. We must put our heads together to try and make the St. Lawrence route the best. It is the shortest route, and we have only to exert ourselves to make it the best.
In the summer time, you mean ?

Of course. The port of Montreal was closed last year only four months and twenty-five days. It is too often said that the port of Montreal is an ice-bound port. I feel that I am on safe grounds in saying that the port of Montreal is open about seven months in the year, and during these seven months it is at the head of ocean navigation and at the foot of the great lakes, which are the reservoirs of forty million tons of freight each year. I feel that when the port of Montreal is equipped as we are equipping it now ; when the St. Lawrence route is dredged and widened as it will be within a couple of years ; when my hon. and distinguished friend, the Minister of Marine (Sir Louis Davies) will have made the improvements that the trade requires ; I believe that then the St. Lawrence route will be one of the best Commercial routes in the world. Some little accidents happen. A day or two ago a ship grounded through the chain of her rudder breaking, but that was an accident over which the government had no control. The Tiverton grounded at Contrecoeur. She was drawing 18 feet of water, and there were 38 feet of water in the channel that day. The pilot had evidently lost his head, if he had ever a sound head on his shoulders, and he grounded the boat in full daylight. We cannot help such things happening.
You are to blame for having such pilots.

I am very glad my hon. friend interposed that remark. I quite agree with him. I have followed all the inquiries into accidents from 1896 to 1898, and I am sorry to say that in nearly every case it was found that the pilot was responsible. That state of affairs has to be put an end to. and without any delay.
Hear, hear.
I have no hesitation in saying, that, speaking for myself, and I am sure for all my colleagues, we have no desire that that state of affairs shall continue any longer.
Hear. hear.

There are able pilots, but there are pilots that are not able. Let the able pilots stand on their own merits, but let the bad pilots be dispensed with. In other words, in my humble opinion, free pilotage should be the order of the day.
Hear, hear.
Stick to it.
It seeems to me that in matters of trade like this, we should have no hesitation to apply a radical remedy where it is clear that there is a radical evil.

I wish to ask the minister a few questions. What is the capacity of the Canadian Pacific Railway elevators which load direct into the ships in Montreal ; what quantity of grain was handled to these two elevators last year ; will the proposed elevators be erected near the Canadian Pacific Railway elevators ?

Oh, no. The Canadian Pacific Railway elevators, if I am well informed, handled last year five or six million bushels of grain. Of course, I do not know the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's plans very well, but I know that they have made up their minds to handle a great deal more grain in Montreal, and they will have to have more elevators. The elevators that are intended to be built are not in that locality at all.
How far away are they?
Not very far. The Canadian Pacific ele-

vators are located on the shore wharf, where there is a pretty strong current. The other elevators will be erected in the centre of the harbour in still water. 1 am not authorized to speak for the harbour commission. All I know is that I have been asked to approve of an enlargement there so as to allow of the erection of an elevator. There are three large wharfs to be erected in the centre. One is completed, another will be completed in a few weeks, and the third the next season; and there will also be three large basins. The Montreal Board of Trade insist very strongly that two elevators should be built to serve the trade that will take place in these basins and on these wharfs. In other words, these elevators will serve the same purpose that is served by the elevators at Portland. Big ships will come to the wharfs, load and unload produce, cattle or anything else, and at the same time the grain in the elevators will be loaded into the whole of the ships. The whole operation will be done simultaneously, as on every well equipped wharf. The question is whether two elevators are immediately necessary in the centre of the harbour, because we must not lose sight of the fact that we shall have to deal to a very large extent with all-water trade. I am sure that ships will come down by the canals in greater numbers than hitherto.
What will be the capacity of these elevators ?

The plans have not yet been decided upon. Perhaps a million bushels.
