I cannot say as to that, because the whole thing will be under the contrpl of the harbour commissioners, subject of course to my approval and the approval of my colleagues, because I take pride in submitting all such questions to my colleagues; I think it is my duty to do so. As to the exact location of these elevators, I am not prepared to say. A large warehouse is also to be provided, because we must not forget that the grain trade is not the only one we shall receive from the lakes. A great deal of flour, molasses, sugar and package freight will be handled in the ports of Montreal and Quebec. Mr. Booth handles to-day a large quantity of package freight between Philadelphia, Buffalo, New York and western ports. What we have done on a smaller scale in the past will be done in the future on a larger scale, when we are better equipped-when. Port Col'borne, Parry Sound, Collingwood, Goderich and all the other ports on the lakes are better equipped. I have confidence in every port on the Georgian Bay and the lakes. Each one will be a gatherer of trade, and what we have to do is to supply means for handling that trade by the St. Lawrence route. I see that my hon. friend from Toronto is getting anxious
about Toronto itself. He wants me to speak of Toronto.
Certainly; always glad to hear you.

I have no objection to say that, in my opinion, no scheme should be discarded without being considered carefully. I have given my best attention, and I am going to give more attention in the future, to that air line project which has been often suggested in the House. If it is the shortest route, it will become one of the best; there is no doubt about that. Two and two make four, and when a route is the shortest and the best, the trade has to flow there. But of course this is a question at which any man who does not want to commit himself without knowing should look carefully. I know that the Grand Trunk people have settled in Portland; but I am glad to say that they have intimated to me and to some of my colleagues that when the port of Montreal is fully equipped, they will take down the St. Lawrence route as much trade perhaps as we can handle. I am not going to speak of plans which some gentlemen may have in their minds. The Department of Railways and Canals have plans which have been submitted to them for the further improvement of the port of Montreal. These are not before the House at the present time; but I feel that tiie port of Montreal, being at the foot of the lakes and at the head of navigation, will always be the most important distributing point in Canada. Am I unfair to any other port in speaking as I do ? Decidedly not. I know that Quebec will have a large share; we all hope it will. The larger the ships will grow, the more trade Quebec will have. Quebec has that great advantage of being open to navigation longer in the year than the port of Montreal. We Montrealers are well-wishers of the port of Quebec. Speaking for myself, nobody has lived happier years than I have in Quebec. I have kept an affectionate souvenir of that fine old capital, and there is no one more anxious than I am to do for Quebec everything in my power. Nature has done a great deal for Quebec. It is one of the most magnificent ports in the world.
Where is the Grand Trunk at present bringing its grain from to Montreal ? And where does the Grand Trunk carry it to from Montreal ?

The Grand Trunk is still sending some grain to Montreal from American ports. Midland has become one of the important gathering points of the Grand Trunk system; but it is well known that the Grand Trunk Railway is sending more and more of its freight to Portland, for the excellent reason that it can handle its freight there

cheaper than in Montreal, because Montreal Is not equipped as it should be.
I would like to compel the Grand Trunk Railway, not by force, except by the force of low rates, to come back to Montreal, and I have no doubt that if Montreal be well equipped, if the St. Lawrence route, which is the shortest, is also made the best, the Grand Trunk Railway will have to come back to that route. Railway companies are not actuated by sentiment, but by their own interests.
Will the hon. gentleman permit me to put him a question V Is the Grand Trunk Railway carrying more grain from Montreal to Portland than it did before it acquired the Drummond County Railway ?
This has not the slightest bearing on the question. The piece of railway that the Grand Trunk Railway then acquired is still owned by the company.
But the traffic that used to go over that road is now going to Portland.

It is not in the same direction at all. The Grand Trunk Railway has been for years using its road between Quebec and Montreal as a local road, and as nothing else, and the question the hon. gentleman has put has no bearing at all on the point. My hon. friend from Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) has asked me what I mean by free pilotage. I mean that every navigation company should be free to choose its own pilots. There is now in force a system of what is called le tour de role. In other words, when a pilot has made thirty trips, though he may be the best pilot in the world, he is not allowed by the rules of his corporation to make any more.
That is between Quebec and Montreal ?

Yes, I am not speaking of below Quebec, because there is a different pilotage corporation governing that route altogether. The pilots between Quebec and Montreal pool their receipts, and each one enjoys an equal share; and under the rules of their corporation, no one pilot can make more than thirty trips in one season. That is a dangerous policy to which this country cannot submit any longer. The navigation companies must be given the right to choose the pilots they want. In that respect it is that I use the term ' free pilotage.' I hope also that in the near future we -will have a dis-tinot tribunal to judge the pilots, although my hon. friend has already taken a step in the right direction in appointing a pilot commissioner. It is to my certain knowledge that in the past, pilots who were guilty of the greatest negligence, found a means of Mr. TARTE.
escaping punishment. That state of affairs must cease. The interests connected with this matter are so large that no petty question of English or French Canadian must be allowed to have any weight. I am in favour of having pilotage open to the world, so that every competent man, no matter where he comes from, may become a pilot.
Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the resolution.

The hon. Minister of Public Works has explained the basis upon which he is asking for this appropriation, but the question I put him was not as to the desirability of making a large appropriation, but as to whether the government had sufficient technical knowledge to say that this will be sufficient for all purposes, or whether it is merely the insertion of the small end of the wedge, and that in two years hence we shall be called on to contribute another large appropriation.
We know how appropriations have been voted for canals in times past. When the Trent canal was about to be built, we were never told that it would cost what it did. The first vote was for $1,000,000, but that vote was merely a small instalment of the [DOT]entire cost.
This vote which is now asked for the harbour of Montreal is no doubt intended for the benefit of the whole country, but we have nothing to show that ultimately the policy we are adopting will prove the proper one. We have no means of knowing whether other railways may not find the port of Portland the one to which they had better ship their freight if they want to control the business. I am quite satisfied that each of the ports of Quebec, Montreal and Halifax has its merits. For the last ten years I have been importing millions of dollars worth of goods, and I do not allow one pound of freight I import to come into Toronto over an American road, and I find that 1 am able to compete with those who bring in their goods through American ports. But when I am shipping goods to the English market, where they have to compete with American goods, I must send them by such a route that they will he able to compete in the matter of price.
There are two questions to be considered in this connection. One is the question of imports and the other of exports. On the question of exporting goods, we should have a little better information than we have at present. To go on voting millions upon millions will not make Montreal or any other inland port an all the year round port. Business in this country is conducted in such a way by banking and shipping interests that merchants want to draw continually against the goods they are shipping anil cannot keep these goods locked up six months of the year. It is the duty of the government to have a fixed plan laid before the country, and that plan they would as-

certain if tliey would appoint a commission as suggested by my bon. friend from Jacques Cartier, which would furnish us with expert evidence, so that we would not merely have the dictum of a minister, who asks us to vote a million dollars in order to equip a certain port, which may equip that port, as far as the minister knows, for the present, but which equipment would be utterly inadequate three years hence. We should have more information than we appear to have at present to justify our inserting the small end of the wedge, when it may afterwards be found that cattle and other products could be carried past Montreal to Quebec, by an extra line of railway, probably, the building of which would not cost anything like what we may have to expend if we are to keep continually adding to the equipment of the port of Montreal. It may appear that I am speaking against Montreal, but in reality I am not doing so. On the contrary, I am anxious to make Montreal a great city, and I think we can do so without making it a great exporting centre. The city of Quebec we should assist at present in every way possible ; and if we were to spend a few million dollars in the construction of a railway, we might make of that city a winter port. If that be the case, this enormous expense for the purpose of making Montreal harbour suitable for large vessels could be done away with, and it would still remain a great distributing point. If the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Finance will go on from year to year appropriating millions of dollars for the benefit of the harbour commissioners of Montreal, these gentlemen will no doubt honestly expend the money, but I fear it will not be expended with good judgment unless we have more information than we have now regarding the general transportation needs of the whole country.

The committee perfectly appreciate the motives which have prompted the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) to ask the question he has just put to the hon. Minister of Public Works. It has always seemed to me, since I have had a seat in this House, that on this transportation question we have not that technical information to which my hon. friend referred. It was under that impression that I urged-and, I think, with some degree of justice-that we should imitate the American government and have a commission appointed to investigate continuously the whole question. The hon. member for Maisonneuve and for Terrebonne (Mr. Prefontaine) took exception to my remarks in that regard, considering them as a reflection upon the Montreal Harbour Commissioners, which was never intended in any degree. But I maintained that the commissioners of any one port, particularly gentlemen as busy as these gentlemen, cannot have the necessary qualifications to deal thoroughly with such
an immense question as that of transportation viewed from the different points from which it is necessary to view it. And so I claimed, as I still claim, that, under our present system, the Minister of Public Works, having sources of information on which no one body possesses, can best consider the pros and cons of the transportation question. But, in view of the remarks of my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock), I think we have enough information to convince us that we must provide additional facilities at Montreal. We have spent immense sums upon the canals ; and information which comes from all sides shows us that immense quantities of grain would be brought to Montreal if we had there even the most elementary facilities for handling it. In my discussion of the matter I showed the immense difference in the facilities at Montreal and another port, Buffalo or Duluth for handling grain, and how simple and unavailing were the facilities we had in Montreal. We are not absolutely paying out tile country's money for the purpose of providing the facilities required ; but rather making advances. And the advances which have been made to the port of Montreal in the past have been so treated that we should not be discouraged from making the advances now contemplated. I think we must gradually accustom ourselves to look upon expenditures of this kind and upon the whole transportation question from a high standpoint rather than from the point of view of any local interest. For my part, I quite agree with the Minister of Public Works, having managed to rid myself of the spell under which we were on our visit to Quebec owing to the extreme kind treatment which we received there. Before I went to Quebec I had the opinion that I now have, that it is absolutely certain that Quebec will become a very important port and that it will fulfil many wants which it is impossible for Montreal to meet at present. But what has happened in the case of the Grand Trunk Railway and the port of Portland is an intimation that we must do something ; and the first step, it seems to me, is to provide Montreal with improvements in the shape of elevators. And in this connection I would ask the Minister of Public Works if it has been possible for him to secure information as to what should be done-for that is as essential as the improvements at Montreal- at the port of distribution on the great lakes. Has the hon. minister-and this is the part of the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Brock's) question in which I join-has the hon. minister any comprehensive scheme in connection with the improvements of Montreal, which improvements, I agree, are necessary ?

I quite understand the point of view which my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) takes. As a sound business man he wants to know on what

plans we are working. Well, during the last five years the plans on which we are working have been discussed by the board of trade, by the harbour commissioners, by the railway corporations, by the navigation companies. Plans were prepared fifteen or sixteen years ago. When X took office I thought-I do not mean to put forward my own personal opinion except as it was formed after having taken the advice of competent men-that these plans should not be carried out. They provided for narrow and long wharfs and narrow basins. Those who know the port of Montreal will remember that there is a pier which is called the Guard Tier, which was erected to form a still basin and protect the port from the rapid waters of the lake. In my humble opinion, if the plans formerly prepared had been carried out the port of Montreal would have been altogether spoiled. 1 consulted engineers and gave my best attention to that important question. I have travelled a good deal keeping this matter in view. The harbour commissioners themselves made a tour of American ports. Finally, we came to the conclusion that the present plan was the best that could be adopted. We are carrying out that plan. I think that when the works are completed the port of Montreal will he one of the best-equipped on this continent. My hon. friend asks if we are sure that this is the last time we shall apply to parliament. I am not going to say that I am quite sure, hut I am convinced that it is about the last call that we shall make. Still, the trade of this country is developing to such an extent that nobody can tell. If we have dozens and dozens of big ships coming to Montreal, if we have hundreds of barges taking down grain and package freight to the port of Montreal by the St. Lawrence route, we shall need more accommodation and parliament will be obliged to provide that accommodation. We cannot tell where this country is going to stop. I hope before we die we will see in this country a population of 10,000.000 or 12,000.000. When we have that population we will necessarily have more trade, and we will have to equip our harbours and rivers in a more thorough manner. Let my hon. friend who speaks of the expenditure remember that we are at the end of it. When the harbour commissioners took charge of the St. Lawrence between Quebec and Montreal, there were only 11 feet of water in Lake St. Peter ; now we have 27 feet and a half, and within two years we will have 30 feet. The St. Lawrence has been deepened 271 feet its whole length. Last year my department dredged ten miles and a half to a depth of about thirty feet and a width of 450 feet. We are completing our route. Would we be jsutified in now folding our arms ? We are completing our work, in my opinion a most necessary work. There will always be big ships coming to the port of Montreal. Perhaps the giants Mr. TARTE.
of the sea will have to stop at Quebec, the 15,000-ton ships will stop at Quebec ; but the 8,000 and 10,000-ton ships will always go as far as they can inland. That is the law of trade, my hon. friend knows it as well as I do, because he is an able business man. We are now contemplating the idea of opening a great national highway from Montreal to the lakes by the Ottawa and the French river. The tendency of trade is to go deeper and deeper inland. Montreal, therefore, will always remain a most important trading port.
Now, my hoh. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has asked me a very proper question, he wants to know what we are doing on the upper lakes. We had a debate on that subject a few nights ago, I am sorry he was not here. Both the Department of Public Works and the Department of Railways and Canals are carrying out important works at Port Colborne. Port Colborne had not even a harbour, and how could our canal system expect to compete with American ports when we have not even a place where a ship could throw anchor ? It was out of the question. But we have so many things to do we cannot do them all at once. I do not blame anybody for that, as we have been going on most successfully indeed. At Port Colborne the Department of Public Works has awarded a contract to Messrs. Morgan & Macdonald; the hon. member for Jacques Cartier knows them, they live in Montreal. That work will be about 5,000 feet long. We have awarded only part of the contract, because parliament has not voted all the money. The first part of the work that has been awarded will be far advanced this coming fall, but it will not be completed. I expect the whole breakwater will be completed by the end of next season. The Department of Railways and Canals are deepening the entrance to the Welland canal. They are also contemplating the erection of two piers adjoining the canal. I am told my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals has brought down the plan. There will he two piers on which terminal facilities will have to be erected. At this moment a large American company is trying to arrange to take down trade through the St. Lawrence route and the Welland canal. They have not yet made up their minds how much trade they will take to Montreal or to Quebec ; but Mr. Wolvin, whose name Is well known, has made an offer to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, and negotiations are going on between them. His view would be to use large freight carriers on the lakes to take cargoes of grain and package freight to Port Colborne, there to tranship it into smaller barges, barges with a capacity say of 250,000 bushels, and take this freight to Montreal or Quebec, or Three Rivers. I suppose they cannot make up their minds

as to which port they will go, it will depend on the advantages that will be offered to them. The question will then be between the water bound interests on the lakes and the water bound and railway interests, in other words, between the St. Lawrence route and the American route. Here is Buffalo at the right hand of the Erie canal, and here is Port Colborne twenty miles away. Prom Buffalo grain has to he carried by rail to American ports. Now, from Port Colborne grain and package freight and trade in general will have to be carried by water. Let us not forget that there are only about seventy miles of canals from Port Colborne on the St. Lawrence route, the balance of the route being fine open lake navigation. Now, these American and Canadian capitalists believe that they can carry a cargo of grain much cheaper from Duluth, from Chicago, from Milwaukee to Liverpool by the St. Lawrence route, a water route all through, than they can carry it by the American routes. They make a vast difference in the cost of freight between the two routes.
Of course, to have low rates we must have accommodation, we must have the best possible handling facilities. In Montreal, up to a year or two ago, and even to-day, we have not such facilities. Those who have visited ports both in the United States and in Europe know that Montreal is not in it in that respect. Not one of our Canadian harbours is able to compete with the United States from the modern standpoint. We have not the modern equipments. The most important part of the work, however, is done, we have laid the foundation, we have now only to crown our work ; and it is with that object in view that we are asking parliament to advance, not to give, $1,000,000, on which interest will be faithfully paid, to complete one or two elevators, one large warehouse, to lay down tracks for the accommodation of trade in Montreal. At present a great deal of freight in the port of Montreal has to be moved by hand at a great cost. It is indeed marvellous that we have been able to do as well as we have, with our imperfect means of handling freight. Our natural advantages must be immense to have enabled us to compete with American routes even to the extent we have done. Let me say that when I speak of the St. Lawrence route I speak of it as a whole. I applaud with both hands the national and patriotic statement made a minute ago by the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock). He is a great importer of trade, and it is cheerful to hear a man of his standing say in the House that he does not allow a pound of his trade to pass through American channels. Let us be a nation, let us be Canadians before everything else, and it is with that object in view that I would not hesitate to spend a
large sum of money to make of this Canadian nation, a nation independent of our American neighbours. We are on good terms with them, but we are on better terms with ourselves. St. John, Halifax- all these harbours should be equipped and everything that parliament has in its power to do to make of St. John and Halifax winter ports, so that we may have winter ports of our own, should be done without any hesitation whatever. I do not like to spend money uselessly. I believe I am a fairly sound business man in that regard. I do not like to waste money, hut I like to have money spent in developing the trade of this young and enterprising nation. I may be a little enthusiastic over the S1. Lawrence route. I feel at times that I am a little bit crazy over it; I dream abut it, but I think a public man may have worse dreams than to dream of advancing the natural advantages of this country.

I agree with every word uttered by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I think if there is one feature more than another in the outline of the undertaking of the hon. Minister of Public Works, it is that one particularly mentioned by the hon. member, that it has not been carried out upon a comprehensive and intelligent plan. I think there is no doubt whatever that all these ports are valuable, but there must be in the future some of them that will be winter ports and some of them summer ports only, some that will be suitable for boats drawing a great depth of water and others suitable for boats of light draft. We have Halifax, St. John, Quebec and Montreal. We have been trying to build up a trade at the port of St. John lately, but the result is that the trade during this last winter, as compared with last year, has fallen off about one-third. What is the reason of that ? Is it because the Grand Trunk Railway are taking the trade to Portland ?
The Grand Trunk never sent a pound of freight to a Canadian winter port. St. John has never received a pound of freight from the Grand Trunk.
The Canadian Pacific Railway has ?
Yes.

At any rate there is some cause for it. Is it for want of proper accommodation to handle the trade, or, is it on account of the distance that the trade must be drawn before it reaches the winter port ? There must be some cause, and it seems to me that if we were able to get that information by a commission it is very desirable that we should have a commission appointed independent of all these ports so that it might be in a position

to make comparisons as to the relative merits of these different ports and report the results to parliament. My own opinion has been for a good while that the head of ocean navigation will he Quebec. I entertain that belief on the ground that it is closer to ocean navigation than Montreal, and that it has a greater depth of water, and that the influence of the tide is felt there. If the trial which the government propose to make during the coming season by putting on a boat to ascertain whether winter navigation is practicable in the St. Lawrence, proves successful, Quebec will afford ocean navigation the year round. If that be the case, then it is the most Important jjort in Canada to-day, because it brings ocean navigation so much farther west than any other port we have while affording a sufficient depth of water to ensure a safe passage to the very largest ships that traverse the ocean. That is why I think it may be a valuable port. I think It will be a valuable port because it will be found in the future to be a port for twelve months In the year, a port that makes shorter railway hauls than the port of St. John, or Halifax, or Portland. If that be the case it seems to me It is a very important port, but notwithstanding all that, Montreal will always also be a very valuable port. Iu saying what I have It is not for the purpose of opposing the proposal which the lion. Minister of Public Works is making, because, In my judgment, there cannot be too many facilities for handling the trade of the country. Until we have better facilities for handling the trade it will go to other ports, whether to Portland or elsewhere, wherever these facilities are provided. As to whether this sum will complete the work or not, I have not the slightest hesitation in saying that instead of $1,000,000, it will require from $4,000,000 to $7,000,000 before it is completed. To me It appears doubtful whether we will ever be able to get a sufficient depth of water between Montreal and Quebec for the largest vessels. I think that with the ice in the winter and the Ailing in of the channel in the summer
It does not fill in at all.

Well, whether it is In the depth, or the width of the channel, or the danger of rocks falling down from the side, there is something that will prevent it from being navigable for vessels drawing the greatest depth of water, and with the trend towards larger vessels this will be a disadvantage. The celebrated engineer, Mr. Sawyer, who spoke to us the other day, said that in his judgment we had reached the maximum of the size in vessels, but there are a great many who disagree with him because they are building larger and larger vessels all the time, and they believe that the same increase in size will go on in the future Mr. SPROULE.
as has gone on in the past. That will bring us very close to the time when we require 30 foot navigation and perhaps even more for the use of these large vessels. I do not think that the channel to Montreal is likely to afford that depth of water.
We have it now.
Hear, hear.

If we do not encourage them they might be obliged some day to do, perhaps, what the Grand Trunk Railway has done. I know from my personal knowledge, that the Canadian Pacific Railway would be in a position to make advantageous arrangements to-day at Boston, and even at Portland. I am sure they do not contemplate anything of the kind. But, Canadian public men. and this Canadian parliament, must not lose sight of this natural fact: That if we want to do the export trade by our winter ports we must take the necessary means to do so. So much for our winter ports. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has paid a good deal of attention to the transportation question, but I am afraid he loses sight of the facts to a pretty large extent. The navigation between Montreal and Quebec is not dangerous. There may be some little accidents, but there cannot possibly be any serious wreck. A ship may ground, but she cannot be lost. The navigation between Belle Isle and Quebec is the great trouble, and the greatest part of the marine losses have always been on that part of the route.
I understand that in some place between Belle Isle and Quebec the navigation is not deeper than on Lake St. Peter, and I have never been able to get assured on that point.

There is nothing of the kind. There is abundance of water. At Crane Island there
is a little 'spot of about 1,500 feet that has to be dredged, but that is a question of detail. The trouble is that there is a fog at times, but there is also fog on the American routes. I have travelled enough to be often caught in a fog going by an American route. But, with the improvements on the St. Lawrence route that are in sight ; with an improved system of fog-signals, of dredging, lighthouses and beacons, that route between Belle Isle and Quebec can be made, and will be made, a great deal safer than it has ever been in the past. In the supplementary estimates, my hon. friends will find a pretty large amount of money to complete-perhaps not to complete, but to improve our system of fog-signals and lighthouses. I am asking this year a pretty large amount of money-
Hear, hear.
A pretty large amount of money, but not too much, to build powerful dredges.
Hear, hear.

The entrance at St. John harbour has to be dredged. At low tide there is only 18 feet there now, and there is no sense in that. In the maritime provinces there is also a large quantity of dredging to be carried out. Within two or three years after we get these powerful dredges we can create a kind of commercial revolution on the great lakes. When the Canadian people once get started, they go at a pretty high 'speed of progress and development.

May I be permitted to call attention to the fact that this debate is only partial in its scope. I have great hopes in all that has been said, and I cheerfully vote for this, or for any other sum that may be necessary to make the St. Lawrence route a good route. Perhaps we may have to spend money in order to get information. A nation has to spend money to get information as well as an individual, and that information may not be all that we may desire. There is one thing certain, and that is, that the conditions at present existing, both at Montreal and Quebec. are not such as to make for the betterment of the transportation question. I vote for this appropriation because it will tend to bring about that which must come ultimately in Canada. All the ports named on the whole St. Lawrence route, including Montreal and Quebec, must be ultimately the collecting points for the sea-shore ports in Nova Scotia.
Oh.

I admit that if it can be shown that Quebec is navigable during the whole year, the transportation question from that side will be solved ; because you can bring by rail to Quebec the wheat and other products cheaper than you can bring

them to the lower provinces. But having a strong doubt on that point, I think we should bear in mind that all these expenditures are summer expenditures and somewhat tentative of what must in the end come. I am sure the lucid explanations given by the Minister of Public Works, indicating a clear understanding of the question, and the broad views he has enunciated, whatever may be the feeling of hon. gentlemen as to his political views, must commend themselves to every Canadian.
These are my political views.

They could not be otherwise, believing as the hon. minister does politically. Of course, where nature is lavish, art has to do less. So far as Montreal is concerned, if shipments can be made to Montreal with larger ships, as the hon. minister hopes, then Montreal has the advantage that the expenditure of carrying by rail to Montreal will not be as great as Quebec ; but, on the other hand, there are the difficulties which I have pointed out, and we have always to bear in mind the question of the ultimate result. There is Nova Scotia, the vestibule of the Dominion, with the ocean always open, with ports like Halifax, Country Harbour, Whitehead, the Straits of Canso, Louisburg, Sydney, and other harbours which I have not mentioned at all. Going around the coast of Nova Scotia, at every ten miles you will come to harbours which would be considered in the less favoured parts of the world, like Ontario and Quebec, as magnificent harbours, and they are never mentioned at all.
Yes, and a lot of suckers in them, too.

Not a sucker in them. Suckers are fresh water fish ; they are never found in the sea. They are mud fish, found up in the lakes and the small streams of Ontario. Salmon, and cod, and mackerel, nice large trout, and sportive -whales, you find in the ocean ; but turtles, suckers, and flat fish you get inland.
And eels.

Yes, and eels of the most slippery character. My firm conviction is that we must turn our attention to transportation by land, and in some way make it cheap and effective. Our railways must in some way, by means of larger locomotives, a better road-bed, or other facilities, be enabled to do the work quicker and cheaper than they do it now. In a country like Canada, with the St. Lawrence frozen for a part of the year, we shall always be subject to difficulties which our neighbours to the south of us are free from. Their ports are open all the year, and they have to use their railways a good deal more than we do. The Mississippi and Missouri form a mightier avenue than the St. Lawrence ; but some-Mr. FRASER.
how or other it is a wonderful fact that they do not carry one-tenth of the trade in proportion to population that the St. Lawrence does. As to these expenditures, I am for them with all my heart. I believe that expenditures on transportation, though lavish, if wisely and honestly expended, are the best investments Canada can make. We need not be afraid of such expenditures. Why, I see that some of the small nations in Europe are almost doubling their expenditures in building ships, preparing for war, and that sort of thing. If we in Canada understand the value and extent of the wealth we have, we shall not stint our expenditures. We will lay our foundations deep on the broadest and most liberal grounds, to serve, not simply the trade of to-day, but the trade of a quarter of a century afterwards, that those who come after us may have the advantage. I was struck with a remark made by the hon. minister to the effect that the plans of sixteen years ago, if they had been followed, would have ruined the harbour. Let us not forget that the same thing may happen sixteen years hence if we are small in our plans and ideas to-day. With regard to large ships, I see there is a ship now being built in England of 18,000 tons. I do not see why, with the increased knowledge of materials and construction, we should not be able to build ships in the next ten or fifteen years that will carry 30,000 tons and if mid-ocean caravans carrying 30,000 tons are crossing and recrossing the ocean, do what you will, there will always be danger if they come inland. Therefore, let us spend wisely and liberally to-day, with the fullest information we can get, and with hope and confidence in the future. I am not going to say anything about what the hon. member for Jacques Cartier said. I have often thought of that. I do not know of any better expenditure we could make than to take three of the ablest men we could find in Canada and give them $25,000 or $30,000 a year each to take this whole question into consideration. You cannot get a good man now except at a large price, and you want the very ablest business men in Canada for this work. Hon. members may think that the sum I have mentioned is a very large one, but I only mention it as one I would willingly give to the right men to solve this question.
In the exercise of his duties, no minister who has ever occupied the position of Minister of Public Works has shown better results than the present incumbent; but he is a very busy man, and when he has to attend to all the work of his department, when he has besides to run an election and keep the opposition from doing wrong, and do the thousand and one things which a minister has to do, even if he were an intellectual giant beyond any man living, he could not give that study to this subject which would enable him to find out what is really the condition of things in Canada.

You want, for example, one of the best engineers in America or Europe to ascertain what should be done. 1 remember the (ate premier Sir Mackenzie Bowell going to a gentleman in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway and saying to him: I want a good man for the Intercolonial Railway. What kind of a man do you want ? Sir Mackenzie went on to describe the kind of man he wanted, and then this gentleman asked: What are you ready to pay him. Well, said Sir Mackenzie, 1 might give him $6,000 or $7,000, if I could get a man like that. You would, would you, asked the other. Well, I have been looking for a man like that for ten years, and if I can find him I will give him $25,000 per year. We make a great mistake in taking a man who may be good, but who is not the best, and I thoroughly approve of the suggestion of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. We have a number of ports, each one claiming that it is the best. Naturally enough, the members of the various constituencies urge that the particular locality in which each is interested is the one in which our money could be expended to the best advantage. But an engineer of great ability would not pay any attention to the views of men influenced by local preferences, but would come to a decision apart from such views altogether, and no doubt tlie employment of such a man would be one of the best investments we could make.
Let me again remind the House that all this work must end as I have indicated. Let me remind them that the ocean, which never ceases in its inflow, and is always open inviting the commerce of the world, is the ultimate point at which the shipments of Canada must be made.
ing to do what we can for them, and so on, but he submitted to this House no systematic plan. These hon. gentlemen come down year after year deploring that things are as bad as they are, deploring that there are no facilities in Montreal for carrying on the business, and that the Grand Trunk Railway is forced to go to Portland. Well, what are the government there for ? They did not come into power yesterday. They have been here five years. They told us that the canals would be finished at a certain date, but that certain date has long since passed, and the canals are still unfinished. Those terminal facilities necessary for the carrying on of the business, and the elevators, are still not completed. The government has done nothing except spend money in a reckless fashion without having any matured, well-considered scheme. They have been simply going on spending money, as the Minister of Public Works has been doing, for instance, at Port Colborne. He produced a plan by the engineers of his department which called for an expenditure of five and a half million dollars at that port. He told us that he did not want to spend five and a half million dollars, and was only asking a vote of a million or two. and he said: Just vote me the money, and I will show what I will do with it. He comes before parliament with the crudest possible ideas as to what he is going to do, without any well-considered scheme for the expenditure of that money which _ he calls on us to vote. When we hand this money, which he is now asking us to vote, over to the Montreal Harbour Commissioners and they spend it, they will be responsible to the Dominion for the payment of 3 per cent interest, but the principal will be paid by the people of Canada and not by the harbour commissioners at all. How much money do the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal owe the Dominion to-day ?
I have a statement here showing $1,700,000.
I think they have drawn something since, and the amount is now about $2,000,000.
The statement was made by the Minister of Public Works a short time ago that it was $3,800,000.
That is the whole indebtedness of the board, but not to the government.
To whom do they owe the rest ?

I punk that the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) has made out a very good case for the appointment of a commission, and he indicated, I think, that he himself would be just the style of man to fill the bill.
You mean the size of man.

Yes, the hon. member is, according to his own opinion, just the man to suit, and the salary would be just about the size suitable for him. He has eulogized the Minister of Public Works untii the hon. minister had to clear out.
No, he knew that you were going to speak.

I have listened to the Minister of Public Works for almost several hours, and I never heard a speech so absolutely destitute of information. He just indulged in a lot of platitudes about Montreal being a great port, and Quebec being a great port, and Halifax and St. John being great ports, and about our hav-

To different parties. They have simply issued bonds which they sold in the ordin-

ary way, and on which they pay the interest.	.
And the Dominion guarantees the bonds ?
Not all of them. The government guarantee bonds for the amount advanced and nothing else.
$2,000,000 under the one statute, and an outstanding power for $2,000,000 which has not yet been used.
That makes $4,000,000 which the Dominion will become liable for?
The second part is not yet paid.
But the harbour commissioners can draw upon it ?
To be expended in accordance with the plans- yes.

Since the present government came into power, the liabilities of the harbour commissioners to the government of Canada have increased from $385,000 to about $2,000,000; and the harbour commissioners have power to expend $2,000,000 more as it is required, under approval of the government. [DOT] The Minister of Public Works prepared one scheme, found it a failure and adopted another, and yet the facilities that should have been provided when the canals were completed are not provided. And we are told that it will be years before the port of Montreal will be equipped. In the meantime, the Grand Trunk Railway lias sought its port at Portland, the reason being as the Minister of Public Works tells us that proper facilities have not been provided at Montreal. It is a great humiliation to the people of Canada after we have been spending money thus copiously, to find the business leaving Canada, and Portland becoming the summer and winter port of the Grand Trunk Railway system. We have just two great railway systems, the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Grand Trunk has its ramifications through the most productive parts of the Dominion and naturally does the largest freight business. And when this great system establishes its terminus in a foreign country the government stands idle, helpless; it has no programme, nothing to recommend as a means of keeping the business in Canada The only thing they have to suggest comes from the Minister of Public Works who tells us : Give us more money and we will spend it for you. The government should have retained the business on this side of the line so far as the Grand Trunk is concerned. The government, when extending the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal, gave the

Grand Trunk immense sums of money for the Improvement of their bridge, sums of money out of proportion as we contended to the service rendered by the Grand Trunk. And now we find the president of the Grand Trunk in the old country boasting that they have received enough money to doubletrack the road almost from Montreal to Portland, thus facilitating the carrying or the business away from this country to which it naturally belongs. This is the government that claims to be a business government and that claims to be looking after the interests of the people. They are neglecting the interests of the people. We look over the supplementary estimates and we find that they have about $3,309,000 for the balance of this year to the 30th of June, and they have other supplementary estimates to the amount of $8,300,000, which will be available for the government works during the coming summer season, in all, over $.12,000,000. These are supplementary estimates that are simply unrivalled, unprecedented in the history of this country. The government have been unequal to the task imposed upon them-they have not shown adequate results for the money entrusted to them. For my part, I enter my protest against voting away euormous sums without knowing how the money is to be expended. We are told that this money is to be spent under the approval of the Minister of Public Works. But when the minister comes before parliament asking for a vote of $1,000,000 to be expended in this way he does not come with any programme or scheme showing how that money is to be expended. I listened with a good deal of interest to the statements made by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) with regard to the port at Quebec, and I think he has fairly stated the case. The port of Quebec is the great ocean port of Canada, leaving out of consideration for the moment the Atlantic ports of Halifax, St. John, Sydney and the others to which reference has been made to-day. The freight carried on the inland waters will go to Quebec and will there be loaded on the enormous steamers that are to do the business in the future. Even on the great lakes we see vessels larger than those that were used for sea-going commerce a few years ago, vessels so large that until within recent years no one would have dreamed of utilizing them for inland commerce. The ocean vessels also are being built larger. And the port of Quebec meets the requirements of these vessels. A few years ago I was in the city of Quebec when the first-class man-of-war Blake came there. They found that they could not go up the stream to Montreal, the vessel being of too large a size.
Quebec will no doubt capture the trade; and the business should be arranged on that basis, on an intelligent basis, instead of doing a lot of work this year that he will

have to undo next year. The minister should have his schemes ready, his plans ready, his business ready, instead of coming here and saying, we deplore these things, we have 'to acknowledge that the Conners syndicate is broken down, and we are trying to get somebody else to take their place. That is not the way to do. The money of the country is being expended, its business is being retarded, and the canals, though completed, are not producing that benefit which these gentlemen had predicted. I remember the First Minister, in a speech in Toronto shortly after he became premier, saying : The first thing we did when we came into power was to recognize the fact that the transportation question was the great problem of the future in Canada. He said : We undertook to dig the canals-indicating that there were no canals before he came into power. It was like his inspiration, like his creation of the Dominion in one night ; he dug the canals while we were all asleep. They were to have them all ready by a certain date. Well, year after year has passed by, and the predictions of the right hon. the First Minister have not been verified in any degree. The business of the country along those lines has actually decreased. While they are boasting of the enormous increase of business, the business at Montreal has actually decreased, the canals have not done the business that they were going to do, we do not see that enormous increase that we might have fairly expected if proper facilities had been provided for doing it. Now I protest strongly against these enormous expenditures. I protest against the minister coming here with an off-hand demand for a million dollars, and uttering a lot of platitudes, meaningless, without information, in order to get the House to vote this money. Let him come here with a well-defined specific plan. The resolution says that the expenditure must meet with the approval of the Minister of Public Works. Well, he has no doubt the plans before him, else he should not have come to parliament and asked for this money. Has he a plan, has he a specific arrangement ? He has not told us so this afternoon, he has not given us information that would justify us in voting a million dollars for the purpose he has indicated.

My hon. friend is the first member of parliament during this debate who has placed it on party ground, and he will be the last one, I am sure, because the opinions that have been expressed on both sides of the House have not been in that direction.
That clap-trap is all played out.

The hon. gentleman is himself played out. If he goes on as he is going we will not hear much of him in a short time, and the less, perhaps, the better for the country. However, the hon. gentleman has a right to his own policy. He has a policy of his own, we saw that yesterday evening. On this occasion also he has a policy of his own. I would like to see him have the courage of his policy. Is he opposed to this grant for the improvement of the St. Lawrence and the port of Montreal ? If so, let him make a motion. That is a practical way of proving that he means what he says. The hon. gentleman says that I am uttering platitudes. Well, the country will judge between his speech and my modest utterances as to who is uttering platitudes. I do not profess to be anything else than a very plain man, and on this occasion I am only stating plain facts to parliament. When we took office the port of Montreal had not been attended to. We discussed plans that had been prepared but that had not been carried out. The plans were changed. After consultation with the great commercial bodies of Montreal, we agreed on plans that are now being carried out. The hon. gentleman says that we are doing nothing, that we have no policy. Well, let the hon. gentleman, who is still under the impression of his trip to Quebec, come and see what we are doing in Montreal. He will have an opportunity of making another conciliatory speech like the one he made in Quebec, and which, I understand, has made him one of the most popular men of the whole party that went down to Quebec. The hon. gentleman intends to be a candidate in Joliette. We will be glad to see him there. He has a perfect right to ask for the suffrages and votes of the French electors. To gain their favour he has but to read his speech that he made at Quebec and he is done for. He will never be elected in a progressive province with utterances like the ones we have heard. As I have said, we are carefully carrying out plans that are prepared. The hon. gentleman says we have nothing to show. Well, we have already done work in Montreal to the value of $2,000,000. Let the hon. gentleman come and see that work, and he will find that we have not wasted out time nor the money of the country. The hon. gentleman has thought proper to speak of Port Colborne, and to rehash the old story that there is an expenditure of $5,000,000 in view. The hon. gentleman knows right well that he is only talking to the moon.

I said nothing of the kind, I did not say that. the government were contemplating an expenditure of $5,000,000 or $5,500,000 at Port Colborne. But the minister told us distinctly that he was not going to adopt that $5,500,000 plan of expenditure. Now he turns round and puts words into my mouth the very opposite of what I used.

Well, the hon. gentleman is just taking back water, as he has often done before when

lie lias found liimself in a corner. He is intimating

I won't permit any one to misrepresent what I stated. What I said was that his engineers had a plan for that amount of expenditure, but that he himself did not propose to adopt that plan, but said : You give me a much smaller sum and see what I will do with it. That is the statement I made to the House, not that he had adopted the $5,500,000 plan, but that he had repudiated the plan of his engineers, and was adopting a plan of his own.

The hon. gentleman is again talking to the moon. My engineers did not suggest that expenditure of money. There was a plan prepared, not for the immediate expenditure of money, not for the purpose of any expenditure of that amount ; there was a plan prepared by which it would be possible, if trade developed, to spend that money later on. Those plans have no immediate importance at all, but the hon. gentlemen are trying to create the impression that we contemplate spending millions and millions of money. That is just what they have tried to do. The work that we are carrying out at Port Colborne is a very simple one, but a most useful one, indeed. There was no harbour at that point. Big ships could not unload. The Department of Public Works is building a breakwater inside of which large ships will be able to load and unload. The Department of Railways and Canals is building piers and docks, at which large Ships will be able to load and unload. The plans have been placed before parliament. It will be great pleasure for me to put the plans on the Table of the House. That work is being carried on under well-defined and well-prepared plans, and it is no use for hon. gentlemen to say that we are coming to parliament without any definite plans. The works have been awarded and the plans prepared. As far as Montreal is concerned, there is a part of this plan completed. One large work is completed and the other one will be completed in a few weeks. Three large piers will be completed next year. To handle the grain at this port at these three wharfs the Board of Trade of Montreal believe that two elevators are necessary. Whether there will be two elevators built or only one at that particular spot, I am not prepared to say. It is an open question, upon which I am not prepared to say anything to-day. I must have more information. But, in the meantime, we are asking parliament to allow us to advance $1,000,000 to the harbour commissioners so that they may build elevators and warehouses, and other terminal facilities, on plans to be submitted to us. I do not see what more we can place before parliament to justify us in asking this amount of money. If we did not ask for money this year before the plans of the elevators are prepared, we might Mr. TARTE.
be open to reproach of having wasted time. We are asking for the mouey in advance so that the plans may be prepared immediately and the work may go on without delay. The hon. gentleman has made a mistake from a party standpoint in talking about politics. I am not going to follow him. I am not going to recriminate because the Conservative party when they were in office accomplished some important things. They built railways and harbours, but they have not been able to do everything. It is well known that the port of Montreal was not equipped and that the port of Quebec was not equipped. I am not going to make it a crime to the Conservative party that they have not been able to do that. Things come in their time and in their day. We are doing good work now we are in office, as our i>re-deeessors did good work when they were in office. God forbid that I should forget myself to the extent of making party politics out of a question of such importance. I will leave that to the hon. gentleman if he is not able to rise higher.

Mr. Chairman, when the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) introduced these resolutions, I was very much pleased with the manner in which he treated the subject. It is certainly a national question, a question which ought to receive the very best consideration of both sides of this House, apart from any political feeling whatever. 1 confess I regret that an hon. gentleman occupying the position of the hdn. Minister of Public Works should have turned the whole debate along the lines of making it simply a political question. He has done his utmost to show the advantage politically that would accrue to him and to his party by the expenditure of this money, and if perchance any hon. gentleman should say one word not in sympathy with his views, then he declares it would be impossible for that man to be elected in the city of Montreal or in the province of Quebec. I hope the hon. gentleman will take back something of what he said and that he will endeavour to undo the mischief, if he intends to get these resolutions passed with the unanimous consent of the House, which, to my mind, ought to be done if done at all. To my mind, the government, before they proceed to authorize the expenditure of any large sum of money for the purpose for which this resolution is designed, ought to have some definite policy. I think they ought to arrive at some conclusion as to which port is to be the great national port of Canada. I do not say that whilst we select one port and expend money to make it a port at Which great vessels can come from the ocean, can land their cargoes, we ought to neglect other ports, but, we ought to make a selection of the port on which we are going to expend the largest sum of money for the reception of the very large vessels that must of necessity come to this

country to do the trade of the country. 1 say, therefore, that the government ought to have some definite object in view so that, whether it be Montreal,or Quebec, or Halifax, it shall be a place that we can rely upon. It seems to be a little dangerous for an hon. member to speak his mind upon this question, but at the risk of falling out with the hon. Minister of Public Works, I would venture to say that there is one port in this country which has advantages far above and beyond that of any other port for carrying on the trade of the country. At the city of Quebec we have deep water and abundance of water, and there is a probability of that port being open for ten or twelve months in the year. That harbour can be made an excellent harbour without the expensive dredging that is incidental to almost every other port in the country. Large ships can come into that port and facilities can be arranged by which the largest vessels that sail the ocean can come in there, receive and discharge their cargoes. Well, now, if that port is placed over all the other ports of Canada, if with the expenditure of the same amount of money it can be made advantageous to the country, to make it the national port, why cannot the government decide upon the scheme that they are going to aid for the next ten, fifteen or twenty years, and let us know exactly the aim and object they have in view ? I have nothing to say against the port of Montreal. Montreal will be a port. There will always be a large amount of trade carried on at Montreal. The largest vessels that come may not be able to come to Montreal, but there will be a class of vessels that will always come to Montreal, and it will be necessary that Montreal should be equipped and maintained as a port. But, I believe that the national port of Canada will be the port of Quebec ; that in the future it will be the port where the great vessels that trade between Canada and other countries will receive and discharge their cargo. Now, in reference to the vote that is before us, I desire to say that I think this is a very large sum of money for this parliament to vote to be controlled by the hon. Minister of Public Works. I do not think it is good policy. I think the whole government should have something to say as to how that money should be expended, and that its expenditure should receive the approbation of the government, and the government be held responsible for its proper outlay. I therefore take exception to the wording of the resolution so far as it declares that the money is to be expended entirely upon the approval of the Minister of Public Works. It places a tremendous lever in his hands, and from the exhibition of political feeling he has given us to-day, I am very much afraid that this money may be used for a very improper purpose.

This point has not been raised before, but
I may say that the wording of the resolution ,1s identical with that used in the resolution of 1894, when the first advance was made to the harbour commissioners, and when my friend, Judge Ouimet, was Minister of Public Works. What was good for the goose then ought to be good for the gander now. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) says they were wrong, we are wrong ; but, if they were right in 1894, we are right to-day. The hon. gentleman was then a member of parliament, and he did not object to it.

My views on the transportation question are well known. I suggested in the House some time ago, that as part of a proper transportation scheme, it was absolutely necessary to afford the very best kind of facilities at the port of Montreal. But, the Minister of Public Works should have given more information to the House. The Harbour Commissioners of Montreal have stated to him what they wanted to complete their port, and amongst other things, elevators are mentioned. Now, one million dollars will build four large elevators, containing nearly two million bushels. The minister stated that we were to have besides elevators, terminal facilities, warehouses and other necessary adjuncts. He praised his Montreal harbour scheme, but, it is my opinion that a great waste of money will be entailed by it, because the scheme is not as comprehensive as it should be. The present scheme will afford only a moiety of the facilities necessary to make Montreal a first-class port. If you have elevators it will be necessary to have them connected with the main lines of railway, and you should have warehouses large enough for the port, but it will be difficult for you to make railway connection under the present scheme. We should have before us the plans which the minister has approved of, as well as the other plans which he has rejected. I was on a committee for the purpose of adopting plans for the Montreal harbour improvements, and one plan commended itself to me more than any other, which proposed to improve the facilities along the river which at present exist, and which would include an inland harbour or dockage connected with all the railway lines. The railways would have their terminals,.and there would be ample room for elevators and warehouses. Montreal will never be the port it should be unless there is a radical change made in the arrangement of its harbour.
At what part of the harbour would that be ?

speechtext: The plan I refer to, and which was approved by the department to a certain extent, was a little below where the old barracks used to be.

Yes. I would have made a good job of it while I was at it. I agree with the Minister of Public Works, that the harbours which are the furthest inland from the sea, and which require the shortest railwas' haul, are the harbours that will be utilized. No man can make me believe that railways can compete with water communications. I stated the other day that freight can be carried by sea for one-tenth of a cent per ton per mile, and that cannot be done by any railway system that ever existed. Look at Germany to-day, improving its canal system. Why was the Manchester ship canal built ? It is because . it is known to all practical men that water transportation is the cheapest. An hon. gentleman has said that the St. Lawrence is closed for five or six months of the year, and that our traffic must be done by ports which are opened all the year round. Does he not know that more than one-half of the trade of the United States is done under circumstances similar to those existing in Montreal ?
We are now loaning to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal one million dollars. They have faithfully kept their bargain with us in the past, and have returned every cent of interest on the loans they got from us. I believe that in the near future the people of Canada will insist that the harbour dues shall be taken off from the port of Montreal, and as a pre-requisite, we shall be compelled to assume the whole debt of that harbour. We must, therefore, look to the future. Although they are able to repay us, and will repay us. yet, the future of the country demands that the expenditure in Montreal shall be the best and the wisest. Harbour dues are like tolls on country roads, a relic of barbarism.
Hear, hear.
We must get rid of them. I will say that the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal have spent the money they have got from us wisely.
Hear, hear.

They have done the best they possibly could with the money but that money has not been applied to the best possible advantage, because the plans are defective. I do not know whether or not that plan was forced on them by the Minister of Public Works, but, at all events, it is behind the age, and is not sufficient for the requirements of a port like Montreal. There must be a bigger plan, a broader plan, and a better plan adopted. From the remarks which the Minister of Public Works made three or four years ago, I thought the hon. gentleman agreed with me. and that he was not going to go along ' futtering,' as the Scotch say. with little expenditures and little improvements.

After all, the prosperity of this country depends on the development of the St. Lawrence as our natural highway to the ocean, and on proper facilities being afforded in the port of Montreal; and these elevators and warehouses, as well as the terminal facilities for the railways, could, I think, be all placed in a better location than they are at present. However, I rose particularly to say that I am in favour of a large expenditure for the purpose of developing the port of Montreal to the fullest extent. It is a disgrace to this country to have its exports carried past our own maritime ports and taken to ports in the United States. We should make every effort to build up our own maritime towns, and not the towns of a foreign country. To that extent I am with the minister in any expenditure he can possibly make. I am a firm believer that, with proper facilities at the port of Montreal, our western sea-bound traffic will go by that port as the cheapest and best possible route to foreign markets, and not by ports in the United States; because nature has given us advantages in that respect above those of the United States. Let the minister be sure that his plans are of the best; but I doubt that they are. We have not had an opportunity of judging them. The plans ought to be spread broadcast; we ought to have them in the House. We ought to have before us the proposals of the harbour commission as to the building of these elevators, the terminal facilities, and everything else. It is a large sum of money, and if we are not ourselves able to judge mechanically as to the proper location for these works, we ought to be able to consult people who are. We are totally in the dark. We are asked to vote a sum of money for a laudable purpose if it is properly expended; but the information necessary to judge as to that ought to be furnished to the House.

Of course, I have not the slightest objection to bring down the plans of all the works now being carried out; but the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals must not forget that these plans were submitted to the House three years ago. Rightly or wrongly, they were adopted then, and we are simply carrying them out.
Our memory does not go back for years.

I quite remember bringing those plans before the House. I quite know what my hon. friend means. The port of Montreal is divided into two parts-the central part, where the most important works are being carried out, and the eastern part, where a certain amount of work has been carried out in the past, and where I am now erecting a large pier. My hon. friend I am sure remembers all the difficulties which the late government had when they attempted to

deal with his plans. They could not carry them out, so great were the influences against them, although I agree with him that they were the best. My hon. friend means an inland basin in the eastern portion of the harbour.
You have no such trouble as that to contend with.

Well, I have had a great deal of trouble when I have attempted to carry out the same plans. When I first said that certain works had to be carried out in the eastern part of the harbour, I had to face a great deal of opposition and difficulty. I have carried out parts of our common plan, and I am carrying out part of it now. If trade develops as we expect, 1 have no doubt that portion of the harbour has a great future before it. It cannot be otherwise; it is bound to be the natural port of Montreal. But works of improvement were begun when we took office, and we have simply improved on the improvements that were carried out in the past. My hon. friend will agree with me that the work which is now being carried out will be a most useful one. The piers now being-erected will be a splendid improvement. An inland basin would have given better facilities, I grant; but an inland improvement could not be made in the centre of the harbour. We are now completing the improvement of the western part of the harbour; and when that work is completed, if the trade of the future is what we all expect it will be, my notion is that it will have to go down to that inland basin. But for the time being, I am doing the only feasible thing. There was such a strenuous and powerful opposition that I could not do more. I am perfectly frank about that. My hon. friend could not do anything; but I have done something, though not all I wanted to do. In politics we must understand that we cannot always get our own way; we must do the best we can with the means available. The work that is being carried out now has been approved by the most important commercial bodies of Montreal. I am glad my hon. friend has borne testimony to the good work done by the harbour commissioners. There is no party politics in the harbour commissioners. Mr. Creighton, Mr. Allan, Mr. Torrance, and other Conservative gentlemen have just as much influence with this government in regard to these improvements as our political friends have. If Mr. Creighton were to speak, he would say that he has exercised perhaps more -influence on certain decisions we have made than any other man on the harbour commission. I am glad to say that the harbour commissioners are working hand in hand. My hon. friend should not ask for more information than I can give. I cannot possibly give all the information as to the site of the elevators, for the excellent 162
reason that we do not know yet what may happen. There are big American companies who want to come to Montreal, and; who ask that a large elevator be placed on the Windmill basin. The Montreal Board of Trade want two elevators in the centre of the harbour. My hon. friend has very properly said that with $1,000,000 we could construct four elevators. He is right there; but the harbour commission do not intend to construct four elevators. They intend to construct two elevators, a large warehouse equipped with all modern conveniences, and to use the balance of the money, I suppose, in laying down rails, &c. All the expenditures will be connected with the improvements in the eastern part of the harbour, where the Canadian Pacific Railway is located, and which will be used largely by the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Grand Trunk Railway is not located in the eastern part of the harbour; but I hope that with the new plans we are now carrying out the Grand Trunk will find its way down to the spot which is near to the heart of both my hon. friend and myself, because I believe it is the most important part of the port of Montreal.
This very morning a large capitalist from Ontario called on me and asked whether the government could not do something in the way of providing facilities at the port of Montreal for the export of cattle, as he thought of organizing a big company for that purpose, but there were no decent facilities for a cattle port. That gentleman said to me, just what my hon. friend has stated, that the eastern portion of the harbour is the best adapted for that trade. All things come to those who know how to wait, and I have no doubt that he and I will live long enough to see our plans in the eastern part of the harbour carried out. In the meantime, we are accommodating the trade in that part of the harbour where the work was begun before he and I were in public life.
