Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of the government, and more particularly to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture, a question that is of very deep interest to the people of Manitoba and the North-west Territories. I refer to the establishing of remount stations or some similar arrangement which would enable the government to give such assistance to the producers of -horses in that country as would enable them to reach the markets of the purchaser of those animals. There can be no question as to the



suitability of that particular portion of Canada for the raising ot' horses such as arc now being purchased in very large numbers in other portions of the world, and of which large numbers are now being purchased in other sections of the Dominion. 1 may say that no portion of Canada, or for the matter of that of the world, can produce such animals, as are now being raised in our western country. As an evidence of this, I need merely refer to our North-west Mounted Police. I know whereof I speak, and other lion, members will bear me out, When I say that as many as twenty or thirty horses of that force, carrying on their backs from 150 to 170 pounds each, have been known to cover 120 miles in 12 hours in the pursuit of horse thieves. And I may add that although the horses we sent to South Africa were not by any means the best we raise, I have been assured by men who served throughout the campaign there, and who were mounted on Canadian North-west horses, that they have ridden the same horse from the time they landed in South Africa untn they came away. I saw a smile on the face of the Minister of Agriculture when I made the statement of what our horses had done, but if he wants the evidence he will have no difficulty in obtaining it. We can, in fact, grow any kind of horses that are needed for any purpose. We have an enormous territory, and can raise any amount of them ; and it is quite evident that the British army, benefiting from past experience, will require a very large number of those animals in the future. Their eyes have been opened, and I maintain that it is the duty of this government to assist that great industry by doing for it what the Department of Agriculture has done for the industries of cheese and butter by the establishment of cold storage and other facilities. The government are just as much entitled to come to the aid of this great industry as to grant a vote to the extent of $100,000 for a steamship, which we have done to-day. Why should the government not advance $50,000 or $100,000 in order to build up that industry ? And the government can do it through their police department or in many other ways. If they ask me to devise a scheme to bring together in trade the producers of these animals and the parties who need them, I think I can do it very readily. Now the difficulty with regard to sales to the Imperial authorities is this-these animals run wild from the day they are foaled until the day they are sold for some purpose. If the owners gather these animals when five or six years old, break them, train them as it were for the work they are to do, they are not certain of being able to sell them for that work. If they were certain of a purchaser, any number of horses could be provided. Probably as many as a thousand head could Mr. BOYD.
be got there now. But these men cannot go to the expense of gathering these horses, training them, making them as quiet as these people demand they shall be, if there is nobody to buy. What I ask the government to do is to devise a scheme and provide the means to bring the producers and the purchasers of these animals together. You have a body of mounted policemen there, you might increase the number and start a remount station or breaking station. Then when the horses have become sufficiently tractable and ready for the market, they could be shipped and the trade started. This could be done much as the cheese industry was encouraged under plans started by the late government and followed up by their successors who are now in office.
I would direct the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture to the possibilities of this trade as one that is as well worthy of attention as the production of cheese. And, while I am on my feet, it might not be amiss for me to say that the influence of the present government might be brought to bear upon the Imperial authorities by showing them that there is no better place for a military station, where a regiment might be trained in the arts in which the Imperial forces showed themselves deficient in the last struggle they were engaged in-scouting, horsemanship, and so on. There are the plains, there are the mountains or hills or kopjes or whatever you choose to call them. There could be no better training ground. I do not wish to occupy more time, but I would again urge the government to give attention to this trade, the possibilities of which are unlimited.

I have very much pleasure in saying a few words in favour of the proposition presented by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd). I think it would be a step in the right direction if the government endeavoured to induce the Imperial authorities to turn their attention to the Canadian North-west as a source of supply for horses. There is no doubt that, as the hon. member for Macdonald says, we produce the best horses in the world" for this particular service. I can bear out what the hon. gentleman says about the endurance of the horses used by the North-west mounted police. Horse ranching was a flourishing industry in the North-west some years ago, and many horses were produced as suitable for remounts for the army. Unfortunately, however, prices dropped so low that it did not pay to breed these horses, and the ranchers were obliged to turn their attention to the raising of cattle, which does not pay the people of the North-west so well as horse-raising did. Another important point is that you can raise horses where you cannot raise cattle. Any one who knows anything about the grazing lands of southern Alberta knows

that it is only where there are streams that cattle can be raised, the animals ranging only about three miles back from the water. All the land back of that is useless for raising cattle. But the horses roam much further back. Consequently millions of acres might be used for raising horses that cannot be used for cattle-raising. The industry would be very profitable for those engaged in it. As my hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) says, if it is right and wise, as I believe it is, to assist in the production of butter and cheese in the North-west, why should not the attention of the government be turned to this great industry of horse-raising. There are portions of the Territories where dairying cannot be carried on successfully, but where horse-raising could be carried on with the greatest success. It would be of untold advantage for the people to have a remount station in the North-west Territories or in Manitoba. I have no doubt that if the government opened negotiations with the Imperial authorities their attention could be turned in this direction. We could raise all the horses that are desired, and, if a market is furnished, the people of the North-west will turn their attention to this industry in order to meet the demands.

I desire to say a few words in support of the suggestion that steps should be taken to establish a market for the horses of the Northwest. It may not be within the knowledge of the members of the House, but it is nevertheless a fact, that there are very large areas of the North-west that, by reason of natural conditions are suitable to the rearing of horses, but are not suited to the rearing of cattle or the production of grain. In fact, that there are large areas of the North-west Territories that must come into use as horse-raising country, or they will be of no practical use. There is, therefore, substantial reason from a national point of view why the question of securing a market for the horses of the North-west should engage the attention of parliament. The general idea in this eastern country is that horses are more delicate than horned cattle. That is not the case; the horse is the hardier animal of the two. He can paw a living in the winter where cattle cannot; he can get his living under conditions where horned stock would die. In the summer time, also, in districts of the country where water is scarce, cattle cannot live, because they cannot travel far for water, as horses can. Consequently in those vast areas where winter is too severe to admit of cattle pasturing out, and where water is too scarce for them during the summer, horses could be produced in large numbers, becoming a source of great wealth to this country. I am not prepared to suggest any scheme of operation, I merely want to bring to the attention of the House existing conditions. Let me say that it is not for any lack of enterprise which has been 162}
displayed by horse ranchers in the Northwest that the enterprise has so far failed. I may say that hundreds of thousands of dollars have been spent in the district that I represent in the enterprise of breeding horses for the Imperial army. The ranches were established, but the market was not reached, and the industry turned out to a large extent a failure. It turned out a failure at any rate on the scale that was intended. To-day many of these ranches are for sale, or are turned into cattle ranches. Iam not able, in the time at my disposal, to give the particular reasons why the industry was not successful; but I believe that the conditions have so changed that where failure occurred before, success is within reach now. In former times the demand of the British army was for heavy cavalry horses, and there is a difficulty in rearing the highest class of heavy horses on the ranch ; it can be done, but the expense is increased to such an extent that the profit of the ranch is minimized. Now the conditions have changed, so that the army does not require such high class horses as it formerly did. They are buying horses that are well within the capacity of the North-west to supply.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock, I was speaking of the efforts that had been made in the North-west, for the supply to the British army of cavalry horses. This is not a new idea. It is an old idea ; the effort has been made at the expense of many hundreds of thousands of dollars. The fact that it was not successful in the past is no indication that it will not be successful, or that it cannot be successful, in the future. As I have already remarked, the conditions have changed, so that the class of horses which was demanded for British cavalry purposes ten years ago is not the class of horses that is in demand to-day. A different class is in demand, and it is a class particularly available on the ranches of the North-west. There are difficulties in the way of the development of this trade. The chief difficulty is not in the production of horses, is not in the securing of capital to rear the horses, but, the difficulty is in making connection between the market in Great Britain and the scene of production on this side of the water. It may be asked : Why does not the trade develop itself, just as did the trade in cattle and in wheat ? The reason is, because this is a special article, required only for a special market. If it were an article of world-wide demand, there would be no special effort necessary in the way of bring-

ing it to market; but, the conditions in regard to the horse industry, that is, the feature of supplying army horses, is that it is a special industry to supply a special market, just as is the cheese industry or the butter industry, which supplied a special market. In that case the conditions were such that something more than the mere natural course of trade was necessary in order to bring about the desired results. It is so in the case of this horse industry. Although we have the horses, and although Great Britain furnishes a market, it remains a fact that while Great Britain has purchased, during the past year or two, not less than 100,000 horses in the country to the south of us, and not less than 200,000 or 300,000 horses in other parts of the world, Great Britain has, so far, not purchased a single horse from the Canadian North-west, although the horses are there for sale, and although the horses are of the quality they were proven to be by those who went to South Africa as mounts for the second Canadian contingent, and, for the Stratheonas. The very reason that there was a difficulty in the way of producing range horses suitable for cavalry in the past is the reason of the advantage of these horses at the present time. What the British cavalry wanted years ago was the largest and heaviest animal that could be produced of the class required,, in order to carry weight. The conditions had to be adapted to the production of that class of animal; that is to say, conveniences of stabling, feeding and breeding had to be all of the most complete character. Such conveniences do not exist on the western ranches, and as a consequence, horses were not reared of the size then demanded by the British army. But, to-day, the British army is not asking for such large horses. What is wanted now is a horse of possibly smaller size, but with greater endurance, and it is in that feature that the horse of the Canadian Northwest excels, we claim, any other country in the world. As compared with the stable-reared horse, there can be no question that the horse reared on the plains, on the range, which has faced the heat of summer and the cold of winter, which has been on the prairies all his life, is certainly an animal which can stand the vicissitudes and hardships of a military campaign in a way that the stable-reared horse cannot possibly be expected to do. Taking horses of an equal weight from the prairies and from the farms, the prairie horse is worth far more for practical army purposes than the stable-reared horse. But, the very fact that he has been reared on the range, that he is not a gentle horse, is the very reason of the difficulty that exists in marketing him for army purposes. When the army wants a horse it wants a gentle horse, a horse that can be handled. The prairie horse is good, but he is not gentle, and he has to be gentle before he can be used. There is the difficulty which is now in hand, and there is Mr. OLIVER.
the difficulty that is asked to be met by the establishment of an Imperial remount depot in the North-west, where it will be possible to break these horses, or have them broken for military purposes. The reason why it is necessary that there should be special conveniences fob this purpose is, that while it costs practically nothing to rear a horse, it costs a good deal to break him, and he must be kept in use or the advantage of the breaking is lost. The ordinary horse rearer cannot keep on his range a number of unused, broken horses. The expense of breaking them and the impossibility of keeping them broken absolutely prevents this. A horse, then, must be broken immediately previous to his being sold, in order that the full advantage of his breaking shall be secured. It is because of this condition that the necessity exists for some general arrangement whereby horses can be marketed in large numbers, and brought together for the purpose of being broken economically, and disposed of at the time.
I would call the attention of the House to the fact which I mentioned a few minutes ago, that the British army has purchased within the last few years several hundred thousand head of horses, and of the hundreds of thousands of head of horses purchased, the Canadian North-west has not had the privilege of selling one single animal. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that, under all the circumstances, something, perhaps, might have been done that was not done to secure for us the benefit of this market. Only a few days ago, 1,200 young Canadians sailed for South Africa to take part in the operations there as a mounted force, and they are to be mounted on horses brought, probably, from the other side of the line. It seems to me reasonable that if Canada can supply the men Canada can supply the horses, and especially as the Canadians supplied are acknowledged to be the best men so Canada can supply what are acknowledged to be the best horses. It seems to me that this was an opportunity which should have been availed of, and it is only because the conditions have not been generally understood that it was not availed of. It is because of this patent fact that we desire to bring the conditions to the attention of the House here to-night. .
The hundred thousand head of horses purchased in the United States meant a distribution of English money in the United States of something like $1,000,000, and if a proportionate number of horses had been obtained from Canada there would have been a like distribution of wealth in this country. This is something surely worth considering, something worthy the attention of parliament. It is not that an expenditure is desired to be made. The horse business necessarily involves such a large private expenditure on the part of those connected with it, that a mere matter of expenditure by the govern-

ment makes very little difference. It is not a question of expenditure ; it is a question of bringing together demand and supply. It is because of the stupendous demand that has existed for the past few years for the very class of horse that we can supply, and because that demand has not turned to our advantage at all that we desire to bring to the attention of the House and the country the necessity that exists for something to be done to turn this great source of wealth to the advantage of our people, not only in the west, but also in the east. It is desired that measures should be taken to let the British government understand that there is in Canada a field for the production of the horses that they need, so that the; demand shall meet the supply, and the advantage shall be mutual. The peculiar conditions that exist in the west are such as almost necessarily to produce the class of horses that is required by the army at the present time. There are people there now, and others are ready to go in, to take the means to produce that class of horse, and to add so much to the wealth of the country. But, as long as the market is not found for the horses produced, so long must the industry suffer a drawback, and so long must that wealth be lost to the country.
Everything is at hand. The demand is greater than ever before, and it is probable that this demand will continue, if not in as large a degree, yet in a very considerable degree. Capital is invested for the purpose of producing the animals, and all that is necessary is to establish relations between the producer and the market. At the present time the British government has sent a buyer to Canada, and it is expected that that gentleman will visit the Northwest within a short time. It is because of his prospective visit there, that we desire particularly to draw attention to the question at the present time. This gentleman who is buying for the British army will require his orders filled within a short time, and in the case of range horses it is necessary to make preparations beforehand, so that the order can be promptly filled. I understand that arrangements are being made to meet this gentleman from the War Office with the class of horses he requires. so as to make the experiment successful. We desire to see the British War Office continuously buying horses in Canada. No stock is so profitable as horses if there is, a demand, and no stock so unprofitable when there is no demand. There is no stock which is as easily reared in the North-west as horses, and there is no) stock on which people have lost more money simply because they could not get the market for the ani-mais. It is because of these conditions and the possibility of so vastly increasing our trade in horses in the future, that we bring this matter to the attention of the House to-night.

This question is now attracting the attention of our people to a very great extent, and I am glad that it has been mentioned in parliament. Perhaps the most noticeable thing about the war in South Africa has been the largely increased use of mounted men in the field. We feel confident in Canada that just as our men did good service to the empire, so our horses can be turned to good account in the Imperial service. The Imperial authorities, however, required to get an enormous number of horses at the shortest possible notice during the war, and the contractors for the supply sought them in the cheapest and quickest market. Canada was comparatively unknown as a horse-producing country, and there was unfortunately in the War Office a report furnished some years ago which was rather against the good name of the Dominion as a field for the production of army horses. Strong representations were made to Lord Strath-cona asking the Imperial authorities to send a purchasing officer here, and that was done. He was urged to send forward the animals immediately, and he believed that his duty called upon him to buy his horses last year entirely in eastern Canada. We are glad to know that these horses created a very favourable impression amongst the officers of the army, and showed up well in comparison with any other horses that were sent to South Africa. This year representations came to me from the people of the North-west Territories, and some three or four months ago I sent a cablegram to our High Commissioner asking him to urge upon the War Oflfice, that still large numbers of Canadian horses could be advantageously purchased for the army. As a result of that Colonel Dent, the Imperial purchasing officer, who is at present in Canada, was sent here with instructions to buy two ship-load of horses as rapidly as possible, and then to make a tour of western Canada to purchase other animals, and to make a report upon Canada as a ground for supplying horses to the British forces. Our desire is that not only in the case of an emergency like the present, but that at all times the British War Office should purchase horses in Canada, so that the men in Canada who breed horses may know that there is a market for a certain type of animals, in order that they may take steps to produce that particular type. Up to the present time there has been no such demand in Canada, and the result has been that while one man would take a fancy to a certain class of animal his near neighbour produced an altogether different breed. Consequently when the purchaser sets out to purchase a certain type of animal in large numbers, he has got to travel over a great deal of ground, and he has to lose

a great deal of time. When it is understood that the Imperial authorities are going to purchase a fixed number of horses in Canada each year, then our breeders of horses can govern themselves accordingly.
This subject has been receiving the most earnest consideration of the government. [DOT] I have myself been in constant discussion with my colleague, the Minister of -Militia and Defence (Hon. Mr. Borden), whose work in connection with the armed force of Canada naturally brings him very closely to this subject-as closely as myself, representing the farmers of the country. We have been discussing various plans and schemes which have been put forward ; and I can take the House into my confidence by saying that quite recently a rather elaborate memorandum on this subject has been sent to the Imperial authorities pointing out the advantages of Canada as a breeding ground for horses, and the advantage to the Empire as a whole that such a supply of horses as may be needed for army purposes should be obtained within the bounds of the empire; and pointing out that no part of it is better, if equal, to Canada, for this purpose ; also that Canada, lying as it does between the Atlantic and the Pacific, midway, so to speak, between the mother land and the Orient, is particularly well suited for the supply of horses to the armies of the empire, both eastward and westward ; pointing out further, that if the Imperial authorities would undertake to purchase a reasonable number of horses in Canada year by year for army purposes, the encouragement which would thereby be given to the breeding of horses for army purposes in Canada would tend greatly to strengthen the defensive forces of this colony and promote the growth of armed militia forces within the empire. These views have been presented to the Imperial authorities with all the force possible to us. I hope within a few days to sail for England, and this subject is one of the most important of those with which I shall have to deal while there. I may say that we have been assured already by the Imperial authorities that our views and representations shall receive most careful and friendly consideration. Under these circumstances, the object which the hon. gentlemen who have addressed the House this evening have in view, appears to be almost within sight. Just how the Imperial authorities will view the proposals we may make to them, it is beyond my powers to say ; but I can assure hon. gentlemen that nothing will be left undone on the part of the government or myself in my visit to England to bring about what I believe to be not only in the interest of the horse-breeders of Canada, but in the interest of Canada as an integral part of the empire, as well as in the interest of the strength and effective supply of material to the whole force of the empire when war may arise. I do not need, I think, to take up the time of the House any longer, ex-Mr. FISHER.
cept that I would like to refer to a remark made by my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) a little while ago, when, speaking of the great endurance of our horses in the west, he said that a certain troop had covered 120 miles in twelve hours. If that is the case, it is the most extraordinary instance of endurance and speed known in the world's history of equine animals. I think he must have meant twenty-four hours instead of twelve. He shakes his head, so I suppose he means twelve hours. If the hon. gentleman can prove that that has occurred, he will prove the most extraordinary feat by any horses that have ever existed on the face of this earth. I shall be glad indeed if he can prove that of Canadian horses. Even if they had done it in twenty-four hours, it would' still be one of the most extraordinary feats of endurance and speed I have ever heard of in my reading regarding horses and horse work. I quite understand that Canadian horses will do perhaps more than any other horses, and I would be glad, indeed, to find an instance in which they have accomplished what the hon. gentleman has said.
speakername: The MINISTER OE AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sydney Fisher).

speechtext: If I may be permitted, I would say that the information given to me was that a possfi of mounted police had done as I say-followed some horse thieves a distance claimed to be 120 miles, in twelve hours. That distance in twenty-four hours would not be considered uncommon. There are men in the gallery who have ridden 115 miles in twelve hours, and the riding of 100 miles in that time is looked upon as an ordinary feat in that country.
How long are your miles in the North-west ?

I may tell this House that during the last campaign I was driven ninety-three miles in twelve hours by a team of those horses from the town of Neepawa to a place between Makinak and St. Rose du Lac ; and the man turned round and drove back the next day. So that I am not drawing on my imagination at all, and ordinary horses have accomplished even more than I speak of now.

I thought the hon. gentleman must have made a mistake in the figures. I do not wish to discredit what he has stated at all. Since he has made the statement, I accept it, of course, and I am glad to find that such endurance and power are well known in the North-west, because I confess it is something very uncommon amongst other horses in the world.

The other portion has to do with inducing steamship companies to provide that ventilation which my hon. friend from South Wentworth (Mr. Smith) has urgently been asking for.
While cold storage and ventilated chambers are required for some of our products, our other products do not require the cold storage chambers, but nevertheless it is absolutely necessary that some arrangement should be made to carry them safely and properly across the Atlantic. I propose to make a contract with the steamship companies, by which we will aid the companies to put in the necessary ventilating shafts and cold storage traps, so that cold air may be forced into the holds of their ships. Up to the present the proposition has always been simply to put in ventilation traps in, order to give the air in the hold the same temperature as outside, but we propose to go a step further and
provide a small chamber, in which the air will be cooled and then forced into the hold. The chief products for which this will be used are fruits and cheese. During the last year or two our cheese has suffered in reputation in consequence of heating in the holds of the vessel, and it is well known that our fruits have been cooked a good deal in the tightly battened down holds. These difficulties we propose to obviate, and hope by our arrangement with the steamship companies to bring about a complete revolution in the carrying of these perishable products. The amount may seem a little large, but I am satisfied that the money will be well expended in the interests of the fruit and cheese trade.
This makes a total of $188,600. How many steamships does the hon. gentleman propose to have fitted up with these facilities, and from what ports are they to sail ?

Some seventeen or twenty steamers. We propose to fit up those steamers that go from Montreal and Quebec in the summer and St. John and Halifax in the winter, and which go to Glasgow, Liverpool, Manchester, Bristol and London. Our information is that this amount will fit up seventeen vessels, but I hope it will fit up as many as twenty. This is entirely apart from the cold storage vote.

With what particular steamship lines will this arrangement be made ? We were told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that certain steamships, which came within the mail contract, were not to have any cold storage facilities.

I think the hon. gentleman slightly misunderstood my colleague. The supplying of cold storage accommodation is not a portion of the mail contract given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but in many cases we make a contract with the same ships that carry the mail. I have the assurance from the following lines of their willingness to enter into these contracts on the terms we stipulate : The Beaver, the Manchester liners, the Elder-Dempster, the Thomson people, and others. The Furness Withy steamers, which go to Halifax and St. John, have not been satisfactory to us. I say this with regret, but am constrained to say it, because we made the same kind of contract with them as with the other companies, and they did not carry it out. We may be able to make better arrangements with them in the future, and hope to do so. I should be glad if we can make arrangements with the other lines. There is a line subsidized by the Minister of Trade and Commerce which is to run, I think, from Kingsport and Annapolis. If that line is running, as I trust it will be, as I understand it is specially intended to

carry fruit, we will be ready to give them the same encouragement as the other lines. The question of a French line arose this afternoon. Our fruits at the Paris exhibition astonished the people there, and I believe there is a great opening for us in that line. In some fruits, such as pears, the French are themselves our keenest competitors in the English market, but in other lines they make a demand for our fruit.
How many steamers are there on each line, and between what ports do they run ?
The Donaldson line runs to Glasgow, the Allan line to Glasgow, Liverpool and London.
Do they make their trip every two weeks ?

The arrangements differ with the different ports. The Allans run every week to Liverpool and every week or fortnight to London. I think they send a boat every fortnight to Glasgow. We hope to have a weekly service to Liverpool and London and fortnightly to Glasgow, weekly to Bristol and fortnightly to Manchester. Then, if we have a service from the maritime ports, Halifax and St. John, our facilities would be sufficient.
What freight rates do you charge ?
The ordinary rates.
I understood that the rates last year were raised one-half. Has the minister been able to make better arrangements this year ?
That was for freight in cold storage chamber. This is for freight in the ordinary hold of the vessel, and one of the conditions is that the rates shall be the ordinary freight rates.
Has the hon. gentleman made up his mind with regard to the line to France ?

I was saying that I hope to make such arrangements. But we cannot say to-day what the trade would justify. If they begin this season, as I trust they will, we can see how the trade develops. We will try and keep a little in advance of the development. But I cannot say as to the number of steamers.
Do you put in the same construction as for the ventilation of the chambers ?

I do not think my hon. friend has appre-Mr. FISHER.
bended the idea. We have steamers with insulated chambers in which goods are placed that need a low temperature. But the arrangement that we are talking about is to force cold air into the hold of the vessel, the 'tween decks, as it is called. We are proposing, as in the other case, to pay within the course of three years half of the first cost of this apparatus, that is, to pay one-sixth of the total each year for three years.
How does it compare in cost with the Mackenzie cold storage ?
The cost on a steamer of the ordinary carrying size would be about $8,000. We would pay $1,333 each year for three years. This is for the ventilation of the hold of the vessel.
Is that without the mechanical cold storage ?

We must cool the air by mechanical apparatus, the cost of which, with ventilating shafts, is about $8,000. The other arrangement was a mechanical apparatus to cool the air in a closed chamber into which articles like butter and poultry, which require low temperature, were placed. But vessels carry in their holds in the ordinary way thousands of barrels of apples or thousands of boxes of cheese. When the hatches are closed tight, the cheese or the apples develop a heat of their own, the effect of which is to reduce their value. We propose to arrange the hold so that there will be ventilating shafts through it and out of it, and an intake of air from the outside. This air would *be cooled by mechanical apparatus and forced through the hold, cooling the air about the barrels or boxes. This system has been adopted in the new line of steamers running from England to the West Indies, put on practically by the Imperial authorities, to aid the West Indian fruit trade. The same system is used in the fruit-carrying steamers from St. Michaels, the Azores and the Canary Islands, to England.
I understand we have cold storage for one class of produce and the ordinary ventilated chambers for another, both in the same steamer.

In some cases. In the cold storage chamber we permit certain extra charges to be made. The last contract was at the rate of 16 shillings per ton. In this arrangement, goods will be put in the ordinary hold, and they will not be charged any extra, but just the ordinary freight rates on the same kind of goods.

The minister says that this $48,000 would equip sixteen steamers, or perhaps twenty. Now, there must be some

minimum amount required to equip a steamer for tlie purpose of carrying fruit properly. It would be, I think, bad policy to equip a steamer unless you made it thoroughly efficient. It would be much better to spend all this money on ten steamers, if it requires that amount to make them efficient, than to spend it on twenty steamers none of which will be thoroughly equipped. I understood the minister to say that they would equip sixteen steamers, and he hoped twenty. But if it is going to take all that money properly to equip sixteen or seventeen steamers, it would be a great mistake to spread it over twenty. I am in accord with this vote, I am willing that the amount should be amply sufficient for all the purposes ; but from what the minister says I fear he is trying to produce quantity rather than quality.

I quite agree with my hon. friend, but I think he misunderstood me, because the apparatus would depend upon the size of the steamer. If we were to take seventeen average steamers such as are now engaged in the trade, it would take the whole of this. But we may undertake to equip some smaller steamers, in which case it will cost a little less. For instance, we have one steamer we propose to equip that is undertaking to trade between Prince Edward Island and England, devoting itself to that tra'de exclusively. That trade only requires a comparatively small steamer, and the equipment will not cost much more than half what it would for one of the larger Elder-Dempster boats sailing from Montreal to Liverpool. The reason I left a margin as to the number of steamers, was that I do not know yet which steamers we are going to equip, and we cannot say how much it will take. But we propose to use the whole of this money if we can make a contract with steamship owners, and we propose in any steamer we do equip to give the full capacity of cooling power.

I desire to ask the minister what will be the capacity of the steamer for Prince Edward Island, what date the first steamer is expected to call there, and the extent of the cold storage appliances he is to put into that steamer ?

I am not very familiar with shipping questions, and would not like to state the number of tons of the vessel. Perhaps the hon. gentleman may know the vessel, it is a vessel called the Micmac. She has been twice to South Africa with hay for us, and we are expecting soon to close an arrangement with the owners of that vessel. The vessel was chartered to go to South Africa again, and they have asked us to release them from that charter that they may take up this other trade. She will be equipped with a
cold storage chamber for carrying butter, poultry and such things as require extreme cold in the insulated chamber, also with a cooling apparatus and a fan to force cold air through the hold where apples and cheese may be stored.
About what date do you expect that steamer to sail from Prince Edward Island, and how many trips will she make ?

It is not yet settled when she will commence. When she does commence she will make as many trips as possible. I understand that it will take a little over a month to make the round trip, and it is expected that she will start on her first trip in the month of June.
Does she sail direct from Prince Edward Island, or does she go first to Montreal ?
Her duty will be to ply from Prince Edward Island to England and back.
And she will make possibly five trips during the season ?
It is expected she will make five trips this season, and six trips afterwards.
I would ask the hon. gentleman if a careful investigation has been made into this system of driving cool air through the holds. It seems the operation must necessarily be slow ?

We have been examining the reports of these other vessels which have been equipped with this mechanism, and it seems to work well. We have also had the advice of the Cold Storage Equipment Company who have equipped ships similar to these, and who are now prepared to equip these ships on our Canadian trade. I may say that a number of leading cheese buyers and exporters of the city of Montreal who have been in England quite recently, have strongly recommended this system, and have been in consultation with Prof. Robertson and myself in reference to the matter. The best example that I know of is the line from Jamaica and the West Indies to England, which has recently been established.

Has the hon. gentleman made any arrangement in England by which, on the landing of goods in cold storage, the temperature may be gradually lessened ? I believe that a large part of the loss that occurs almost every year in some of our cold storage shipments arises from the fact that the goods are taken out of cold storage at once and placed in warmer air, moisture condenses on the surface, and gives the fruit a mussy appearance, detracts from its value. Al-

though it does not rot it, it makes it look bad. I think that could be obviated by gradually warming the cold storage chambers.
We were rather expecting that these ventilated holds would cease to operate a few days before the vessels got to England and allow the temperature to rise.
I am referring to the old cold storage.

We have not ourselves undertaken to deal with the situation in the old country. As a matter of fact the goods which are now being sent forward in these cold storage chambers are not goods that are handled in the way that was mentioned. At one time they tried to send eggs in these cold storage chambers and also fruit. But they have practically given up the eggs altogether. Cheese also has been given up in so far as sending it in the old cold storage chambers is concerned, which are now used almost entirely for butter, for iruits, poultry, beef, and other meats. As far as fruits are concerned it is a very difficult problem unless we provide something of the nature of a chamber in England for the purpose. I do not know how the difficulty can be avoided, but the trade object to that because they say that when the fruit gets to England they want to put it on the market as rapidly as possible without any detention.

I should think that a short delay of twenty-four hours to bring the temperature back gradually to its normal condition would be time well spent. Of course, we must send pears to England in cold storage chambers. The complaint which has been made most frequently is that they present a mussy appearance.*
Our agents in England are watching the trade and keeping in view its special requirements.

I hope the hon. minister will see his way clear to sending a fruit-grower or an expert over in charge of these shipments next year. I think that the men looking after the fruit department, while perhaps perfectly efficient in other departments, are not experts on fruit. I believe four men went over last year.

We have two fruit men there now, a well-known fruit man from Peterborough, in Ontario, was over there and a well-known fruit-grower from the Cornwallis valley in Nova Scotia who was in London all last fall.
I understood the hon. minister to say that they have given up sending cheese over in cold storage.
Yes.
In regard to butter, meat and fruit, what was the experience last year, because most of these were trial shipments, I understand, with this new system.

There was no new system last year particularly. Butter has always been sent over and occupied the greater part of the cold storage. There was a good deal of fruit sent over last year. Speaking from memory, I would say that the pears went over most successfully. There were comparatively few peaches sent over last year, and I could not speak with positive assurance as to the success. I dare say that the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith) knows better than I do the details of these shipments. Although I have had them before me, I would not like to make a statement from memory in regard to them. Grapes were also sent over, and I think more successfully than heretofore, but in regard to that I am also speaking from memory. I can say positively that pears were sent over most successfully with profit to the growers.
How about butter and meat ?

There was hardly any other meat than poultry meat sent over last year. We are now sending over other meat. The poultry meat went over most successfully. There was one single instance where it did not go over successfully, and that was because some butter was put into the cold storage chamber with it.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if he has made any arrangement for shipping fresh meat. I am interested in that trade.

There is now every week going over fresh meat in cold storage. There is a firm in Ontario that has made arrangements by which they send over fresh meat regularly. I do not think I need mention the name.
Is that Mr. Harris ?
I know them as the William Davies Company. I think Mr. Harris is in with them. They have made arrangements by which they get cold storage accommodation for fresh meat.
Will that be continued all summer ?

What arrangements are made in regard to cargoes for these various steamers ? You had a special arrangement last year that after a certain time they might load with anything they could get, provided they did not get a full supply of

Canadian produce. What arrangements have you made this year ?	*
They will take Canadian produce and if there is any space not filled they can take other produce.
What arrangement have you made in regard to filling the space if there is not sufficient Canadian produce offered ?
We take no responsibility.
Then, I understand the hon. gentleman to say that they charge 15s. a ton more than the ordinary freight rates ?
My hon. friend is speaking of thef cold storage chambers, not the ventilated holds.
No.
We have no new contracts with them. The contracts are the same as last year.
What were they last year ?
They called for the payment of 15 shillings extra for cold storage accommodation.
Suppose all the space is not taken ?
Nobody is responsible for it in any way.
Are the same contracts continued ?

Some expired last year, and some are continuing still. I think there are about twenty still in force. I want to explain to the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) that we have no responsibility in connection with any space in the cold storage chambers that is not occupied.

I understood from shippers last year that owing to the scarcity of steamers on account of the South African trade the rates were very much higher, and I understood the hon. minister to say that several of these contracts were made for a longer time than one year and are therefore in existence at the present time. If that is the case the rates will be very high. Could the hon. minister not make better rates this year ?
The contract is for two years. It was made a year ago this spring for two years and I cannot break the contract.

The result will be that the shippers, if they can get cheaper rates from other sources, may not avail themselves of this cold storage, because I understand that last year there was a serious objection on the part of a number of shippers to the freight rates and that they could not afford to send their produce in cold storage.
They would get as cheap cold storage on these steamers as anywhere else.
Many of them decided to run the risk of sending their produce in ordinary storage rather than in cold storage, because they thought the rates were too high.
They have given that up.
How many new contracts have been made this year ?

We have not made any new contracts for the ordinary cold storage. The steamers on which the contracts have run out are still running on the Canadian route and are retained in the service for the Canadian trade as we anticipated they would be. Last year some of these steamers were taken off for the South African trade, but they have come back now and are running with cold storage without any contract, just as we anticipated they would.
At the same rate ?
Yes, I believe so. Of course, we have no control of that, they not being under contract.
What arrangements have been mad^ to see that the steamship people will really keep the machinery in operation ?
Last season we put self-registering thermometers in all the cold storage chambers, so that we have a check upon them.
Does the minister know whether, he will be able to make arrangements for cold storage on the steamers plying to France ?
I have not discussed it with them yet.
As there may be considerable possibilities for us in this trade, I trust the minister will exert himself in that direction.
Have any arrangements been made with the steamers running to Hamburg ?
No.
I believe that a very large trade in apples could be carried on with Hamburg.

I understand that in Alberta the government is carrying on a certain number of creameries and disposing of their produce for the benefit of the farmers. I shall read an article from the Nelson Tribune, of April 10th last, which will explain the grievance to which I wish to call the attention of the minister. It is as follows :
Official Circumlocution.
And the Government Creameries.
A local wholesale firm wrote to the Minister of Agriculture at Ottawa, in December last, asking if they could not have an opportunity of handling a share of the product of the government creameries of the North-west Territories. Several weeks having elapsed without any acknowledgment of the communication, the firm again wrote the department, and received the somewhat unsatisfactory reply that their first letter had not reached its destination. Another copy of the original document was then forwarded, and only yesterday was this acknowledged, through the Commissioner of Agriculture and Dairying. This official conveyed the intelligence that there was no butter available in September last, according to the superintendent of the dairy at Calgary, and that * when we have butter to offer, we are glad to sell it to whatever firm will give the best price.' The firm in question are anxious to make a bid on the product of the creameries, but have not been afforded an opportunity of so doing. They contend that at the time they were apprised that there was no butter available, the article was being supplied freely by another firm, and they reasonably think that they should be in a position to get the butter, provided their price is as good or better than that paid by their rival in business.
It appears that all the butter manufactured in these creameries is disposed of to the firm of J. Y. Griffith & Co., who advertise themselves as the sole agents, and are thus enabled to conduct a very profitable trade, to the injury of others who are engaged in similar business, and who think that as this enterprise is supported by the public funds, they ought reasonably have a share in the trade, and that there should be no monopoly. They think that the butter should be sold to the highest bidder, and that they should not be compelled to go to J. Y. Griffith & Co., and pay an advanced price for this butter. These gentlemen contend that they should be allowed to purchase on the same terms as Griffith & Co., or else that they should have an opportunity of purchasing in the open market. If the butter belonged to a private firm, there could be no reasonable complaint, because that private firm would have the right to dispose of its butter as it thought fit. But, these creameries being carried on by the government, each firm thinks that it should have a fair opportunity of purchasing the butter, and that Griffith & Co. should not have a monopoly on the sale of this superior article.
I ask the minister, if it is the decided policy of the department to give this one firm the sole control of this butter, to the detriment
of other dealers, who have an equally strong claim to a share in the trade?

I am glad that my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) has brought this matter up. My attention has been called to it, and I went fully into the matter with Prof. Robertson. As a matter of fact, Stewart & Co., of Vancouver, get this butter exactly on the same terms a!s J. Y. Griffith & Co. We are responsible to the patrons of these creameries for marketing their product as well as we can, because the profit which they get depends on the price of the butter. The department simply acts as their agents, charging a certain price for manufacture, and whether the butter be sold at 20 cents or 25 cents, the profit goes to the patrons, and we make nothing out of it. It is our duty to sell this butter as well as we can, in the first place because we are acting as agents, and in the second place because, if we make a success of the experiment, it enhances the reputation of the country for dairying purposes. When we inaugurated this business, we sold the butter to any one who would take small lots. The result was that a great many persons purchased this butter who had no proper facilities for its storage, and it was constantly found that butter with the government stamp upon it was being sold all over British Columbia in a deteriorated condition, thus hurting the reputation of the butter. That tended to lower the price, and we decided that only those who had proper warehouse facilities, and who were really in the distributing trade, and not jobbers or agents who would buy and sell anything that they could make a profit upon, would be entrusted with the sale of this butter. We found that there were several houses in British Columbia so situated that they could do that, and we have always given these people every facility for buying all the butter they could handle. But, we came to the conclusion that it was not in the interest of our patrons or of the government creameries, to allow jobbers to buy this butter, and sell it in any way they could to the retail trade. That is the reason why only certain firms have had this butter for sale. I may say that last fall the only firms that would take our butter in quantities were the two I have mentioned- J. Y. Griffith & Co., and Stewart & Co. ; and Prof. Robertson, in the exercise of his business discretion, made a contract with them to give them all the creamery or brick butter, as it is called there. They offered to take all the butter that was made. We could not get any others to bind themselves to take a definite quantity, and Prof. Robertson believed that he was making the best possible bargain in the interest of the government creameries. I may say that at this very moment we are asking for offers from any firms in British Columbia who will be able to handle the butter in the way I have

indicated. I do not care who does so. There are other firms.
Starkey & Co.

They are a jobbing firm only, and it was because they were damaging the reputation of our butter in the way they handled it that we declined to give them the contract. They bought our butter in job lots and sold it in job lots without seeing it at all.

There may be something perhaps in what the minister says ; but there seems to be an impression that these people have been unfairly dealt with, simply because the manager of the firm of Griffith & Co. is very closely related to Prof. Robertson.
Yes, Prof. Robertson's brother.

And for that reason the impression is that he, having the government behind him, is giving the firm of J. Y. Griffith & Co. a monopoly of this business through the Kootenay district. The other firm of Stewart & Co., I understand, sell it in Vancouver.
They also sell it up the country.

That seems to be the impression with regard to J. Y. Griffith & Co., and it is not fair to Prof. Robertson that that impression should prevail if it is not true. Is it possible that they sell to consumers all the butter they handle ?
Oh, no; they are wholesale as well as retail merchants.
Then they are jobbers too ?

No. The other men never see the butter. They simply contract to deliver so much, and then they- buy it from us, and it is delivered to the parties to whom they sell it. They have no warehouses or places to store the butter, and my information is that the butter handled by them has been frequently injured. I may be incorrectly informed, but I have been investigating the matter. Prof. Robertson has shown me correspondence to show that his brother has had no privileges which the other firms in British Columbia have not had, and that J. Y. Griffith & Co. have not been treated differently to several other firms in the same line of business.

The minister says that the firm of Starkey & Co. have no warehouses, and not the same facilities for handling the butter that the others have. I think that is the very reason why the butter would be delivered to their patrons
in better condition than butter delivered by J. Y. Griffith & Co.; because they give the order, say at Calgary, and the butter is shipped directly to the purchaser instead of passing through a warehouse. I fear that the minister has been loaded up by somebody in the wrong way. I hope he will investigate the matter, and not allow one firm to have a monopoly of this business.

I am well acquainted with J. Y. Griffith & Co. I was in their warehouse in Winnipeg last summer, and I may say they have an excellent establishment there, and I have no doubt they have others in other parts of the North-west. I know they were good Conservatives when they went out there, and I believe they are good Conservatives yet; so that I do not think there is any jobbery in the matter.

I did not say anything about their politics, or that there was any politics in the matter. It may be that they have a good warehouse in Winnipeg ; but that does not prove that there are not other firms in British Columbia capable of handling this butter.

I understand that there are three kinds of cold storage : first, on steamships: second, on railways ; and third, in creameries. Will the hon. minister tell us what arrangements he has made for cold storage on railways, mentioning the different lines, and the supply of cars per week or month ?

I am afraid I have, not got with me the details of all the lines. I may say in general terms, however, that all the lines served last year will be served again this year, and that we are adding considerably to the number-that, as a matter of fact, we add to the number wherever there is any demand.
Is it a weekly supply ?

Where there is a large supply going forward, it is weekly, and sometimes two or three times a week. At other places where there is not so much going forward, the supply is fortnightly. Of the forty-two or forty-three lines which had cold storage last year, thirty have a weekly service, and seven or eight fortnightly. To-day there is a net work of the railway system of the country by which the refrigerator cars converge on the shipping ports during the summer time.
What rates are charged on these lines over and above the ordinary class rate ?

The rate is the ordinary less-than-carload rate. There is no extra charge. We guarantee to the railway company that the cars

shall be two-thirds paid for whether they are used or not, and If at any time less than two-thirds of the accommodation is utilized, we pay the difference ; but when more than two-thirds are utilized, the railway companies are obliged to credit us with the extra, and we make up the account at the end of the season. The result is that on most of the old lines there is nothing to pay. On the new lines, in the beginning we pay ; but, as the work goes on, and there is more freight for them, they come to the paying point. That is the system we have pursued all along.
Will the minister tell us what arrangement he has made for cold storage for creameries ?
The same as last year.
That is, you give a subsidy to each creamery that builds a cold storage warehouse of a certain capacity, and the subsidy is in proportion to the capacity ?
Yes.

Perhaps the hon. minister is prepared to give some information with regard to an item to which I called his attention some time ago, the item of Quebec Cold Storage Company, and the cold storage at Charlotte. He promised to lay the contract on the Table.
I think I did.
Perhaps he will be able to tell us how it comes that so large a sum was paid in excess of the contract.

The contract will furnish a good deal of the information which the hon. gentleman requires. When we came to settle, we said the contract bore one interpretation, and the Quebec Cold Storage Company claimed it bore another, and the Justice Department upheld the interpretation of the company. We consequently had to pay.
Is the hon. gentleman continuing that contract ?
No.
Does the hon. gentleman intend to continue the experiments with grapes in the old country ?

Yes.
For the purpose of renewing and improving Canadian exhibit at Imperial Institute, London, $3,000.

Those who are familiar with the Imperial Institute, know that for a long time com-Mr. FISHER.
plaints have been made about the representation of Canada at that institute. The matter was brought up several times in the House, and I replied that it was entirely in the management of the provincial governments. When the institute was first established a special request was made by His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, that the colonies all over the world should provide adequate representation of their products in the institute. Considerable exhibits were sent by the provinces, but the province did not keep them up, and the result has not been creditable to us. Over and over again the Dominion government have been asked by the provincial governments to relieve them of this work, as they could not afford to do it ; and after discussing the matter with Lord Strathcona, when he was here last, and also with my colleagues, I concluded that it was in the interests of Canada that the Dominion government should take hold of this exhibit and see that it was put into proper shape. I hope when over in England to visit the institute and see what is necessary to be done, and I have no doubt that by taking advantage of the exhibition at Glasgow, we will be able to make a proper representation of Canada at this institute. Three thousand dollars will be sufficient to completely renovate the exhibit, and a small amount will toe required from year to year to keep it up.

I agree that this is a wise expenditure, but I have been told several times that our exhibit at the Imperial Institute is not at all creditable to us, and it would no doubt prove of considerable advantage if kept up properly, and a greater variety of exhibits shown.

I am afraid that the sum which the hon. minister is asking will not be found sufficient to put life into the exhibit. Every one who has visited London is greatly disappointed with it. A friend of mine, who visited London during the last three months, told me that it was completely worthless, and it would be better to have none at all. I would sugest that the hon. gentleman should urge on the different provincial governments to contribute towards the expense of making this exhibit creditable to this country. Otherwise it would be better to do away with it altogether. I am afraid that the amounts asked is not sufficient, but do not think that the Federal government should have to bear the whole expense ; and if the provinces will not contribute, better to do away with the thing altogether than keep it up in a half-hearted, [DOT]manner.

It would be a mistake to rely on the province doing any considerable part of the work, not because they have any lack of interest in the matter, but because their financial affairs

are not in such a condition that they feel warranted in engaging in what seems to them ornamental work. I know that when I was in the government of one of the provinces, while we had every desire to aid this exhibition, we found great difficulty in obtaining an adequate grant for the purpose. My hon. friend is right in saying that it is better that we should not have any exhibit than have the one that has been in the Imperial Institute for several years past. Some of the provinces have not prepared an exhibit at all. You will find vacant Avail space which, on inquiry, you are told belongs to a certain province. And even the provinces that have made some attempt at exhibiting have not succeeded very well. The Dominion government contributed to the building, if my memory is correct, $100,000, but left to the provinces the management of the several exhibits. Unfortunately, the provinces were not consulted, and did not feel auy great obligation to exhibit. It is not too much to say that hardly one of the provinces has made a good exhibit. The Imperial Institute is not in the part of London best calculated for a popular exhibition. It is in the south-west of London, and if we were selecting a place for a London exhibit, very few of us would select that locality. Still, this is a great Imperial movement, and other colonies have participated, and my hon. friend will agree that it is hardly creditable to Canada to be poorly represented. speechtext: There is: a subject, having some bearing on this, about which I wish to say a word and to ask the minister to give it a little consideration. It'is well known to all persons who have had anything to do with marine matters that there is a very substantial difference between the pilot rules of the United States and our navigation rules as embodied in our statutes. I have considered the matter and it seems to me most desirable that there should be uniformity in these rules. In many respects the rules are the same, but in very many respects they are entirely different. That desirable uniformity can only be secured by correspondence with the United States authorities, or by commission to consider the matter, or by some action taken by one or other of the two countries. Without going into the details to-night, I would ask the minister if the matter has ever been brought under his consideration, and if anything is likely to be done in the direction I have indicated ?

This is a very important question, and it has had a great deal of consideration from the department. It is not so simple to bring about uniformity as my hon. friend (Mr. Britton) may at first sight think. The British Marine law provides that the Admiralty shall make these regulations as to the number of blasts a steamer must blow in a fog, and so on, and these British regulations are adopted by us. Our rules are uniform with the British rules, so that a certified British captain or a certified Canadian captain understands exactly what the regulations are. If a vessel leaves Great Britain and comes up the Gulf of St. Lawrence to Montreal, and beyond Montreal to the great lakes, the Brit-163*
ish regulations govern her. Unfortunately the American regulations are different. I see the very great advantage that would be derived from uniformity, but if we make our regulations conform to the American regulations we are all at sea with regard to the British regulations. I have never yet been able to find a solution of the difficulty. I have talked it over with my officers and with the captains on the lakes, most of whom desired to have the American regulations, but I have never seen my way clear to make our regulations conform to the American regulations and to differentiate them from the British. So far as sea-going ships are concerned, our rules must be the British rules up to Montreal, and to make a different set of rules above Montreal seems to present difficulties which at present I am not able to overcome.

speechtext: Since my bon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) has brought this matter up, I think it is a very opportune time to discuss it, because the session is coming to a close. I think it is very desirable that we should do something in the direction of satisfying the aspirations of Captain Bernier. What Captain Bernier asks from the government-he is very highly recommended in that-is, I believe, the cost of the vessel. He is pretty nearly certain of getting, in the shape of contributions from the citizens of Canada and from scientific societies, sufficient, or very nearly sufficient money, to equip the vessel. The cost of the vessel would be $60,000, if it were built at Montreal, at Quebec, or in the maritime provinces. If built in British Columbia, it would cost some $80,000, although it would be nearer the point to .which he intends to sail in the first instance, that is to say, Behring Straits. I suppose the hon. minister is aware that Captain Bernier has received very great encouragement from Europe ?
Sympathetic encouragement.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: No, he has received more than that. He has received, I think, subscriptions, and in Canada he has received a great many subscriptions. Captain Bernier

asks nothing whatever for himself. He does not ask the ship for himself ; it will belong to the government. He is ready to give two or three or more years of his time, provided he gets the ship, and provided the citizens of Canada and the subscribers generally furnish him with sufficient to equip it. He is ready to go and devote all that time to his country for nothing. Under these circumstances, and as we have perfect proof that he is not an enthusiast, but a navigator of very great experience, and with a most commendable record, I think it is fair to consider whether we should not give him that much encouragement. We may say that it will not cost us so much, because, unless the vessel is wrecked, it will belong to Canada after his return. I wanted to mention the matter, but I had hoped to do so after giving notice to the hon. minister. I see that the hon. Minister of Public Works has come in. I think he will appreciate the appeal I am making. Captain Bernier is, I think, preeminently qualified to go in search of the North Pole; and if he does not get the necessary encouragement from us, I believe he will get it from the American people. I believe he has already been approached by enterprising American newspapers, with the object of securing his services for that purpose. Under these circumstances, I think this country is interested more than any other country at the present moment in advancing the project which Captain Bernier undertakes. I think we can gain a great deal by discovering the North Pole, if it is to be discovered ; and such an expedition, at a cost of some $80,000, would, I think, be very beneficial indeed. As hon. members are aware, Nansen got within about 300 miles of the pole, and the Italian duke who went afterwards got 60 or 70 or 100 miles nearer. Captain Bernier has the benefit of their experience ; he has given the subject a great deal of study ; and any one who has heard his demonstrations must believe that he will get nearer still-that he will probably reach the pole.
He will get there.
Under these circumstances, I think we should do all we can to encourage him. I am glad the hon. member for West Toronto has brought the matter up.

I do not know any man who is better fitted than Captain Bernier for that expedition. He has a long experience. He was born in a cold country, and he has been a navigator all his life. He is one of the best built men I ever met. I happen to know a good deal about him. He was one of my employees for some time. He is a man who, I think, can live fifteen days without sleeping, and yet remain as fresh as we are here to-night. He is well educated, and he has travelled all over the world. He is a

strong man, physically an>d mentally. I think his plans are good. I happened once to have him on hoard one of the government boats with a couple of my colleagues, one of whom was the Minister of Finance ; and he gave us a private conference on his X>roposed North Pole expedition, which was so interesting that I shall remember it all my life. He is not a public speaker ; he does not appear to advantage before a large public audience ; but, in a room with half a dozen men, let him explain his venture, and he will convince any half dozen capable men that if there is any man living who can discover the pole, he is that man. Well, what is going to be gained financially by that discovery ? I am not quite prepared to say. But, it will be a great advertisement. Highly civilized countries encourage men who are prepared to go on such ventures. Speaking not as a minister, but as a member of parliament, I would be very glad indeed if the government could see their way to help him. Parliament seems to be well disposed, and the nation seems to be well disposed, towards his enterprise. Nansen is an able man, but I do not think he is as well qualified as Captain Bernier for such an expedition. He had not the same experience nor the same physical strength. Moreover, Captain Bernier has the benefit of the experience of those who have attempted to reach the pole.	I am
very glad indeed that both sides of the House seem to agree that Captain Bernier should be encouraged. I think it would be an easy thing to get private subscriptions to a very large amount. I think $50,000 will be raised in a short time in Montreal.
It should be a national undertaking. The government of the country should undertake it.

Of course, I am not prepared to speak as to that. The right hon. gentleman who leads the government and the House is here. It is for the House to express its views, and if there is a strong opinion on both sides, no doubt the government would be largely influenced by it. I may state, from all the conversation I have had with hon. members on both sides, that the opinion is practically unanimous that if the government should see its way clear to make a grant towards this expedition, it would reflect the public opinion of the country.

I have had many conversations with Captain Bernier, and have learned from them that he is a man of very considerable experience, that he comes* from a seafaring stock, that he has been a seafaring man all his life, and that he has thoroughly studied the experiences of Nansen and others who have engaged in arctic explorations ; and every Canadian would be proud if, under the auspices of this government, a Canadian could do what no one
has yet been able to accomplish, namely, fix the location of the north pole. I have no doubt that physically and in every other way Captain Bernier is eminently well qualified to take command of such an expedition, and would do as much as any man ever did to accomplish the result aimed at. Speaking for myself and many other members on this side, we would have much pleasure in supporting a vote to fit out a vessel to enable Captain Bernier to enter on that perilous undertaking.

The accomplishment of the object of this proposed expedition would have a very important bearing on our interests. In the impression of many, the discovery of the north pole would enable us much more easily to determine what is our own in making a dividing line between our territory and that of Russia and the United States, leaving aside altogether the great advertisement which it would give this country. I do not think that the government should give a very large grant; but according to the newspapers, jtiaptain Bernier has. been very successful up to the present in getting private subscriptions, and the hope is entertained that he will succeed in getting all that is needed, through these subscriptions, except the supply of a vessel. If a vessel could be supplied for $00,000, that does not appear a very large sum, and I think we might go that far, if he were able to secure all the additional support he requires.

I think the suggestion a
